This is an initial public offering of shares of Class A common stock of Anthropic, PBC. We are selling
shares of Class A common stock and
the selling stockholders identified in this prospectus are selling an additional

per share will be between

.
We have applied to list our Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the
symbol “ANT.”
We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure. We are incorporated as a public benefit corporation under Delaware law, a structure
consistent with our commitment to artificial intelligence (“AI”) safety and responsibility. As a public benefit corporation, we are required to
balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit
purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation: the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for
the long-term benefit of humanity. We created our Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) to help ensure that
Anthropic, PBC
is managed in a
manner that responsibly balances its goals as a public benefit corporation. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of financially
disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock,
Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of
the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters
submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will also issue a single
share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to a limited liability company organized by our co-founders (the “Founder
LLC”).
Dario Amodei, our Chief Executive Officer and a member of our board of directors, and Daniela Amodei, our President and Chairperson of
our board of directors, together with our five other co-founders, will initially be the sole members of the Founder LLC. Our
Class F common
stock, which will be held by the Founder LLC, will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting power of our
outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than
the Class T directors. Our Class F common stock will not have any economic rights. Upon the completion of this offering, we will also authorize a
special class of our common stock, Class E common stock, which will be issued to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E
common stock will be entitled to vote only on certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. In addition, we have authorized
Class A common stock and Class N common stock. The rights of the holders of Class A common stock and Class N common stock are identical,
except with respect to voting and conversion. Each share of Class A common stock is entitled to one vote per share and shares of Class N common
stock have no voting rights, except as otherwise required by law. The holders of our Class N common stock are primarily strategic business
partners, and shares of Class N common stock will generally convert to Class A common stock upon a sale or transfer to an unaffiliated third
party. Our Class A common stock is not convertible. See the sections titled “Risk Factors—Risks Related to our Governance Structure,” “Our
Governance Structure and Its Goals,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for more information.
We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. See the
sections titled “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals,” “Management,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for additional information.

Select Defined Terms
The following are abbreviations, acronyms, and definitions of certain terms used in this prospectus:
“
agent loop
”
refers to the iterative cycle in which an AI agent receives a task, takes an action, such as planning
a project, running code, or calling a tool, observes the result, and decides its next step, with this cycle repeating
until the task is complete. The agent loop is the core execution pattern underlying agentic AI behavior.
“
agentic AI
” refers to AI systems that, with varying degrees of autonomy, can plan, determine, and sequence
actions and execute them to accomplish defined objectives, including through interaction with external tools,
services, datasets, and environments on behalf of a user.
“
AI
” refers to artificial intelligence, a machine-based system that learns or is trained from data and, for explicit
or implicit objectives and with varying levels of autonomy, processes that data to infer patterns, generate
outputs—such as predictions, content, recommendations, and decisions—and act upon physical or virtual
environments.
“
AI accelerators
” refer to processors purpose-built or adapted for the large-scale computations required to
pre-train, post-train, refine, and run AI models. These processors are significantly more efficient and faster
than general-purpose processors for AI workloads.
“
API
” refers to application programming interface, a standardized interface that allows external software to
access a system’s capabilities programmatically. AI model providers may offer APIs that allow software
developers to send inputs to an AI model and receive outputs, enabling integration into the software developers’
products and workflows.
“
Applied AI
” refers to a discipline and organizational function focused on embedding AI capabilities directly
into production business environments to address specific customer requirements. Applied AI teams, which
include forward-deployed engineers, work with enterprises to design and deploy custom solutions, specialized
workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to a customer’s own systems and processes.
“
closing the loop
” refers to a development cycle in which successive versions of an AI model assist in building
the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time.
“
compute
” refers to the computational processing resources used to train and run AI models, including,
without limitation, specialized AI accelerators, memory, networking, storage, and power systems that are
deployed in data centers or other physical computing environments.
“
compute multipliers
” refer to algorithmic and methodological improvements in training and inference that
increase the effective output of a given amount of compute.
“
computer use
” refers to an AI capability that allows a model to observe and interact with a graphical user
interface, such as clicking, typing, and navigating applications, similar to how a human operator would.
“
Constitutional AI
” refers to an approach to training AI models using a set of written principles, which we
refer to as Claude’s constitution, currently organized around four priorities: being broadly safe, broadly ethical,
compliant with our guidelines, and genuinely helpful. Under Constitutional AI, our models evaluate, critique,
and revise their own responses against these principles, enabling us to define and control model behavior
through auditable principles, rather than relying solely on fixed rule-based instructions or human reviewers.
“
context window
” refers to the maximum amount of text, code, or other content, measured in tokens, that an
AI model can process in a given request, encompassing instructions, prior conversation history, user input, and
the model’s output.
“
CSP
” refers to a cloud services provider, a technology company that owns and operates large-scale cloud
computing infrastructure and provides on-demand compute, storage, and networking. CSPs may also serve as
distribution channels through which AI products and services are made available to customers. The largest
2
Table of
Contents
CSPs, sometimes referred to as hyperscalers, operate at global scale with significant infrastructure and market
concentration.
“
customer
” refers to a prosumer or an organization that uses our models, platform, or applications.
“
customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis
,” “
customers with $1 million or
more of revenue on a TTM basis
,” and “
customers with $10 million or more of revenue on a TTM
basis
” each refer to customers contributing revenue equal to or greater than the applicable dollar amount
during the trailing twelve-month (“TTM”) period ending on the measurement date.
For purposes of this metric,
we define a customer as a distinct organization, identified by aggregating the accounts that we determine
belong to the same organization based on internal records and available data.
We do not separately define or
internally track a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured
internally by reference to whether a given customer is an “enterprise.” Because spending $100,000 or more on
our products is generally characteristic of organizational rather than individual usage, we use the number of
and revenue from customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis as our measure of enterprise
adoption and engagement with Claude throughout this prospectus, including in references to “enterprise
customers” and “enterprise adoption.”
“
frontier AI
” refers to AI systems at the current leading edge of capability and safety, performing at or near
the highest levels of any existing system across a broad range of tasks.
“
hallucinations
” refer to outputs in which an AI model generates factually incorrect or fabricated information
with apparent confidence.
“
inference
” refers to the process by which a trained AI model processes an input and generates an output.
Inference occurs each time a
user or agent interacts
with an AI system.
“
interleaved thinking
” refers to a capability whereby an AI model interposes discrete reasoning steps
between successive tool calls within a single response, rather than confining its reasoning to a single planning
phase at the outset.
“
interpretability
” refers to research into how and why AI models produce specific outputs, with the goal of
making model behavior more transparent and verifiable, especially in high-stakes applications.
“
knowledge work
” refers to complex cognitive work and related professional activities, including obtaining,
producing, analyzing, and communicating information through tasks such as coding, drafting analyses,
synthesizing research, building financial models, and managing and automating documents and workflows.
“
LLMs
” refer to large language models, or AI models trained primarily on large datasets to understand and
generate natural language and computer code.
“
mechanistic interpretability
” refers to a subfield of interpretability research focused on reverse-
engineering the internal computations of neural networks. Rather than inferring model behavior from inputs
and outputs alone, mechanistic interpretability seeks to identify the specific features and circuits within a model
that give rise to its behavior with the goal of making model reasoning auditable at the mechanism level and
detecting failure modes, including deceptive or unsafe behavior, that may not surface in standard testing.
“
model weights
” refer to the numerical parameters encoding a trained AI model’s behavior, which are the
primary intellectual asset of a frontier AI developer, representing the accumulated investment in compute, data,
and research.
“
multi-agent orchestration
” refers to an architecture in which multiple AI agents collaborate on a shared
task, with one coordinating while others execute subtasks in parallel, enabling more complex, long-horizon
work than a single agent can complete alone.
“
Net Revenue Retention
” reflects customer expansion, contraction, and churn as of a measurement date.
We calculate Net Revenue Retention by dividing the Qualified Customers’ Current Period revenue by their Base
Period revenue. A Qualified Customer is a customer with at least $1 of revenue during the Base Period,
excluding subscribers to our Claude Pro and Max plans, whose fixed-price subscriptions do not reflect the
3
Table of
Contents
expansion and contraction behavior this metric is intended to capture. The Base Period is the three months
ending a year prior to the measurement date. The Current Period is the three months ending as of the
measurement date.
“
open-weight
” refers to an AI model whose trained model weights, or the numerical parameters encoding the
model’s learned behavior, are publicly released, allowing third parties to download, run, and modify the model,
subject to the terms of the model’s license, without necessarily providing access to the underlying training data
or code.
“
pay-for-intelligence
” or “
consumption
” refers to our revenue model under which customers pay for their
usage of our intelligence service, which is metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected.
“
persistent
,” in the context of AI applications, refers to denoting data, state, or context that is continuously
retained beyond the boundary of a single operation, session, or interaction, remaining accessible for reuse
across subsequent steps, sessions, or workflows without requiring reinitialization.
“
post-training
” refers to the collection of techniques applied to a pre-trained model to refine its behavior,
including reinforcement learning, supervised refinement methods, and other alignment methods. Post-training
is the stage in which much of the work to make a frontier model helpful, accurate, and safe is performed,
including the application of safety and alignment techniques.
“
pre-training
” refers to the initial stage of training an AI model, in which the model learns general patterns
and representations from large-scale datasets of text, code, and other data, typically by predicting the next
token in a sequence. The output of pre-training is a base model with broad capabilities that has not yet been
adapted for any specific deployment context.
“
primitives
” refer to the foundational, modular building blocks of a software system from which more
complex applications and workflows are constructed.
“
prompt
injection
” refers to an adversarial technique in which malicious instructions are embedded in
content an AI model is asked to process, such as websites, documents, or tool outputs, with the aim of
overriding or manipulating the model’s intended behavior, typically without the user’s knowledge.
“
prosumers
” refer to individual users who subscribe to AI tools to perform knowledge work.
“
reinforcement learning
” refers to a machine learning approach in which a model learns to perform a task
by taking actions, receiving feedback signals called rewards, and adjusting its behavior to maximize the rewards
it accrues over time. In contemporary AI development, reinforcement learning is widely used to refine model
behavior after pre-training, including to improve helpfulness, accuracy, and adherence to safety guidelines.
“
RLHF
” refers to reinforcement learning from human feedback, a specific form of reinforcement learning in
which human evaluators rate the model’s responses, and those ratings are used as the reward signal to guide
training.
“
Run-Rate Revenue
” is an operating metric that refers to the estimated annualized value of our revenue-
generating activity as of a measurement date, calculated as the sum of (i) our consumption-based fees during
the trailing 28-day period ended on the measurement date, multiplied by 13, and (ii) our aggregate monthly
subscription fees as of the measurement date, multiplied by 12. For purposes of calculating Run-Rate Revenue,
consumption-based fees and subscription-based fees are derived from customer usage and active subscriptions.
“
SIs
” refer to systems integrators, or third-party technology and professional services firms that design, build,
and deploy integrated solutions for customers by combining products and services from multiple technology
vendors into unified systems tailored to customer needs.
“
tokens
” refer to numeric units into which an AI model converts the data it processes, including text, images,
audio, and video, the number of which varies by the model and tokenizer applied. Tokens are the smallest
individual units of a language model and can correspond to words, subwords, characters, or bytes. A tokenizer
is the component of a model that converts customer inputs into the sequence of tokens the model processes and
then converts the processed tokens into the outputs provided to customers.

Overview
For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason,
analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this
abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of
industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. AI that truly delivers on its potential—with the
risks well managed—could significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for
people around the world.
Anthropic
was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for man
y of the breakthroughs that define
AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is the responsible development and maintenance of
advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and
culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the
core
advantages
that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier AI and shape
the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier AI, Claude, is delivered to customers
through our models, platform, and applications.
Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any
technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of
2023 to $
for the three months ended September 30, 2026.
This rapid and growing adoption generates
two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps
fund our continued research in frontier AI.
Our Core Advantages
Mission & Focus
. All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to
concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid
conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while
mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together.
Talent & Culture.
Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including
researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a
low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier AI capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. We
believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
Frontier & Safety Research.
We believe that sustained, focused research at the frontier of intelligence is
required to build the most capable and safest AI systems. Our frontier capabilities and safety research are
deeply integrated and directly shape model design, training, and deployment, helping us produce systems that
are more reliable, steerable, and well-suited for real-world deployment, particularly in demanding enterprise
environments. We translate our research leadership into innovation velocity, and have consistently released
better models, platform capabilities, and applications. Each version of a Claude model assists in building the
next, helping to compress development timelines and produce compounding improvements in the speed at
which we innovate. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop,” and we believe it is one of the most
significant structural advantages in frontier AI.

Our Approach to Compute
. We manage compute as a single, fungible pool from multiple strategic partners, and
we dynamically direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be
most productive at any given time. We believe that this approach to compute enables us to deliver superior
models, serve more customers, and achieve greater productivity from our compute investment. This compute
efficiency creates the foundation for us to advance the frontier of AI capabilities through research and model
development, meet growing demand from customers, and provide for internal usage of Claude.
We have
achieved this through our research breakthroughs and our
multi-chip compute architecture
across AWS
Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs, enabling us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for
price and performance
. To support our research, model development, customer demand, and internal usage of
Claude, we continue to invest at scale. As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into
purchase commitments and lease agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet
commenced, with an aggregate committed spend of more than $
, substantially all of which is related to
compute and infrastructure. These commitments include approximately $
expected to be incurred before
December 31, 2030, and substantially all of the remainder is expected to be incurred between 2031 and 2045.
Approximately $
of these commitments are due in the next 12 months. See the section titled
“Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and
Capital Resources—Contractual Obligations” for more information.
Enterprise Strategy.
Our enterprise strategy is built on the belief that frontier AI is most valuable in real-world
settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest and where the improvement
loops from customer feedback are richest. Accordingly, we have organized our research priorities, our product
roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, which range from routine
knowledge work to the most complex problems. The customer feedback we gather directs our research focus
and makes Claude more
capable
over time. This broadens where Claude can be deployed and further expands
enterprise adoption, which helps ensure that the benefits of our AI reach people and organizations at scale.
AI is Transforming Intelligence
We believe that Powerful AI, a highly capable and impactful form of frontier AI characterized by the following
key attributes,
will
become widely available within a few years:
•
cognitive capabilities matching or exceeding those of top human experts across most professional and
scientific disciplines;
•
the ability to navigate all interfaces available to a human working virtually, including text, audio, video,
and direct computer control;
•
the ability to reason through complex tasks autonomously over extended periods—lasting hours, days,
or weeks—and seek clarification and feedback when needed;
•
the ability to coordinate across multiple instances and collaborate with both humans and other AI
systems; and
•
the ability to interface with the physical world by digitally controlling laboratory equipment, robotic
systems, and other machines through digital connections.
If Powerful AI is directed at solving humanity’s hardest problems and the risks are managed responsibly, the
potential is
extraordinary. The
possibilities include compressing decades of scientific progress into years;
accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy; providing individually
tailored education and expert financial and legal advice; advancing power grids and battery design for greater
efficiency and reliability; and extending to the developing world capabilities that took wealthy nations
generations to build.
A Near-Term Opportunity to Transform Cognitive Work
Frontier AI is transforming cognitive work—the application of knowledge, reasoning, and judgment to produce
economic value. We believe it will make humans far more capable and expand the world’s overall capacity for
that work, including accelerating scientific discovery and helping businesses grow. Knowledge workers are the
leading edge of this opportunity. As frontier AI advances, more capable models can unlock entirely new use

Frontier AI May Reshape Entire Sectors and Accelerate Novel Discoveries
We believe frontier AI represents a larger opportunity than any prior technology cycle, and Claude is already
demonstrating this potential. Claude can now execute complex projects autonomously and turn open-ended
tasks into finished, high-quality deliverables. These capabilities enable it to transform the largest sectors of the
economy, driving meaningful gains in productivity and output. Frontier AI’s capabilities may extend beyond
current markets to open entirely new ones, reaching domains such as robotics, advanced manufacturing, and
logistics, and accelerating progress in scientific research, including drug discovery and materials science. For
example, in the life sciences sector, where annual global pharmaceutical spend is expected to exceed $2 trillion
in 2026,
3
Claude is used in drug discovery and development by our customers, our biotechnology partners, and
our own researchers. We are also extending Claude into robotics, where our Model Hardware Standard enables
AI agents to operate lab and manufacturing equipment such as microscopes, liquid handlers, and off-the-shelf
robotic arms. Ultimately, we believe frontier AI will help drive global economic growth. As frontier AI makes
workers and organizations more productive, becomes embedded in the products and services they deliver, and
unlocks new business models, it creates economic output that did not previously exist. We believe our
opportunity is to capture a share not only of today’s economic activity but also of that newly created output as
the global economy expands.
The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
While the potential benefits of AI are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society
in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if the technology is not developed and deployed
responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using AI’s capabilities to
discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse,
including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. AI deployed at scale also has the potential
to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm
society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned AI systems could corrupt institutional decision-
making or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their
users and operators. We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure
the responsible diffusion of this technology. We also believe that safety, alignment, and ethical behavior
resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and
demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting an AI partner for mission-critical
workloads.
Claude as a Virtual Collaborator
We believe we have reached an inflection point where AI systems can function as genuine collaborators in
professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional
for several hours, a full day, or longer. AI systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks
that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses. We refer to
these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional levels as
Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights, system connections, and context that their
organizations grant them, which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can navigate and
use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained reasoning. Virtual
4
IDC, Worldwide Developer Population Growth Forecast, 2025–2029, doc # US53789825, September 2025.
8
Table of Contents
Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to continue extending
them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in 2028.
4
Claude Code.
The clearest manifestation of Virtual Collaborators today is Claude Code, our coding agent and
the product we believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like. Claude Code shifted
the market’s understanding of what an AI system could do in collaboration with software developers: the model
suggests the next line of code and goes further by planning, writing, testing, and debugging—a process that
results in production-grade code. Within months of its release, autonomous coding became the reference point
for measuring the progress of frontier AI. For enterprise AI use cases, we believe the launch of Claude Code was
comparable in its impact to the introduction of the first widely adopted conversational AI assistants. What
makes Claude Code a Virtual Collaborator is its sustained reasoning, a harness that translates intent into
actions, an execution environment that maintains a persistent state whether on a developer’s machine or in a
sandboxed cloud environment, integration with existing tools and systems, and a user-friendly interface. Its
uses are highly varied and often surprising: for example, NASA engineers used Claude Code to plan and write
navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover, resulting in the first AI-planned drive on Mars.
Software developers are powerful advocates for Claude—they understand how systems work, have credibility
evaluating technical tools, and often serve as internal champions for adopting new technologies. Winning their
trust creates a foundation for broader diffusion of Virtual Collaborators across enterprise workforces. We are
already seeing this pattern play out with non-technical teams increasingly adopting Claude Code and Claude
Cowork to manage their own workflows.
Claude Cowork.
All digital work is ultimately an expression of code, and Claude’s mastery of it powers Virtual
Collaborators capable of handling complex work far beyond software development. Claude Cowork extends the
same agentic architecture of Claude Code to knowledge workers broadly by translating a user’s intent into
completed work, autonomously reading files, navigating applications, and executing multi-step workflows on a
user’s desktop while the underlying code is abstracted away. By extending beyond Claude Code with
applications purpose-built for specific professions and industry verticals, we accelerate Claude’s diffusion into
new categories of knowledge work and deepen our presence across the enterprise.
As of September 30, 2026,
adoption of Claude Cowork, which we made available as a research preview in January 2026, outpaced the
adoption Claude Code achieved at the equivalent point following its research preview release in February 2025.
In September 2026, we began merging Claude Cowork and Claude.ai, bringing agentic and conversational work
into a unified application. Users can now move from a simple question to complex, multi-step tasks in the same
conversation.
Extending Virtual Collaborators.
We believe the trajectory for Virtual Collaborators is clear and accelerating.
Each
generation
of Claude models has expanded along multiple dimensions: the depth and rigor of their
reasoning, the duration and autonomy of the work they can sustain, the complexity of tasks they can complete,
and the volume of useful output they can produce.
Capability evaluations and benchmarking have shown
substantial improvements across Claude model versions in the duration and complexity of tasks that can be
completed reliably, with more recent model versions demonstrating particularly significant advances.
We are building towards a world where Claude can be given open-ended tasks lasting hours, days, or weeks,
and then execute them autonomously with the judgment and initiative of a brilliant colleague. Ultimately,
millions of Virtual Collaborators can run in parallel, each working independently on unrelated problems or
collaborating seamlessly to achieve a shared objective. The result is something without historical precedent:
what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a data center, available to every organization and sector of the
economy.

trustworthiness and judgment that we believe was not previously available from earlier generations of AI.

embedded intelligence in their products. As Claude’s capabilities grow, our customers benefit and often
broaden their adoption of Claude in new workflows. This expanding role reflects a broader shift in how Claude
is used inside the enterprise, from a tool that responds to discrete prompts to a Virtual Collaborator.
We drive the diffusion of Claude primarily by making it accessible across multiple product surfaces. For

•

scale codebases.
•
Claude Cowork, our knowledge work agent, has computer use capability that enables it to work with
professionals on end-to-end business tasks: autonomously researching, drafting, analyzing,
synthesizing, and executing other knowledge work.
Much of the diffusion of Claude has been organic. We amplify this with our go-to-market and Applied AI teams,
which extend our reach by meeting customers where they are through distribution partnerships that place
Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks. For example, Claude is accessible on all three major cloud
platforms—Amazon Web Services (“AWS”), Google Cloud Platform (“GCP”), and Microsoft Azure (“Azure”). We

with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure allows us to foster stronger commercial

compute efficiency improvements.

Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop
Claude itself has become one of the most powerful drivers of our progress—each new version of a Claude model
directly accelerates development of the next. Many aspects of the research, training, and testing of subsequent
model generations now involve Claude, including running experiments, generating and processing training
data, automating evaluations and safety audits, and writing and reviewing code. We refer to this recursive
dynamic as “closing the loop.” A direct expression of this dynamic is our accelerating pace of producing
compute multipliers. More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn,
more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more
efficiently.

Our Governance Structure and Its Goals
Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from
that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI
exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings.
Operating as a
public benefit corporation (“PBC”) gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary
interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific
public benefit purpose that we promote. Our specific public benefit purpose is the responsible development and
maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity (the “Company Purpose”). In addition, a
financially disinterested trust, which we refer to as the Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) and which
generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, is
designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this balance appropriately. We also believe that
our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.
13
Table of Contents
Public Benefit Corporation Status
Consistent with our long-term commitment to AI safety and responsibility, we are incorporated as a PBC under
Delaware law. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and operate in a
responsible and sustainable manner. Under Delaware law, a PBC is required to identify in its certificate of
incorporation the public benefit or benefits it will promote, and its directors have a duty to manage the affairs of
the corporation in a manner that balances the pecuniary interests of the corporation’s stockholders, the best
interests of those materially affected by the corporation’s conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose
identified in the corporation’s certificate of incorporation. As provided in our amended and restated certificate
of incorporation, the public benefit that we promote, which we must always consider in the management of our
company, is the Company Purpose.
Long-Term Benefit Trust
In 2023, we implemented an innovative governance structure featuring the LTBT, which is designed to ensure
that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: the pecuniary
interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company
Purpose. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of five financially disinterested voting
trustees (“Trustees”) with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through
a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and
remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of
directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights on matters submitted to
stockholders generally.
Founder Voting Structure
We believe that our seven co-founders, Dario Amodei, Daniela Amodei, Tom Brown, Jack Clark, Jared Kaplan,
Sam McCandlish, and Christopher Olah, as a group, are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our mission.
Immediately prior to the completion of this offering, we will issue a single share of Class F common stock, a
special class of our common stock, to a limited liability company of which our seven co-founders will initially be
the sole members (the “Founder LLC”).
Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting
power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally,
including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors.
Board Governance
Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors.
Immediately prior to the
completion of this offering, we will enter into a stockholders’ agreement (the “Stockholders’ Agreement”) with
the LTBT and the Founder LLC, under which they will agree to vote their shares and take other actions to give
effect to the board composition, director nomination, and director removal provisions described in our
governing documents.
Collectively, the LTBT and the Founder LLC will have the ability to elect all members of
our board of directors. Regardless of the class or classes of stock by which a director is elected, there is no limit
to the number of terms a director may serve.
While the LTBT has significant influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and
remove a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors, neither the LTBT nor the Trustees have
decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of the company. The LTBT’s role is
to select directors who are well-equipped to make decisions in furtherance of the responsible balancing of the
pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the
Company Purpose, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance.
The Founder LLC will also have significant influence over our business and affairs through its ability to vote our
Class F common stock, which is entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of the total voting
power of our outstanding shares of capital stock with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally,
including the election of our directors other than the Class T directors.

Controlled Company Status
We are considered a “controlled company” within the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate
governance requirements because the LTBT, as the sole holder of our Class T common stock, generally has the
power to elect a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. As such, we are permitted to opt
out of compliance with certain Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements. Accordingly, if
we elect not to comply with certain requirements, you will not have the same protections afforded to
stockholders of companies that are subject to all of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance
requirements. Although we qualify as a “controlled company,” we do not expect to rely on this exemption except
with respect to our nominating and corporate governance committee (“NGC”), which will not consist entirely of
independent directors. Our board of directors currently consists of a majority of independent directors and our
audit and compensation committees currently consist entirely of independent directors. See the sections titled
“Risk Factors—Risks Related to our Governance Structure—We are considered a “controlled company” within
the meaning of the Nasdaq Global Select Market corporate governance requirements, and, as a result, we
qualify for, and currently rely on, exemptions from certain corporate governance requirements,” “Our
Governance Structure and Its Goals,” “Management,” and “Description of Capital Stock” for additional
information.

workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those of our competitors or
adequately serve our customers.
•
Constraints on the critical inputs supporting compute could limit our ability to secure adequate
compute.
•
We are highly dependent on the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and
key technical employees, and the loss of any of these individuals may adversely affect our business,
financial condition, and results of operations.
•
Our company culture has contributed to our success and, if we cannot maintain this culture as we
grow, our business could be adversely affected.
•
We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial
condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
•
If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect or
declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and results of operations
could be adversely affected.
•
If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse by other
third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and
brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
•
Our A
I models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking
harmful actions that no user or third party directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and
brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations.
•
We may be exposed to liability, litigation, and regulatory action arising from harms associated with our
AI models, and our contractual protections and insurance may be insufficient, any of which could
adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
•
A substantial portion of our revenue and accounts receivable is driven by a limited number of
customers and distribution channels, and the loss of, or a significant reduction in, spend from one or
more of our top customers or disruption through those channels could adversely affect our prospects,
business, and financial condition.
•
We have a limited operating history in an evolving and nascent industry, which makes it difficult to
evaluate our future prospects and may increase the risk that we will not be successful.
•
We are at an early stage of our revenue growth, we have experienced rapid growth in recent periods,
and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future performance or our ability to sustain or
forecast future revenue growth.
•
Our business is subject to an evolving and uncertain regulatory and political environment, which could
increase our costs, restrict our operations, or adversely affect demand for our models, platform, and
applications.
•
Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and investment
relationships with us and are our customers, creates complex dynamics that could give rise to conflicts
of interest and adversely affect our access to compute.

Voting rights
Shares of our Class A common stock are entitled to one vote
per share. Shares of our Class N common stock have no
voting rights, except as otherwise required by law. The
share of our Class T common stock has no voting rights
with respect to matters submitted to stockholders
generally, except as set forth within our amended and
restated certificate of incorporation, including with respect
to the election of a majority of our board of directors or as
required by law. The share of our Class F common stock
will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that
represents 50.1% of the total voting power of our
outstanding shares as of the applicable record date on all
matters submitted to a vote of stockholders generally,
including the election of the directors other than the Class T
directors. Shares of our Class E common stock will be
entitled to one vote per share with respect to certain limited
matters.

Risk Factors
Investing in our Class A common stock involves a high degree of risk. You should carefully consider the risks
and uncertainties described below, together with all of the other information in this prospectus, including the
section titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations” and
our consolidated financial statements and related notes, before making a decision to invest in our Class A
common stock. The disclosures in this section reflect our beliefs and opinions as to matters that could
materially and adversely affect us in the future, and are not representations as to whether such matters have
or have not occurred previously, except as otherwise disclosed. References to past events are provided by way
of example only and are not intended to be a complete listing or a representation as to their likelihood of
occurring in the future. Our business, financial condition, results of operations, or prospects could also be
adversely affected by risks and uncertainties not currently known to us or that we currently do not believe
are material. If any of the risks actually occur, our business, financial condition, results of operations, and
prospects could be adversely affected. In that event, the market price of our Class A common stock could
decline, and you could lose part or all of your investment.
Risks Related to our Business and Industry
Our
success depends in large part on our ability to continue to develop the most advanced and
capable AI models, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our business.
Our success depends in large part on our ability to continuously develop, improve, and deploy the most
advanced, capable, and useful AI models.
Achieving and maintaining this position depends on our ability to:
•
advance the frontier of AI capabilities through breakthrough research, innovative architectures, and
efficient training methodologies;
•
ensure our models are safe, reliable, and trustworthy while maintaining competitive performance;
•
secure the compute and infrastructure necessary to power and support our increasing needs;
•
advance compute efficiency through algorithmic and architectural innovations, including compute
multiplier advancements;
•
retain the continued service of our co-founders, senior management team, and key technical
employees, and attract, retain, and motivate leading researchers, engineers, and technical talent in an
intensely competitive and evolving market;
•
continue revenue growth and maintain access to sufficient capital, including through potential equity

Our failure to achieve any of the foregoing could prevent us from maintaining our competitive position, cause
us to fall behind competitors, reduce customer adoption of, or demand for, our models, platform, and
applications, and impair our revenue growth. Limitations to our revenue growth could, in turn, constrain our
ability to fund the substantial and increasing expenditures required for frontier AI development, including
investments in compute, model training, data acquisition, and safety and security systems, as well as our ability
to attract, retain, and appropriately compensate highly skilled technical and operational personnel in a highly
competitive market. Any such constraints could slow our rate of development and innovation, degrade model
performance or reliability relative to competitors, limit our participation in industry standards-setting and
regulatory processes, and reduce our attractiveness to enterprises and prosumers. These effects could create a
self-reinforcing or compounding cycle in which diminished growth limits our capacity to invest in the resources
necessary to remain competitive, which in turn could further weaken our ability to sustain or increase our
revenue growth, making it increasingly difficult and costly to regain technological leadership and operate at the
frontier of AI. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of
operations.
Our ability to maintain our position at the frontier of AI depends in part on our use of AI systems to accelerate
our research
processes, a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” in which successive versions of our
models assist in building the next, with the goal of compounding capability gains over time. Our models have
been and are increasingly becoming critical tools in designing, training, testing, and optimizing next-generation
AI systems. If we fail to direct sufficient compute and research efforts to AI-assisted development, or if our
competitors more effectively leverage AI to enhance their own innovation cycles, we risk falling progressively
further behind as competitors continuously use AI to further enhance their own development capabilities,
enabling the creation of increasingly advanced systems at an accelerating pace. As our reliance on our own AI
systems to write production code, conduct research, and build subsequent model versions deepens, any
systemic flaw, bias, or error in our current models could propagate into the next versions of models and
products built using those systems, compounding across successive versions of Claude models in ways that may
be difficult to detect or remediate. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our ability to deploy the most
advanced, capable, and useful AI models could be adversely affected.
In addition, our increasing use of AI systems to accelerate our own research and development may cause the
capabilities of our models to advance more rapidly than our ability to develop, validate, and implement
corresponding safety, alignment, and security measures. Much of our evidence regarding the pace of such AI-
driven acceleration is derived from lagging indicators, and our ability to forecast or measure the rate at which
our capabilities are advancing, including any acceleration attributable to our most recent or unreleased models,
is limited. As a result, we may not identify a significant acceleration in our rate of development until after it has
occurred. If our capabilities were to outpace our safety, alignment, and security measures, or if we were unable
to anticipate the pace of such advancement, we may be unable to adequately assess or mitigate the resulting
risks, which could increase the likelihood of safety incidents, regulatory intervention, or reputational harm, and
could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. In light of these uncertainties,
including limits on our ability to observe the pace at which our capabilities are advancing, we have adopted, and
may continue to adopt, precautionary safety, alignment, and security measures to allow our safety efforts to
advance together with model capabilities. In the past these measures have included delaying the release of
models and limiting their initial availability, such as with Mythos through Project Glasswing, and in the future,
as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, they could include additional measures that
affect
whether
, how, and when we develop or deploy new models or capabilities.
We cannot predict with precision
when we will determine that such measures are necessary, what measures will be required, or how long they
will remain in place, and as the capabilities of our models advance, such measures may become more frequent
and more costly. These measures could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt
similar constraints, and could adversely affect our competitive position, revenue growth, and results of
operations.

such as failing to achieve the targeted capability or safety thresholds, producing unexpected or undesirable
behaviors that cannot be adequately remediated, or yielding a model that is ultimately not competitive with
alternatives available in the market. We would also face the additional cost and delay of initiating a new training

In addition, innovation in AI involves addressing complex and evolving challenges related to data quality, data
integrity, training methodologies, bias, safety, accuracy, and the behavior of model outputs. AI algorithms may
be flawed, and AI systems may contain bugs, errors, or defects or fail to follow instructions or produce
inaccurate, misleading, offensive, inappropriate, or otherwise harmful outputs; reflect or amplify unwanted or
unknown biases present in training data; or raise concerns relating to intellectual property, privacy, or other
legal and ethical considerations. We must continually invest resources to identify, mitigate, remediate, and
reduce the occurrence of such issues, including through managing and improving datasets, training techniques,
evaluation methods, safeguards, and human oversight. However, we may not be able to obtain the datasets that
we need, including through licenses or strategic data partnerships. In addition, we or our data providers may
use synthetic or AI-generated data in the training process, which could introduce quality issues, amplify biases
or errors, contribute to model degradation, or raise novel legal questions regarding ownership, licensing, or
intellectual property rights that may not be timely or clearly resolved by courts or regulators. Such unintended
consequences, failures, or misuse of our models could impair customer trust, slow adoption, expose us to legal
or regulatory scrutiny, or adversely affect our brand and reputation.
If we are unable to secure adequate compute or if we fail to direct our compute effectively
across our workloads, we may be unable to train models that remain competitive with those
of our competitors or adequately serve our customers.
Our ability to develop, train, improve, and deploy frontier models depends on our access to enormous and
increasing quantities of specialized compute. The training of Claude models has required, and we expect will
continue to require, substantial compute. Industry participants, academic researchers, and our own experience
suggest that, in certain contexts, applying greater amounts of compute during model training has been
associated with improvements in model capabilities. These observations are consistent with aspects of broader
empirical relationships among model performance, model size, training data, and compute scale that are
commonly referred to as “Scaling Laws,” although the extent, efficiency, and durability of such improvements
are uncertain, and these relationships may plateau, diminish, or fail to materialize at larger scales or under
different conditions. Accordingly, our ability to remain at the frontier of AI capabilities is substantially
dependent on our ability to secure compute at the scale required to sustain all our workloads, including to train
30
Table of Contents
next-generation models, and we cannot provide assurance that increased investment in compute will result in
commensurate improvements in model performance.
The market for compute is intensely competitive. We compete for access to compute with some of the world’s
largest and most well-capitalized technology companies, many of which develop their own competitive AI
models and have significantly greater financial resources than us. Many own and operate cloud computing data
center infrastructure, maintain captive chip manufacturing or design capabilities, have long-standing strategic
relationships with key hardware suppliers, or have significant equity investments from, or other financial
arrangements with, such suppliers. These competitors can outbid us for scarce compute, secure priority
allocations from chip manufacturers and CSPs, and make long-term capital commitments that we cannot
match. We expect demand for advanced compute to continue to grow, and the cost of compute could rise
significantly, particularly if AI-driven demand accelerates or if the ability to build highly capable models
becomes more broadly available and shifts competition toward access to advanced compute. Additionally,
numerous well-funded AI companies are pursuing large-scale AI model development, further increasing
demand for limited compute. Certain CSPs from which we obtain substantial compute also develop and offer
their own AI models and related services. As a result, our commercial relationships with these providers may
not always be fully aligned with our long-term interests, and if the compute we have access to from third parties
is curtailed, repriced, or terminated, whether for competitive reasons or otherwise, our business, financial
condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
In addition to competition from third parties, our ability to secure compute is subject to allocation decisions by
our CSPs. Although our CSPs are generally subject to contractual commitments with us regarding the provision
of compute, our ability to obtain such capacity remains dependent on those providers’ operational execution,
adherence to the terms of such contractual provisions, and broader business considerations, such as capacity
constraints, internal demand for compute to support their own AI and computing operations, relationships with
or contractual obligations to third parties (which may include other AI companies), and risk management
considerations. As a result, we may not receive the full amount of compute we seek, or such compute may not
be delivered on the timelines we require, even where contractual arrangements are in place. Additionally, we
have in the past sought quantities of compute from CSPs in excess of what those partners were willing to
provide. If our CSPs reduce, limit, or fail to increase our allocations to keep pace with our growing requirements
for any reason, we may need to seek alternative compute sources on less favorable terms or timelines, and we
may be unable to secure adequate alternative compute, or any at all. Any such shortfall could constrain our
ability to train models, serve customers, or maintain our competitive position.
Even if we are able to secure compute, we must still direct it efficiently across the full range of workloads that
are a part of our business, including research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of
Claude. While we manage our compute as a single, fungible pool and direct available compute between
workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be most productive at any given time, there can be
no assurance that this approach to compute will be the most efficient or that it will support the needs of each of
our workloads. Because demand for compute has historically exceeded available capacity, any constraint on our
ability to procure, maintain, or expand that capacity could adversely affect multiple aspects of our business
simultaneously, including our ability to serve customers at the quality and scale they expect, to train and
improve our models, and to develop new products and capabilities. While we actively manage and balance such
compute capacity across these workloads via our capacity management system, if this system fails to perform as
intended, or if our ability to dynamically rebalance capacity across workloads is disrupted, customer-facing
service quality or model and product development timelines could be adversely affected. There can be no
assurance that we will make optimal resourcing decisions, and any significant inefficiencies, including those
related to deployment and rebalancing, could adversely affect both our near-term results of operations and our
long-term strategic position. These compute resourcing challenges are heightened by the growth of our agentic
offerings, which involve multi-step reasoning chains, iterative tool invocations, extended context windows, and
sustained inference sessions that consume significantly more compute per user interaction than single-turn API
calls or chat-based interactions. As agentic workloads grow as a proportion of our total compute demand, the
aggregate compute required to serve our customers could increase disproportionately relative to the associated
revenue, placing additional strain on our compute workload management decisions.
The majority of our compute is procured under multi-year commitments that are typically entered into well in
advance of the periods in which that compute is deployed. Because different AI accelerators have varying

If we fail to secure sufficient compute, or if we fail to effectively direct the limited compute we have across our
workloads to develop and deploy models with capabilities at least comparable to those of our competitors, we
risk falling behind the technological frontier. The pace of AI development is extremely rapid, with successive
versions of models emerging in compressed timeframes, often measured in months rather than years. As a
result, even a brief period without access to sufficient compute could cause us to fall behind quickly. With AI
development, the gap between frontier models and those one or two versions behind can be significant in terms
of capability, performance, and commercial applicability. Customers, partners, and software developers may
shift to competitors whose models offer superior capabilities, and we may be unable to attract or retain the
technical talent necessary for frontier research if our researchers lack access to adequate compute or if we are
not perceived as operating at the forefront of model development. Any inability to maintain our position at the
frontier could result in loss of customers and revenue, diminished brand and reputation, and a decline in our
competitive position, each of which may be difficult to regain. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks,
our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
If our actual compute requirements differ materially from our projections, we may fail to
secure sufficient compute to meet our needs or we may be committed to excess compute that
remains underutilized.
The competitive and structural dynamics of the compute market require us to make binding financial
commitments for compute months or years in advance of our day-to-day delivery and use. Chip manufacturers,
CSPs, and data center developers require advance commitments in order to allocate production capacity, plan
infrastructure investments, and manage their own supply chains. As a result, we must forecast our compute
requirements well in advance of their deployment and commit capital accordingly, often with limited ability to
adjust commitments if our needs change.
These forecasts for future compute usage are inherently uncertain. Our actual compute requirements depend on
numerous factors that are difficult to predict, including the pace of our research progress, the compute intensity
of training techniques we develop or adopt, changes in the competitive landscape that may require us to
accelerate or modify our development plans, customer demand for inference compute, and the evolution of
hardware or other technological efficiencies and changes. If we underestimate our compute requirements, we
may be unable to secure sufficient compute to support our forecasted customer demand and model
development roadmap. In the past, we have significantly underestimated our compute requirements, which left
us capacity constrained and impacted both product development and deployment. Further, the timing of
compute coming online may not align with the timing of demand growth, which could result in periods of
excess or underutilized compute and committed cash outflows that do not produce immediate revenue.
Our ability to forecast and secure the compute we need is further challenged by our ongoing transition from a
cloud-only, fixed-time arrangement compute model to a hybrid model that includes directly leased chips that
are hosted in dedicated data center facilities leased and operated on our behalf, to our specification. This
transition introduces additional variables into our procurement planning, including the timing of facility
completion, the pace at which newly commissioned facilities achieve full operational capacity, our ability to
operate, maintain, and integrate on-premise capacity with cloud-based infrastructure, the operational
execution of our suppliers, and the performance of hardware in new facility environments. Delays in securing
energy, water, and other critical services for these facilities could further slow the pace at which newly
commissioned compute becomes available for use. Errors in forecasting any of these transition-related
variables could compound our risks related to securing sufficient compute and result in either capacity
shortfalls or underutilized capacity during the transition period.

Supply and Concentration of Chips, Memory, and Data Center Equipment
The specialized chips required for AI workloads, particularly high-performance AI accelerators and memory,
are produced by a limited number of manufacturers. The production of advanced chips is extraordinarily
complex, requiring manufacturing processes at the leading edge of technological capability.
The majority of the world’s most advanced chip manufacturing capacity is concentrated in Taiwan, primarily at
Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (“TSMC”). This geographic concentration creates significant
risks, including exposure to natural disasters such as earthquakes and typhoons, potential disruption from
geopolitical tensions between Taiwan and China, vulnerability to any interruption in Taiwan’s power grid, water
supply, or other critical infrastructure, and susceptibility to developing trade regulations and restrictions. Any
military conflict, tariffs and trade restrictions, economic coercion, blockade, natural disaster, or other incident
affecting Taiwan could severely disrupt the global supply of advanced chips, with effects that could persist for
years given the time required to construct and qualify alternative fabrication facilities. Efforts to establish
sufficient advanced chip manufacturing capacity outside of Taiwan, including in the United States, remain in
early stages and may not produce adequate compute to materially reduce these concentration risks within the
foreseeable future. In addition, due to the demand for advanced chip manufacturing, TSMC has, at times, been
unable to fully satisfy market demand for chip manufacturing capacity, and as a result, we have not always been
able to obtain sufficient quantities of chips on a timely basis. Accordingly, any restrictions or delays on the
supply of advanced chips out of Taiwan or TSMC would adversely affect our business, financial condition, and
results of operations.
In addition, both high bandwidth memory, which is a key component in high performance AI accelerators, and
other high performance memory products used in compute infrastructure, are largely manufactured by SK
hynix Inc., Samsung Electronics Co., and Micron Technology, Inc. Each of these manufacturers is working to
expand its production capacity to meet demand. However, there is no guarantee that these efforts will result in
adequate supply fast enough to meet demand, particularly if large customers or competitors secure exclusive
supply commitments or otherwise reserve substantially all of a manufacturer’s available production capacity.
The concentration and constraints in manufacturing supply expose us to the risk that manufacturers may make
allocation decisions or strategic shifts that adversely affect our access to the advanced chips needed for our
business. We also face risks that specialized chips may contain defects, or that their production or delivery may
be delayed or disrupted, which, given long replacement lead times, could constrain available compute and
adversely affect our operations and ability to
scale
. A meaningful portion of the components we and our
partners rely on is sourced from or manufactured outside of the United States
,
and new or increased tariffs,
import restrictions, or trade disputes could delay deliveries, force supply-chain changes, or raise our costs,
some of which we bear directly under pass-through arrangements. For more information, see the section titled
“—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs requirements, and
related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our ability to compete in
certain markets.”
We also depend on third-party chip design and services companies for the design, manufacture, and support of
