data centers, constrain our international expansion, or increase our costs.
Electrical Power and Fuel Constraints
The operation of data centers at the scale required for frontier AI development and deployment consumes
substantial quantities of electrical power. The availability of sufficient electrical power has emerged as a
significant constraint on data center development and expansion in many geographies, including the United
States. Electrical grid infrastructure in the United States and other countries was not designed to accommodate
the rapid increase in demand associated with AI development, and the lead times required to build new
generation capacity, transmission infrastructure, and grid interconnections can extend for years. Demand on
electric grid infrastructure is also increasing as a result of the increased electrification of homes, vehicles, and
industry, and this growing demand is occurring at a time when power generation capacity additions,
transmission expansion, and grid modernization efforts have not kept pace and certain existing generation
resources are being retired, all of which has contributed to higher electricity prices and longer interconnection
timelines in certain regions. We have publicly committed to covering the cost of electricity price increases to
consumers caused by our data centers, including both the cost of electricity itself and the infrastructure
necessary to deliver it.
Our access to electrical power also depends on our ability, and the ability of the third parties on which we rely
for the construction, management, and operation of our data center facilities, to negotiate and maintain
contracts with utility providers and grid operators and to obtain approvals from public utility commissions and
other regulators. These parties may be unable or unwilling to approve, or may condition or delay, the
connections, capacity expansions, special or negotiated rate arrangements, and infrastructure investments
necessary to support data center growth, or may grant them only at costs that limit the economic efficiency and
viability of certain facilities, such as by requiring us to bear grid upgrade or interconnection costs beyond those
attributable to serving our facilities—representing a larger share of costs than is required under existing or prior
regulatory constructs. Interconnection queues for large new electricity loads have also lengthened substantially
in many regions, which could delay or limit our access to grid power. Utility providers and regulators may also
reallocate previously committed capacity that our data center facilities may require. In many jurisdictions, a
single utility provider has substantial control over the terms, timing, and cost of the service and infrastructure
necessary to power our data center facilities. The commercial and regulatory priorities of utility providers may
differ from ours, including with respect to which infrastructure investments are made, how their costs are
allocated, and whether alternative or self-supplied generation arrangements are permitted and on what
conditions. Utility providers and other stakeholders may also seek regulatory or legislative measures affecting
large electricity loads, self-supply, or alternative power generation arrangements. The outcomes of our
negotiations and regulatory proceedings involving utilities are uncertain, and unfavorable results could increase
our costs, delay our projects, or limit the alternatives available to us. More broadly, regulatory proceedings
35
Table of Contents
relating to cost allocation, rate design, and the treatment of large electricity loads are ongoing in numerous
jurisdictions, and adverse outcomes, changes in policy, or the imposition of new tariffs, surcharges, or
curtailment obligations applicable to data centers could increase our costs or limit our access to electrical
power.
In addition, the construction of the generation and transmission infrastructure on which we depend is itself
capital-intensive and exposed to labor shortages, supply chain disruptions, permitting delays, changes in
interest rates, tariffs, other cost overruns, and financing constraints. The significant and increasing capital
required to fund these generation, transmission, and related infrastructure investments, whether incurred by
us, our utility and energy supply providers, or our data center development partners, is sensitive to prevailing
interest rates and the availability of debt or equity financing on acceptable terms. Any inability of our partners
to access capital when needed, and the limitations, cost, and competition for such capital, could increase the
cost of the power on which we depend, delay or halt projects, or render certain facilities commercially unviable,
and under certain of our arrangements, we bear these financing and capital costs directly or on a pass-through
basis. Furthermore, newer sources of generation, such as solar, wind, battery storage, nuclear, and geothermal
power, may not be available in the quantities or on the timelines we require, or may be available only at higher
cost. Our facilities separately depend on access to reliable water for cooling, which in some regions is scarce,
subject to use restrictions, or increasingly costly. Any of the foregoing could adversely affect the availability of
the power or water we require, increase our costs, or limit our ability to develop, expand, or operate our data
center facilities, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Competition for access to electrical supply and data center locations with adequate power availability is intense,
and we compete for such access with well-capitalized CSPs, some of which produce and develop competing AI
models, cryptocurrency mining operations, and other large-scale electricity consumers. In addition to, or
sometimes in lieu of, grid-based electricity, an increasing share of data centers are being developed with
dedicated on-site power generation capacity that supplies electricity directly to the facility independent of any
utility-operated electric grid. The reliability of such off-grid power generation solutions varies by the underlying
technology, the equipment used, and the operator and will reflect site-by-site operational and environmental
profiles. Development of this new capacity in turn requires power generation and electrical infrastructure that
are themselves subject to supply challenges and operational complexity. For example, certain of our planned
data center facilities rely on dedicated on-site natural gas-fired generation, which exposes us to fuel price
volatility and supply disruptions that are outside of our control and for which we bear the cost on a pass-
through basis. These facilities are also subject to constraints on pipeline capacity and firm fuel transportation
necessary to deliver natural gas. As data center operators increasingly rely on natural gas-fired generation, and
because behind-the-meter and on-site arrangements are feasible only in some jurisdictions given the applicable
regulatory frameworks, we expect increased competition among users for the same natural gas supply and
pipeline capacity in those areas. This competition could drive up the price of natural gas in such areas and may
adversely affect our ability to contract for firm fuel supply and transportation and to secure the pipeline
connections and laterals our facilities require.
These dynamics present several related risks. We may be unable to secure firm gas supply and transportation
during the development of a facility, causing a planned site to be delayed or abandoned; we may face fuel supply
or delivery disruptions once a facility is operating; and because our arrangements generally provide for fuel and
related costs to be borne by us on a pass-through basis without cost caps, we remain exposed to increases in the
cost of natural gas and its transportation. More broadly, the cost of electricity is subject to significant variability
that is largely outside of our control, as wholesale electricity prices fluctuate with changing supply and demand,
weather, fuel prices, tariffs or surcharges, and grid stress, and can rise sharply during periods of peak demand
or constrained supply, and such increases in energy costs could adversely affect our results of operations.
In some regions, including certain regions where we have contracted compute commitments, data center
development has prompted public controversy and regulatory scrutiny regarding environmental impact, land
and water use, and the allocation of limited power resources. For example, if our efforts to secure electrical
power are perceived to affect other utility customers and the broader grid, regulators may impose conditions,
standby charges, or other requirements intended to address such impacts. More broadly, our access to electrical
power is subject to an evolving regulatory framework characterized by complexity, jurisdictional overlap, and
rules that were largely designed around service by incumbent utility providers and existing generation
arrangements and that may not readily accommodate new entrants or alternative approaches, which can result
36
Table of Contents
in significant delay or prevent the development of the generation we require. Grid-tied electrical supply, for
instance, is subject to the jurisdiction of federal and state energy regulators, regional grid operators, and public
utility commissions, while behind-the-meter and on-site generation is subject to a distinct set of exclusive
service franchise protections, permitting, environmental, air quality, interconnection, and siting requirements.
In addition, environmental standards applicable to power generation continue to evolve, including as a result of
changing governmental priorities and shifting public and political views regarding climate change and the
appropriate treatment of various power generation sources. Any failure to secure access to adequate electrical
power, any legal, regulatory, or other administrative action or change limiting the availability of electricity, or
any significant increase in energy or compliance costs, could adversely affect our cost structure and limit our
ability to scale our compute infrastructure, develop and deploy our models, and service our customers. We have
also made, and may in the future make, voluntary commitments to offset the impact of our data center energy
consumption on local communities and electricity ratepayers, including commitments to cover grid
infrastructure upgrade costs, procure new power generation to match our energy needs, invest in curtailment
systems to reduce strain on the grid during peak demand periods, and address environmental impacts. These
commitments have increased, and we expect will continue to increase, our operating costs. Moreover, we
believe this is part of a broader emerging trend in the AI industry, and such commitments, or similar
obligations, may become increasingly standard or required, which could further increase our costs. In addition,
the physical effects of climate change may increase our operating costs over time, as higher average
temperatures can increase the power consumption and water usage required to cool equipment at the facilities
on which we depend.
Data Center Infrastructure
Even where chips and electrical power are available, the development of data center facilities requires
substantial time, capital, and specialized expertise. Data center construction involves lengthy permitting
processes, complex supply chains for specialized equipment, and significant lead times for the installation and
commissioning of cooling systems, electrical infrastructure, and networking equipment. Labor shortages,
including shortages of, and competition for, electricians, facility technicians, and other skilled tradespeople,
supply chain disruptions, permitting delays, and other factors can extend construction timelines and increase
costs
. Further, given data center development projects require advanced and significant capital commitments
with dedicated end users, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements for
financing or with partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center
capacity that is expected to host such partner’s chips or computing infrastructure. In addition, there are a
limited number of qualified third-party vendors with the expertise we require and that support the particular
infrastructure we wish to implement. Accordingly, we rely on this limited number of third parties for the
construction, management, and operation of certain of our data center facilities, some of which have limited
operating history or may have less experience operating data center infrastructure at the scale and complexity
our operations require. In certain cases, these third-party operators are trained or supervised by our chip
partners to manage facilities on our behalf but are not affiliates of those partners and may not have the same
depth of expertise, operational resilience, or resources. Any failure by these third-party operators to perform as
expected could disrupt our access to compute. In addition, safety or environmental incidents at facilities built or
operated for us, whatever their cause, could expose us to claims, fines, or suspensions of construction or
operations, the costs of which we may bear. We also depend on an extended network of suppliers, builders, and
facility operators. If any of them engage in practices that are unsafe, unlawful, or contrary to the labor, human
rights, environmental, or other standards we or our partners require, we could face legal liability, lose the
ability to use affected suppliers or facilities, and suffer harm to our reputation, even where we did not direct or
know of the conduct.
Our collective data center infrastructure is currently concentrated primarily in the United States, which exposes
us to risks associated with regional regulatory changes, power grid constraints or failures, disruptions to
network connectivity between facilities, natural disasters, physical attacks—including those motivated by
geopolitical events, opposition to AI, and opposition to data center development—and other disruptions that
could affect multiple facilities. Certain state, local, and municipal jurisdictions in the United States are also
considering or have approved moratoriums on new data center construction, citing public health, safety, and
environmental concerns. Such jurisdictions and other regulators, grid operators, or utilities may also adopt
other measures that subject users of large electricity loads, including data centers, to curtailment, interruptions,
forced reductions, disconnection, or other restrictions during periods of grid stress, whether through changes in
37
Table of Contents
law or policy, market or reliability constraints, limits on transmission and distribution infrastructure, or a
preference for protecting other utility customers and the broader grid. New large loads on the electrical grid
may be increasingly subject to mandatory curtailment in regions where there is insufficient grid-connected
power generation to reliably supply existing and new electricity loads. For example, states such as New York
and Texas have recently moved to regulate large-scale data centers, whether by pausing state permitting for
new large facilities, as New York has, or by subjecting large electricity loads to curtailment or disconnection
during grid emergencies, as Texas has. Such moratoriums, or similar actions, could delay or prevent the
construction or expansion of facilities on which we depend for compute. Opposition to data center development
has also become more organized and coordinated across jurisdictions and our public profile may draw
particular attention to projects associated with us. The loss of, or a significant disruption at, any major facility
may not be readily absorbed by our remaining or future infrastructure. We are expanding our data center
capacity internationally as part of our efforts to diversify our infrastructure footprint and reduce concentration
risks associated with operating a significant portion of our compute infrastructure in the United States and to
support our international growth strategy, including by entering into letters of intent and negotiating lease and
related agreements for data center facilities in multiple non-U.S. jurisdictions, which exposes us to additional
risks related to foreign regulatory requirements and approvals, data sovereignty and localization laws,
governmental access or assistance requirements, cross-border data transfer restrictions, foreign tax regimes,
and increased operational complexity. Our ability to enter into definitive agreements for data center capacity
and operations in non-U.S. jurisdictions depends on the timely formation, registration, and receipt of
governmental approval of local subsidiaries, as well as the establishment of local banking arrangements, and
any delay or failure in completing these steps could delay or prevent us from mitigating our infrastructure
concentration risks, executing our international growth strategy, securing planned compute capacity, or could
result in substantial additional taxes, penalties, or other liabilities. In addition, regulatory, legal, and other
constraints in many jurisdictions may limit the locations in which we can practically site or contract for data
center capacity, which could constrain our ability to diversify our infrastructure footprint as quickly or as
broadly as we currently intend.
We and our principal competitors rely on substantially similar inputs to develop and deploy frontier models,
including advanced chips sourced from a small number of suppliers and data center capacity and compute
obtained from CSPs and other third parties. As we and our competitors increasingly pursue vertical integration,
the basis of competition could shift over time to encompass not only which company can develop the most
capable models, but also which company can develop the best underlying components. Our future
competitiveness may depend in part on our ability to successfully develop vertically integrated compute
infrastructure on competitive terms and timelines, and there can be no assurance that we will be able to do so.
Our competitors may be better positioned, or may invest greater efforts, to vertically integrate across the
compute supply chain, including through proprietary chip design, fabrication, ownership or long-term control
of data center infrastructure, access to dedicated power generation assets, exclusive supply arrangements with
hardware manufacturers, or by securing the limited sites suitable for large-scale data center development ahead
of us. Competitors that succeed in controlling a greater share of these supply chain layers may be able to secure
compute at greater scale, lower cost, or with greater reliability than we can, particularly during periods of high
demand or supply constraint, when captive supply relationships may confer certain advantages over
participants that depend on third-party providers. Such competitors may also develop proprietary hardware-
software co-designs that optimize compute efficiency for their specific model architectures, which could
compound any capability gap across successive model versions. While we are pursuing initiatives to develop
dedicated data center infrastructure, there can be no assurance that these efforts will be completed on the
timelines or at the costs we anticipate, or that they will be sufficient to offset any structural advantages that
vertically integrated competitors may achieve. Competitors that succeed in these efforts may be better
positioned to remain at the frontier of AI regardless of broader market constraints.
Natural hazards, extreme weather, or other disruptions affecting the regions where these inputs are produced
or where our facilities are located could further constrain the availability of chips, power, water, or data center
capacity on which we depend. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our business, financial condition,
and results of operations could be adversely affected.

Our mission-driven culture is one of our core characteristics that helps us to attract and retain key personnel

We face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business,
financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
The market for AI models, platforms, and applications is rapidly evolving, intensely competitive, and subject to
frequent and significant changes in technology, evolving customer requirements and expectations, shifting
industry standards, regulatory developments, new market entrants, and new models, platforms, and
applications. We face competition from a wide range of companies across multiple categories.
We compete directly with companies developing frontier models for third-party software developers and
enterprises. Our primary competitors in this category include Alphabet Inc. (together with its affiliates,
“Google”) and OpenAI Group PBC (“OpenAI”). These competitors are developing increasingly capable AI
systems and compete with us for customers, talent, compute, and strategic partnerships. Many have
substantially greater financial, technical, and marketing resources than we do, their own or greater access to
sources of compute, longer operating histories, greater brand recognition, and established relationships with
current and potential customers and partners, which facilitates their ability to integrate their models into first-
party applications sold directly to businesses.
We also compete with a broader set of model providers operating at or below the frontier, including large
companies, specialized AI labs, and a growing range of other open-weight or open-source (shared weights,
training data, and code) models released by international and domestic organizations. Such providers compete
for a growing range of enterprise workloads that prioritize cost efficiency over intelligence. In particular, certain
large companies compete through proprietary AI models, integrated AI capabilities in existing products, and
control of cloud infrastructure and distribution channels. Some of these companies also have substantially
greater financial, technical, and marketing resources than we do, their own or greater access to sources of
compute, longer operating histories, greater brand recognition, and established relationships with current and
potential customers and partners. In addition, some have substantially broader and more diverse product and
service offerings and may be able to leverage existing relationships with distribution partners and customers to
gain business in ways that discourage customers from purchasing our models, platform, and applications. For
example, competitors may bundle AI capabilities with other products, integrate AI functionality into products
that customers already use, offer closed technology platforms that lock customers into their ecosystems, sell
products at zero or negative margins to gain market share, or use their substantial financial resources to
subsidize the cost of AI models, platforms, and applications. Customers may prefer to purchase from existing
vendors with which they have established relationships, even if our models, platform, and applications offer
superior features or performance. Further, large companies that are currently our customers may choose to
develop their own AI capabilities internally rather than purchase our models, platform, and applications.
Specialized AI labs, on the other hand, are competitive due to their ability to offer specific AI applications and
differentiated business models. These companies can move quickly, attract top talent, develop novel
approaches, platforms, or business models that disrupt existing competitive dynamics, and introduce
technologies or products with greater performance or functionality, lower cost, ease of implementation, or other
advantages.
Some competitors or customers may have access to proprietary datasets, distribution channels, or
domain-specific expertise that we do not possess, or new competitors may emerge that address particular
industries or use cases more effectively than our models, platform, and applications, which could enable them
to develop more specialized or higher-performing AI systems. In addition, competitors, customers, or other
third parties have attempted in the past and will likely continue to attempt to replicate, distill, extract, or
otherwise derive the functionality or capabilities of our models through permitted or impermissible means,
including through our research previews. These actions could reduce the technological differentiation of our
offerings; enable the development of competing products at lower cost, with reduced research and development
investment,
or that replicate our models without safety controls or safeguards that were incorporated in our
versions; implicate national security concerns or strain geopolitical tensions;
and intensify competitive
pressures. In addition, efforts to prevent or mitigate model replication, distillation, or other forms of extraction

may require us to modify our models, platform, and applications, limit features or use cases, or implement

A significant portion of our customer base consists of startups and technology-oriented enterprises that may be
more sensitive to adverse macroeconomic conditions and may reduce or delay spending during a downturn.
Because our cost structure limits our ability to rapidly adjust spending, a sustained economic downturn could
disproportionately disadvantage us relative to larger, better-capitalized competitors. Such competitors may be
better positioned to absorb or withstand adverse economic conditions or reductions in customer technology
spending due to their greater financial resources, diversified product offerings and customer bases, and more
stable revenue streams. It could also disadvantage us relative to smaller startups with leaner cost structures,
lower fixed overhead, and fewer long-term contractual commitments that could help enable them to adjust
spending more rapidly than we can. As a result, competitive pressures on our business could intensify, which
could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
If we are unable to differentiate our models, platform, and applications from competing offerings through
enhanced functionality, superior performance, better safety features and reliability, lower cost, or other factors,
demand for our models, platform, and applications may decline. The rapid pace of technological change in AI
means that models, platforms, and applications can quickly become outdated. We must continuously invest in
research and development to maintain our competitive position, but there is no guarantee that our investments
will result in models, platforms, and applications that customers prefer over competing alternatives. Moreover,
we are first and foremost a research lab, and our strategy prioritizes frontier research and model capability. We
believe the advancing intelligence and capabilities of our models are the principal drivers of their adoption, and
we have historically prioritized research and model development rather than new products and applications or
sales and marketing. This approach assumes that model capability will continue to be a meaningful source of
competitive differentiation. However, as the AI industry matures, the degree of differentiation among advanced
AI models may narrow. This convergence may result from factors such as overlapping or similarly sourced
training data, the widespread adoption of comparable model architectures, training techniques, and
optimization methods, shared access to computing infrastructure, and the rapid dissemination of research
advances across the industry. To the extent competitors are able to achieve comparable model capabilities with
lower development or deployment costs, our ability to differentiate our models, platform, and applications on
the basis of performance, functionality, or cost may be diminished. If differentiation among advanced models
narrows, or if customers increasingly select AI providers on the basis of application features, user experience,
distribution, integration into products they already use, or the strength of a sales organization rather than
model capability, competitors that have invested more heavily than we have in those areas could be better
positioned than we are. Responding to such a shift could require us to increase our investment in product
development and sales and marketing substantially beyond our current plans, which could take longer or cost
more than we anticipate and could reduce the compute and other resources available for frontier research, and
we may not be able to execute such a shift quickly or effectively. See also the section titled “—We have a limited
history under our current go-to-market strategy, and our efforts to scale and evolve our customer acquisition,
engagement, and retention model may not be successful.”

If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops more slowly than we expect

The market for AI technologies, including frontier AI and related models, platforms, and applications, has
grown rapidly in recent years, but is still relatively nascent and evolving rapidly, and it is uncertain whether the
market for such AI technologies will achieve or sustain widespread adoption at the pace or to the extent we
expect. Our ability to generate revenue and achieve sustainable growth depends in significant part on the extent
to which enterprises, software developers, and other users adopt AI technologies, integrate them into existing
workflows, expand usage over time, and are willing to pay for our models, platform, and applications at levels
that support durable economic value at scale. Market adoption may be slower than anticipated due to factors
such as uncertainty regarding the cost, performance, reliability, and perceived value of AI solutions; increased
regulation; concerns about security, privacy, legal and regulatory compliance, or ethical considerations;
technological challenges; level of effort and expense associated with integration efforts; competition from
alternative or emerging technologies; the availability or adoption of complementary infrastructure and
workflows; or reductions in corporate spending due to macroeconomic conditions. Moreover, demand for
frontier models may decline if customers determine that less advanced, lower-cost models are sufficient for
their particular use cases. As AI capabilities improve across the industry and a broader range of models
becomes available, customers may conclude that incremental performance gains at the frontier do not justify
the additional cost, and may migrate toward smaller, cheaper, or open-source alternatives that adequately
address their needs. If we are unable to demonstrate sufficient differentiated value from our frontier models
relative to less capable alternatives, our revenue and growth could be adversely affected, even in a market where
overall AI adoption continues to grow. Further, while AI adoption may continue or accelerate in certain areas,
the long-term trajectory of this technological trend is uncertain, and market understanding, acceptance, and
valuation of AI-enabled models, platforms, and applications may be inaccurate or change over time and
adoption may occur unevenly across industries, geographies, and customer types. If growth in the AI market
does not translate into sustained customer demand for our offerings, expanded usage, and increased revenue,
or if anticipated use cases fail to materialize, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of
operations could be adversely affected.

Even isolated or simulated instances of such behavior, whether occurring in testing or real-world deployments,

in actual harm. For example, state attorneys general in California and at least 15 other states have announced
investigations of another company in our industry regarding AI safety. Concerns have been raised both within
our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently

and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were

our models are contributing to the pace of our own research and these risks will increase as AI systems
substantially automate AI research and development if, for example, they accelerate AI progress beyond our
ability to evaluate and safeguard new models, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition,

Our development of highly advanced models, platforms, and applications and expansion of use cases could
further increase the risk that our models cause harm. For example, agentic AI systems are capable of
autonomously taking actions on behalf of users, interacting directly with external systems, executing code,
making API calls, sending communications, or completing transactions with limited human oversight. These
systems are designed to possess enterprise-level permissions, integrations, and contextual awareness and to
operate autonomously for extended durations, including sustained multi-step workflows lasting hours or days,
which amplifies the potential severity of any errors, misalignments, or security incidents that may occur during
such extended autonomous operation. These autonomous capabilities could increase the potential for harm, as
47

errors, misalignment, or security exploits may result in real-world consequences—including consequences that
may be difficult or impossible to reverse, such as committing code changes, deleting or modifying data, or
completing financial transactions—before effective intervention is possible.
In an agentic workflow, an error or unintended action at any individual step may propagate through subsequent
steps, compounding the severity of harm before detection or correction. The pace and volume of autonomous
execution, particularly in enterprise deployments, may also exceed the capacity of human reviewers to
meaningfully understand and evaluate whether each action is appropriate. The effectiveness of human
oversight over our agentic offerings may be limited by the speed and volume of autonomous agent actions, the
complexity of multi-agent and multi-step workflows that may make it difficult for reviewers to assess whether
an agent’s actions are appropriate, and organizational pressures within customer environments to maximize
agent autonomy in order to achieve productivity gains. Human reviewers may experience alert fatigue, may lack
sufficient context to evaluate agent decisions, or may not review agent actions in time to prevent harm,
particularly in high-volume enterprise deployments where agents operate concurrently across multiple
workflows or in manners outside of a human’s awareness. In addition, agentic systems may pursue stated
objectives in ways that are technically consistent with their instructions but contrary to the user’s actual intent.
Moreover, our ability to anticipate, detect, or test vulnerabilities or other design or implementation
shortcomings in such systems may be constrained, particularly where agents operate across complex, multi-
step workflows or interact with third-party services outside our control, and the breadth and complexity of
potential interactions across such multi-step agent behaviors cannot be exhaustively tested prior to
deployment.
Separately, models may behave in a misaligned manner and take harmful actions that are not
directed by a user or third party, pursuing objectives or acting on dispositions that diverge from those intended
by human users or developers. Misaligned behaviors of this kind, whether occurring in testing or real-world
deployments, have been observed both in our models and elsewhere in the industry, including in testing and
internal use, models circumventing network and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they
had not been given, taking unintended actions in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and
misrepresenting whether tasks had been completed or verified, and as models are granted greater autonomy,
permissions, and integration with external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior increase. For
example, during cybersecurity evaluations built by a third-party evaluation partner, a misconfiguration in the
testing environment left the model under evaluation connected to the open internet despite instructions that it
had no internet access. Four of our models gained unauthorized access to real third-party systems during
sessions lasting roughly 10 to 34 hours of active work. In one incident, after being unable to abort an impossible
task, an early version of a model used a password it found to gain administrator access to a third party’s system,
harvested additional credentials, changed system settings, and read one individual’s personal information. The
affected parties were notified. Each incident involved a single instance of a model working in isolation on its
assigned exercise, and our investigation found no evidence that any model coordinated with other agents,
pursued goals beyond its assigned task, or attempted to evade oversight.
These risks may be heightened where
multiple AI agents operate together. Agents that interact or coordinate with one another may amplify,

intended or endorsed by any user, or take coordinated actions against systems or targets unrelated to their
assigned tasks, in each case, in ways that may be difficult to anticipate, detect, or contain. Incidents of this kind
have occurred, and we expect the deployment and interaction of larger numbers of autonomous agents to
increase these risks over time.
Our ability to detect and mitigate misaligned or unintended behavior depends in part on the effectiveness of our

have become better able to circumvent such techniques, including by concealing misaligned objectives or
behaviors, and the effectiveness of our evaluation, monitoring, and control measures, and our ability to
measure the degree to which our models are aligned, may decline as a result. In addition, models, including our
own, have attempted, in incidents observed in our industry, to interfere with, manipulate, or subvert the
mechanisms used to evaluate, grade, or oversee such models, including the systems responsible for assessing
their performance or alignment. Models used, including our own, to assess the behavior of other models have,
and may in the future continue to, engage in misaligned behavior. Such conduct described above could cause
our evaluations to overstate the safety or alignment of our models and could further limit our ability to detect
misalignment. If we become less able to detect or assess misalignment as our models advance, we may deploy

We are also extending our models, platform, and applications into scientific, biomedical, and physical domains.

In addition, maintaining comprehensive records of the actions, decisions, and reasoning of our agentic systems
across complex, multi-step workflows is technically challenging, particularly when agents interact with third-

forms of such behavior.

A substantial portion of our traffic is subject to Zero Data Retention (“ZDR”) terms under which we retain only
classifier scores, not prompts or outputs. For that traffic, we cannot conduct offline analysis, cross-conversation
investigation, human review, or otherwise analyze historical data to detect, investigate, and document security
events or incidents, which thereby reduces our ability to detect misuse. ZDR may also prevent us from
producing records for subpoenas, regulatory examinations, or incident-reporting obligations, and there is no
certainty a regulator or court would excuse non-production based on a lack of available records, and such
regulators or courts may construe the lack of records against us through unfavorable inferences or other
sanctions. As our models become more capable, our safety framework has required and may continue to require
monitoring and retention incompatible with ZDR for certain model classes. Because ZDR is a competitive
expectation for enterprise customers in regulated industries and on third-party cloud platforms, these
requirements have caused and could continue to cause customers to migrate to other providers or to
deployments where our visibility is more limited.
In the European Union (“EU”), the United Kingdom (“UK”), and elsewhere, cybersecurity and AI-related

provide detailed information about incidents under several laws and regulations, which we may not be able to
provide within the prescribed time frame. Similarly, in the United States, companies are increasingly subject to
incident reporting obligations. In addition, other jurisdictions around the world have adopted, or may adopt,
similar laws and regulations with similar implications. Any of the foregoing could result in regulatory action,
litigation, customer attrition, or reputational harm that adversely affects our business. For more information

The legal frameworks governing liability for actions taken autonomously by AI systems, including our agentic
products, are unsettled and could expose us to significant and unpredictable legal claims. Existing legal
doctrines governing agency, product liability, and professional negligence were developed in the context of
50
Table of Contents
human decision-making and have not been authoritatively applied to autonomous AI systems. We believe our
provision of intelligence service is considered a “service” in the context of legal frameworks addressing product
liability, but courts and regulators may reach different conclusions across jurisdictions. In addition, it is unclear
whether, and under what circumstances, actions taken by an AI agent could be deemed to create binding legal
obligations on behalf of the user or deploying enterprise, or whether our contractual protections, including
limitation of liability and indemnification provisions, will be enforceable or adequate in the context of claims
arising from autonomous agent conduct. We may face claims from customers, their end users, or third parties
alleging that we are liable for harm caused by our agents’ autonomous actions, even where the customer
configured, deployed, or supervised the agent. The absence of settled legal standards creates significant
uncertainty regarding our potential liability exposure and the adequacy of our risk mitigation measures.
Our expansion into new geographic markets further compounds these risks, as we must navigate differing
cultural norms regarding AI use, comply with diverse and evolving regulatory regimes that may impose varying
safety, compliance, or liability requirements, address language-specific vulnerabilities and content moderation
challenges, and potentially face regulatory enforcement actions, litigation, or other liabilities in jurisdictions
where we have more limited operational experience, including heightened risks of intellectual property theft,
unauthorized model access, or misuse associated with operating data center infrastructure in certain non-U.S.
locations.
If our models are involved in causing significant harm, we could be subject to legal claims, including personal
injury or negligence claims, regulatory enforcement actions, criminal investigations, or other governmental
efforts, which could result in costly litigation, significant financial judgments or settlements, disruptive
remediation obligations, or a challenging regulatory landscape. We have taken steps to limit our liability for
such matters—for example, through warranty disclaimers and limitations of liability in our terms of service—
but those contractual protections may not be upheld, or may not apply to certain claims, or may otherwise be
insufficient to limit our liability exposure under applicable law.
Moreover, in some cases we have contractually
assumed additional
liability. For example, to facilitate independent testing and evaluation of our frontier

Although our agreements with external evaluators and testing vendors generally limit the

from such actions could result in substantial liability.

have sufficient capacity or expertise to underwrite insurance commensurate with such exposure.
Further, the insurance market for AI-specific risks is nascent and evolving, and we may be unable to obtain
coverage for certain AI-related liabilities on commercially reasonable terms, or at all, leaving us exposed to
potentially significant uninsured losses. Harmful incidents involving our models, regardless of fault, could also
severely and disproportionately damage our reputation and brand as a safety-focused AI company, leading to
loss of customer trust and customer attrition, reduced demand for our models, platform, and applications, and
difficulty attracting and retaining talent. In addition, because we primarily serve enterprise customers, which
often have heightened expectations around safety, reliability, and compliance, any harmful incident or
perceived lapse in our safety practices could have a disproportionate adverse impact on our brand, customer
relationships, and revenue. Moreover, to the extent enterprises are attracted to our models, platform, and
applications due to our safety-focused positioning, any erosion of that perception could impair our ability to
attract and retain enterprise customers.
There can be no assurances that we will be able to predict, detect, and proactively prevent every harmful use or
harmful output of our AI models, in particular as we continue to rapidly develop our models, platform, and
applications, and expand our operations geographically, and any failure to do so could adversely affect our
reputation and brand or result in costly legal liability. There may have been past instances of harmful use or
51
Table of Contents
harmful output of our models that we did not detect, and there may be future instances that we will not detect.
Any of the foregoing risks could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
If we are unable to manage the risks related to our focus on and commitment to AI safety, our
brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
Balancing Safety and Commercial Objectives
. Our commitment to AI safety requires us to make difficult
judgments that balance safety considerations against commercial objectives, competitive pressures, and
stakeholder expectations. We often make judgment calls with respect to when we determine a model is safe
enough to release and which capabilities to develop or restrict. For example, in April 2026, we initially released
our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available to select
organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to its
advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We expect that frontier models with similar or enhanced
capability profiles, whether developed by us or by other AI labs, will continue to emerge, and that future
Anthropic models exhibiting such capabilities may be subject to access constraints.
More broadly, we believe it
is important to assess the safety of our models not only at release but throughout their development. For
models we anticipate will have novel capabilities or present novel safety risks, we plan to evaluate the safety of
each stage of training, including pretraining, post-training, and internal deployment, and we may delay or
pause a stage when we are not confident in our safety measures for that stage.
For example, we recently chose to
delay pre-training a new frontier base model for more than a month to allow time to further enhance our
security measures related to preventing model weight exfiltration and protecting our intellectual property.
There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that
we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be
circumvented. These judgments are particularly consequential because, as AI systems become more capable,
the potential severity of harm from misaligned or misused models increases correspondingly, and a wide range
of stakeholders, including researchers and policymakers, have raised concerns that sufficiently advanced AI
systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly. Our
safety-focused approach is designed in part to mitigate such risks, but there can be no assurance that our efforts
will be successful or that the broader AI industry will adopt similar safeguards. In particular, as AI systems
become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight, there is a
risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective
specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human
intervention. Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any
frontier AI could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping
regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business.
For example, in September 2026, media reports
citing a senior Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) official indicated that the FTC has opened non-public
investigations into the potential risks that increasingly autonomous AI systems may pose to consumers. In
October 2026, the FTC issued a civil investigative demand to us seeking information about our consumer
protection, data protection, and privacy practices, as well as the safety and security of our products.
The scope
of any investigation of us or its outcome, and any investigation, enforcement action, or adverse finding arising
from this or similar inquiries could result in significant costs, require changes to how we design, test, or deploy
our models, platform, and applications, or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and
results of operations. We may misjudge these trade-offs, either by being overly cautious and potentially losing
market opportunities, or by being insufficiently rigorous and releasing models, platforms, or applications that
cause harm. Even where human oversight mechanisms are in place, such mechanisms may prove insufficient in
practice if the volume, speed, or complexity of autonomous agent actions exceeds the capacity of human
reviewers to meaningfully evaluate and intervene, and any perceived failure of our oversight mechanisms could
expose us to regulatory enforcement, liability claims, and reputational harm. For more information, see the
section titled “—If the use of our AI models results in harm, whether through use by malicious actors or misuse
by other third parties, or if our model guardrails or safeguards fail to prevent such misuse, our reputation and
brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.”
Moreover, governmental authorities have restricted, and may in the future further restrict, the availability of
our models, including based on their assessment of the capabilities or safeguards of our models, independent of
our own safety-based access decisions. For example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department of Commerce imposed
worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models, which we disabled for all customers until
those restrictions were lifted. For more information, see the section titled “—Governmental trade controls,

Internal Governance and Decision-Making
To institutionalize our safety commitments and ensure we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances
our tripartite goals as a PBC, we have established the LTBT, which through a special class of common stock,
Class T common stock, generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will
constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. In addition to the LTBT and our
structure as a PBC, we train our models in accordance with Claude’s constitution, which we make publicly
available, and have adopted and continue to update safety policies, such as our Responsible Scaling Policy. We
also solicit and seriously consider input from a wide range of stakeholders and constituents, including our
stockholders, employees, customers, the LTBT, industry leaders and experts, and AI safety organizations. Such
practices and processes have previously resulted in, and may in the future result in, slower decision-making and
product releases. We may also face potential conflicts when safety and business interests diverge. If we do not
successfully manage these risks related to our AI safety processes and practices, or if there is a perception that
we have not successfully managed such risks, we may face reputational harm, internal conflicts resulting in a
deterioration of our company culture, slower or inferior product releases, or litigation. For more information,
see the section titled “—Risks Related to our Governance Structure.”
We have implemented an external reviewer program and engage researchers, adversarial testers, and other
third parties to support aspects of our safety, security, and model-evaluation efforts. Certain of these
arrangements are novel and may require us to provide such parties with access to internal information,
systems, personnel, or models, which could increase the risk of disclosure of confidential, proprietary, or other
sensitive information. In addition, findings, assessments, or public statements by such third parties may differ
from our views and could adversely affect customer trust, regulatory perceptions, or our reputation.
Heightened Reputational Vulnerability
. As we have publicly positioned ourselves as a safety-focused
organization, we face heightened vulnerability to reputational harm from any perceived inconsistency between
our stated values and actual practices. We are held to higher standards than certain competitors that have not
made similar public commitments, and any incidents impacting our perception as a safety-focused organization
could result in:
•
Employee Disruption
. Employees who joined our company based on our safety commitments may
experience a decline in morale, disillusionment, a loss of trust in leadership, or reduced productivity if
they perceive we are not living up to our stated values. Public disagreements regarding our safety
approach, including criticism from current or former employees, or the departure of personnel
associated with our safety efforts, could amplify such perceptions. Such negative perceptions could also
impair our ability to recruit and hire new talent to the organization. Any erosion of our safety-focused
reputation could also make it more difficult or costly to attract and retain highly skilled employees,
including by increasing compensation or other hiring costs. These dynamics could lead to increased
turnover, loss of institutional knowledge, and reduced effectiveness of our teams, which could in turn
cause disruption to ongoing development and safety initiatives and impair our ability to remain at the
frontier of AI model development.
•
Customer Backlash
. Customers and enterprise partners who choose to deploy our models, platform,
and applications based on our safety positioning may lose trust in us, terminate or decline to renew
their contracts, demand refunds, publicly criticize our company, or switch to our competitors, which
could result in harm to our reputation, revenue loss, and reduced market share. These risks may be
heightened with respect to programs in which we make models available only to a limited group of
vetted organizations, such as Project Glasswing. Organizations not selected for, or removed from, such
programs may perceive our access decisions as arbitrary, exclusionary, or anticompetitive, which could
result in reputational harm, loss of customer or partner relationships, regulatory complaints, or
litigation, including claims under antitrust or unfair competition laws. Conversely, participants in such
programs may publicly criticize us or terminate their participation if program terms, eligibility criteria,
transition arrangements to successor models, or capability levels do not meet their expectations.

Any safety-related controversy or incident, whether actual or perceived, and regardless of fault or frequency,

and reputation, our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected.”
We voluntarily publicly disclose information regarding AI safety challenges, research findings, and limitations
of our models and systems, that exceeds standard industry practice and regulatory requirements. While our
intent with these voluntary disclosures is to advance the safe development of AI and build public trust, these
disclosures create several risks. The AI safety landscape is nascent and evolving rapidly, and our understanding
of and perspective on appropriate safety practices, risk tradeoffs, and deployment contexts may change over
time as technologies, use cases, and regulatory expectations develop. As a result, statements we make today
may later prove incomplete, require modification, or be interpreted differently in light of subsequent
developments. To the extent we adhere to prior public statements or frameworks, we may also limit our
operational flexibility, product development, or deployment decisions, even where evolving circumstances
would otherwise warrant a different approach. Our public statements about AI risks, safety challenges, areas of
uncertainty, or potential societal impacts, including statements regarding job displacement or economic
disruption, may be used against us in litigation, regulatory proceedings, or public controversies, particularly if
our future actions or statements are viewed as inconsistent with our prior statements and commitments.
Regulators have and could continue to use our disclosures as the basis for heightened scrutiny or more
stringent requirements applicable to us compared to less transparent competitors. Additionally, our disclosures
have provided, and may in the future provide, competitors with insights into our proprietary training and other
sensitive processes, research priorities, and strategic concerns, without reciprocal transparency, which may be
potentially competitively disadvantageous to us. If we are unable to effectively manage the foregoing risks, our
brand, reputation, and ability to compete could be adversely affected.
Resource Allocation and Scaling
. Safety-focused development is resource-intensive. We must allocate limited
resources, capital, and talent between safety-focused workloads and other initiatives, often without clear
returns on our safety-focused investments. For example, our investments in interpretability research and
techniques designed to ensure our models’ behavior remains consistent with intended goals, values, and safety
objectives may not yield actual or perceived commercial returns. Additionally, as we develop our models,
platform, and applications, safety testing may become more expensive and resource intensive. Limited-access
programs such as Project Glasswing may also require us to design, operate, and continually maintain bespoke
vetting, contracting, monitoring, and offboarding processes that differ materially from our standard
commercial release processes, including coordination among participating organizations, transition planning to

Our concentration in a limited number of products and applications, as well as our focused development
strategy within specific areas of the broader AI landscape, reduces our ability to mitigate business risks through
diversification. While this focused approach may enable us to allocate resources efficiently and compete
effectively in our prioritized areas, it also creates the risk that significant market opportunities or the largest
addressable markets may emerge in areas outside our current strategic focus. Many of our competitors offer
diverse product portfolios across multiple business lines or pursue broader development across AI modalities,
enabling them to offset weaknesses in a particular area. In contrast, any decline in demand for our core
offerings, whether due to competition, technological changes, pricing pressure, changes in customer demand,
or other factors, would have a direct and disproportionate impact on our revenue and ability to achieve and
sustain profitability. Our concentration also reflects a strategy that prioritizes model capability as a principal
source of differentiation and relies substantially on organic adoption rather than a large direct sales
organization. The risks of that strategy, including the risks that differentiation among advanced models
narrows, that customers select providers based on factors other than capability, or that competitors capture the
individual users from whom our enterprise adoption often originates, are described in the sections titled “—We
face intense competition, and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and

may not be successful.”
The AI industry is rapidly evolving, and it is difficult to predict which modalities or applications will capture the
most durable commercial value or how the competitive landscape will shift. If the market for AI models,
platforms, and applications develops in ways that do not align with our chosen areas of focus, or if competitors
are better positioned to address the areas where the market opportunity ultimately proves largest, our ability to
sustain revenue growth and compete effectively could be adversely affected. If we experience a decline in

revenue to offset any decline in our existing business. Further, technical issues, security incidents, regulatory
restrictions, or reputational harm affecting our models, platform, and applications could have an immediate
and disproportionate impact on our business due to our product concentration where alternative revenue
streams may not be available to offset such impact.
The market for AI models, platforms, and applications is evolving quickly, and customer requirements and

integration and tooling that we do not currently offer and may not plan to offer, or may seek AI solutions
embedded more deeply into enterprise workflows. Enterprises may prefer to develop their own AI capabilities
internally or choose competitors that offer more comprehensive product suites. Moreover, because
substantially all of our models and applications are built on top of our frontier models, any defect, vulnerability,
safety issue, or performance degradation in an underlying frontier model could simultaneously affect multiple

to competitors or fail to acquire new customers.

Our ability to make scheduled payments in respect of, to pay interest on, or to refinance our indebtedness,
including the A&R Credit Agreement and our outstanding convertible promissory notes, depends on our future
performance, which is subject to economic, financial, competitive, and other factors beyond our control. Such
payments will reduce the funds available to us for working capital, capital expenditures, and other corporate
purposes and may limit our ability to obtain additional financing for working capital, capital expenditures,
expansion plans, and other investments. Our business may not be able to generate cash flows from operations
in the future that are sufficient to service our debt and make necessary capital expenditures. If we are unable to
generate such cash flows, we may be required to adopt one or more alternatives, such as selling assets or
obtaining additional debt financing or equity capital on terms that may be onerous or highly dilutive. Our
ability to refinance our indebtedness will depend on the capital markets and our financial condition at such
time. We may not be able to engage in any of these activities or engage in these activities on desirable terms,
which could result in a default on our debt obligations and adversely affect our financial condition. Further, the
terms of the A&R Credit Agreement and the Infrastructure Partner 2026 NPA include a number of covenants
that limit our ability and our subsidiaries’ ability to, among other things, incur additional indebtedness, create
liens, make asset sales or investments, engage in mergers or other fundamental changes, pay dividends or
distributions, repurchase or redeem equity interests, and enter into transactions with affiliates. The terms of the
A&R Credit Agreement may restrict our current and future operations and could adversely affect our ability to
finance our future operations or capital needs. For more information, see the sections titled “—We may require
additional capital to meet our substantial ongoing obligations and support our business growth, and our ability
to generate sufficient revenue and secure additional capital on acceptable terms is critical to our continued
operations and competitive position” and “—If the market for our models, platform, and applications develops
more slowly than we expect or declines, our growth may slow or stall, and our business, financial condition, and
results of operations could be adversely affected.”
We are also subject to variable interest rate risk because the interest rate under the A&R Credit Agreement
varies based on a margin over an indexed rate or an adjusted base rate. If interest rates associated with our
floating rate debt increase, our debt service obligations in connection with the A&R Credit Agreement would
increase even though the amount borrowed remained the same, and our available cash would correspondingly
decrease. Our substantial amount of debt, combined with variable interest rates, could limit our flexibility in
planning for, or reacting to, changes in our business and the markets in which we operate, including limiting
our future investments or our ability to enter into acquisitions and strategic partnerships, and obtain financing
for such transactions.

Our pricing structures for our models, platform, and applications change from time to time,
which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
We have in the past changed, and we expect that in the future we may change, our pricing models, including as
a result of competition, macroeconomic conditions, compliance with increased regulatory hurdles, the
maturation of the market for AI models, platforms, and applications, or changes in how our models, platform,
and applications are broadly consumed. As a result, we may be required to reduce our prices, offer shorter
contract durations or offer alternative pricing models, such as outcome or task-based pricing, any of which
could adversely affect our business. In addition, our agentic offerings are structurally more compute-intensive
than our non-agentic offerings. If we are unable to implement pricing models that adequately reflect the higher
compute intensity of these agentic workloads, or if competitive dynamics constrain our ability to price these
products at levels sufficient to cover their costs, our compute efficiency could deteriorate as agentic usage
grows, which could adversely affect our ability to achieve or sustain profitability.
Additionally, as we continue to target selling our models, platform, and applications to our enterprise
customers, these customers may demand different pricing structures, price concessions, or additional
functionality at the same price levels. If we are unable to modify or develop effective pricing models and
strategies that are attractive to existing and prospective customers, our business, financial condition, and
results of operations may be adversely affected.
If we are unable to attract, retain, or motivate highly skilled personnel, we may not be able to
grow or operate effectively.
Our performance and ability to grow our business depend on the talents and efforts of highly skilled
individuals, and our future success depends on our continuing ability to identify, hire, develop, motivate, and
retain highly skilled personnel for all areas of our organization. Our business is particularly dependent on a
limited pool of researchers, engineers, and technical personnel with specialized experience in designing,
training, deploying, and operating frontier models and the underlying infrastructure that supports them. We
have from time to time experienced, and we expect to continue to experience, difficulty in hiring and retaining
highly skilled employees with appropriate qualifications at the pace that our operations require. Competition in
our industry relating to hiring and retaining employees with appropriate qualifications and on competitive
economic terms is exceptionally intense and has escalated significantly in recent periods, especially in the San
Francisco Bay Area, where our headquarters is located and where we have a substantial presence and need for
highly skilled personnel. A small number of well-capitalized AI labs, large technology companies, and new
market entrants compete aggressively for a relatively fixed supply of individuals with the requisite expertise.
Certain of our competitors have directly solicited, and continue to directly solicit, our employees. Our former
employees are also generally able to join or found competing companies immediately following their departure,
and, subject to their confidentiality and other legal obligations, use the general skills, know-how, and
experience they developed while employed by us. In addition, we have in the past, and may in the future, be
subject to claims or disputes relating to the solicitation or hiring of employees, including allegations that such
hires violated non-compete, non-solicitation, intellectual property, confidentiality, or other employment-
related obligations.
As our company continues to grow and our industry evolves, the incentives to attract, retain, and motivate
employees provided by our cash and equity awards or by future arrangements may not be as effective as in the
past. Many of the companies with which we compete for highly qualified personnel have greater resources than
we have and may be willing to offer more attractive compensation packages. We may need to invest significant
amounts of cash and equity to attract and retain employees, resulting in substantial additional share-based
compensation expense and dilution to the ownership of our existing stockholders, and we may never realize
returns on these investments that are commensurate with the level of our expenditures. If the perceived value
of our compensatory package declines or is subject to significant value fluctuations, it may adversely affect our
ability to attract and retain highly skilled employees. In addition, we have a number of current employees,
including our co-founders, who hold equity in our company or whose equity awards are or will become
substantially vested upon the completion of this offering. This may be particularly true for certain of our longer-
61

tenured and early employees, whose equity holdings may represent a significant portion of their personal
wealth. As a result, it may be difficult for us to continue to retain and motivate these employees, and the value

Historically, our ability to successfully attract, retain, and motivate our personnel has in large part been due to
our company culture and commitment to safety and responsible scaling and development. If we are unable to
maintain our culture, if we make decisions as a company that our employees do not believe align with our
values, or if events take place, regardless of fault, that call into question whether we have operated in
accordance with our values, our ability to attract, retain, and motivate our personnel may be adversely affected.
Rapid growth has also created workforce-planning and execution challenges, including limitations in our ability
to accurately forecast headcount needs, periods of accelerated hiring followed by corrective actions that may
disrupt operations or reduce morale, and increased reliance on managers operating at greater scale than in
their prior experience, which introduces additional operational, legal, reputational, and execution risk as the
organization continues to expand. If we move into new geographies, we will need to attract and recruit skilled
personnel in those geographic areas, but it may be challenging for us to compete with traditional local
employers in these regions for talent. If we fail to attract new personnel or fail to retain and motivate our
current personnel who are capable of meeting our growing technical, operational, and managerial
requirements, our business may be adversely affected.
In addition, heightened public attention on AI has increased physical and informational security risks, and we
have experienced threats to employee safety and attempts to obtain confidential information through physical
or digital means, which, despite the security measures we have implemented at certain facilities, may be
exacerbated by our global and flexible working arrangements and could adversely affect employee morale,
productivity, and our ability to attract, retain, and motivate highly skilled personnel. Addressing these risks also
requires us to attract and retain additional specialized security personnel, and difficulties in recruiting qualified
security engineers could further exacerbate these challenges.
Further, changes to immigration policies that restrain the flow of professional and technical talent, including
but not limited to U.S. immigration policies, may inhibit our ability to recruit and retain highly qualified
employees. If we are unable to effectively manage the foregoing risks, our prospects, business, financial
condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

difficult to evaluate our future prospects and may increase the risk that we will not be

Our results of operations may fluctuate significantly on a period-to-period basis, including as
a result of strategic investment decisions and substantial compute-related expenditures,
which could cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline.
Our results of operations have historically varied from period to period, and we expect that our results of
operations will continue to vary significantly from quarter to quarter and from year to year in the future, such
that the results of any one period should not be relied upon as an indication of future performance. In
particular, our financial performance may be significantly influenced by strategic decisions we make regarding
the allocation of resources and the amount and timing of operating expenses and capital expenditures that we
may incur to maintain and expand our business and operations and to remain competitive. We may make
significant and, at times, discrete investments in areas such as research and development, compute and related
infrastructure, product development, safety and security initiatives, and go-to-market expansion, which may be
uneven in size and timing. These investments may materially increase our expenses in a given period and cause
our results of operations to fluctuate significantly or vary meaningfully from period to period, and may result in
periods of reduced margins or increased losses even if our underlying business trends remain unchanged or
continue to improve. As a result, our financial performance may not follow any consistent pattern, and prior or
interim periods of improved results of operations should not be viewed as indicative of our future performance.
Our revenue in any period has also included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers
that we subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage
policy or commercial terms, and whose revenue would not be expected to recur following restriction or
termination of their access. We believe this dynamic is common in our industry. Detection, investigation, and
enforcement take time, and we cannot assure you that we will identify such usage, or restrict or terminate a
customer’s access, on a timely basis or at all. Customers may evade our controls, and customers whose access is
restricted or terminated may re-register under new accounts. As a result, revenue from such customers may
continue or recur notwithstanding our enforcement efforts. Our continued detection and enforcement efforts,
and in particular, the enhancement of such efforts in August and September 2026, and the timing of any
resulting restrictions or terminations, are expected to reduce the percentage of revenue from customers using
our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms, and may reduce
our overall revenue and growth rates in future periods and contribute to variability in our results from period to
period.
Our results of operations are also affected by seasonal variations in the usage of our models, platform, and
applications. Because our revenue is primarily consumption-based, we have experienced, and expect to
continue to experience, lower usage around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, when
certain customer workflows slow down and overall customer activity declines. Our results of operations may
also vary with the timing and cadence of our model and product releases, which are uneven from period to
period and may cause usage, and therefore revenue, to increase or decline between periods. Our historical
growth rates may have masked the impact of seasonal trends on our results. As our growth rate declines over
time, we expect seasonal effects to become more apparent in, and to have a greater effect on, our period-to-
period results. In addition, other seasonal trends may develop, and the seasonal trends that we currently
experience may become more pronounced, as we continue to scale.
