Any one or more of the factors above, or other factors in this “Risk Factors” section, may result in significant
fluctuations in our results of operations or other key metrics, which may cause such results to fall below our
financial guidance or other projections or the expectations of analysts or investors, and cause the market price
of our Class A common stock to decline.
Certain of our operating metrics are subject to assumptions and limitations. As a result, these
metrics may not provide an accurate indication of our actual performance or future results.
Certain of our operating metrics, such as Run-Rate Revenue, Net Revenue Retention, customer counts, and
Claude’s success rate, are based on numerous assumptions and limitations, are calculated using data from
internal systems and tools, have not been independently verified by third parties, are subject to inherent
limitations in measurement, and may not accurately reflect actual results or provide an accurate indication of
future or expected results.
Run-Rate Revenue is not a substitute for revenue prepared in accordance with GAAP or a forecast of revenue.
Because Run-Rate Revenue annualizes our consumption-based fees for a trailing 28-day period and our
subscription-based fees for a single month, it assumes that activity during those measurement periods has
continued at the same rate for a full year. Because it annualizes a short measurement period, Run-Rate Revenue
measured during a period of seasonally higher or lower usage, such as the reduced usage we have typically
experienced around holiday and vacation periods in the summer and winter, may differ significantly from Run-
Rate Revenue measured at other times, and in each case may not correspond to the revenue we ultimately
recognize over any quarter or fiscal year. Our actual historical revenue and future revenue may differ materially
from this measure. Both our consumption-based and subscription-based revenue may fluctuate from period to
period, and in particular, our consumption-based revenue may fluctuate significantly or decline if customers
reduce, limit, or do not expand their usage or spend, or shift usage to lower-priced models, including in
response to competitive offerings, pricing changes, changes in customer budgets or strategic priorities
regarding AI investment, seasonality, or general economic conditions. In addition, sustaining and growing this
revenue depends on our ability to continue to offer models at the frontier of AI capability, which we may not be
able to do.
Our ability or decision to remain at the frontier may also be affected by the safety and risk mitigation
measures we implement in developing and releasing our models.
Our recent Run-Rate Revenue growth has also
been driven in part by rapid initial customer adoption and expansion often characteristic of an early-adoption
period and the nascency of the AI market that may not be sustainable, and we expect our Run-Rate Revenue
growth rate to decline over time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate, as our
revenue base increases, as the market matures, and as a result of other factors.
In addition, our Run-Rate
Revenue has included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we subsequently
determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial
terms. When we identify such usage, we seek to restrict or terminate the customer’s access; however, because
our detection, investigation, and enforcement take time, our Run-Rate Revenue as of any measurement date
includes amounts from customers that have not yet been restricted or terminated and whose revenue would not
be expected to recur following restriction or termination of their access.
Our continued enforcement efforts may
reduce our revenue, Run-Rate Revenue, and growth rates in future periods. See “—Our results of operations
may fluctuate significantly on a period-to-period basis, including as a result of strategic investment decisions
and substantial compute-related expenditures, which could cause the market price of our Class A common
stock to decline.” Accordingly, our Run-Rate Revenue as of any measurement date is not indicative of historical
revenue and may not be indicative of our revenue for any future period.
The determination of the number of customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis is based on
our internal records and involves judgment, including in determining which accounts should be aggregated and
treated as belonging to the same organization. We apply our most current customer records in calculating this
metric, and our determination of which accounts belong to a single organization may change over time,
including as a result of acquisitions and account consolidations.
We do not separately define or internally track
a category of “enterprise” customers, and our customers are not segmented or measured internally by reference

Certain
success rates and similar AI performance metrics with respect to Claude referenced in this prospectus
are measured using internal benchmarks developed and maintained by us. These benchmarks reflect our

Performance results derived from these internal benchmarks may not be replicable by customers, researchers,
or other third parties who evaluate our models using different tasks, data sets, evaluation criteria, or computing
environments. Accordingly, such metrics may differ materially from performance outcomes experienced by any
particular customer or user in their specific deployment environment or use case, and should not be relied upon
as indicative of the results any customer or user will achieve. Because AI performance benchmarking
methodologies vary significantly across developers, such performance metrics as we measure them may also not
be comparable to similarly titled or analogous metrics reported by other AI developers, and direct comparison
of such metrics across companies may be misleading.
Investors should consider these metrics in light of the assumptions and processes used in calculating such
metrics and the limitations as a result thereof. In addition, our internal systems and tools have a number of
limitations, which could result in unexpected changes to our metrics, including the metrics we publicly disclose.
Further, certain of our operating metrics are based in part on data reported to us by our third-party partners. If
the internal systems and tools we use to track these metrics or if the data reported to us by our third-party
partners undercount or overcount performance, or contain algorithmic or other technical errors, the data we
report may not be accurate. While our operating metrics are based on what we believe to be reasonable
estimates for the applicable period of measurement, there are inherent challenges in these measurements. We
may also refine or change our methodology for tracking certain operating metrics from time to time, to the
extent practicable, including to improve overall accuracy and alignment with management’s view of business
and operating performance and as a result of acquisitions. Any of these updates may result in changes in certain
business and operating trends and may impact comparability of these metrics across periods. Investors should
not place undue reliance on these metrics as an indicator of our future or expected results. Moreover, these
metrics may differ from similarly titled metrics presented by other companies and may not be comparable to
such other metrics. See the sections titled “Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and
Results of Operations” and “Business” for more information regarding our operating metrics.
Our business is subject to an evolving and uncertain regulatory and political environment,
which could increase our costs, restrict our operations, or adversely affect demand for our
models, platform, and applications.
The development, deployment, and use of AI technologies are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly
complex laws, regulations, and governmental scrutiny across multiple jurisdictions. Governments and
regulatory authorities in the United States and in other countries in which we operate or distribute our models,
platform, and applications have proposed, enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance
relating to AI model development and deployment, data usage and privacy, transparency, safety, consumer
protection, content generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For
example, the EU AI Regulation 2024/1689 (“EU AI Act”), which came into force in August 2024 and will
become fully applicable following a transitional period, imposes a range of obligations on AI systems and
general-purpose AI models placed on the market or put into service in the EU, including transparency, risk
management, and governance requirements, and provides for significant penalties for non-compliance. In the
United States, the regulatory framework for AI remains fragmented and uncertain, with evolving federal policy
initiatives, continued debate regarding the scope and durability of executive actions, and a growing number of
state-level laws and proposals addressing the development and use of AI. For example,
several U.S. states,
including New York and California, have passed AI safety laws. More generally, proposed legislation in the
United States contemplates more expansive governmental oversight of AI, including potential nationalization,
mandatory shutdown or discontinuation requirements for frontier AI systems or other strategic measures to
prevent or manage the development of artificial superintelligence.
Further, in June 2026, the U.S. federal
69
Table of Contents
government issued an executive order establishing a voluntary framework for developers of frontier AI models
to engage with the government prior to the deployment of such AI technologies, directing federal agencies to
strengthen cyber defenses, and prioritizing enforcement against criminal misuse of AI; although that
framework is voluntary and does not establish a mandatory governmental licensing, preclearance, or permitting
requirement for the development or deployment of AI models, it reflects increasing federal attention to the
national security implications of frontier AI and the order may be followed by further executive or legislative
action. If executive or legislative action of this nature were enacted to regulate AI technologies, it could
constrain how we operate our business.
We have also advocated, and expect to continue to advocate, for regulation and oversight of frontier AI,
including industry-wide standards primarily relevant to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that AI
capabilities do not advance faster than the safety, alignment, and security practices needed to support
them,
and we have proposed working with the U.S. government and other frontier AI developers to establish safety
standards. Regulatory or other measures of the kind we advocate, if adopted, would apply to us and could
increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and
when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth. The effect that any such measures would
have on the rate at which AI capabilities advance, and on our business, is uncertain and would depend on the
specific requirements adopted and on the extent to which safety, alignment, and security practices advance
together with model capabilities. There is no assurance that policymakers will adopt the approaches we
support, and our advocacy has in the past drawn, and may continue to draw, criticism, heightened scrutiny, or
other challenges.
Regulatory approaches to AI also vary significantly by geography and may be influenced by local political,
economic, social, or environmental considerations. In some jurisdictions, public concern regarding the
potential displacement of labor by AI systems, the perceived societal impacts of automation, or the
environmental footprint associated with AI development and deployment, has led, or could lead, to restrictive
legislation or other governmental actions. In particular, to the extent the rate of job displacement rapidly
increases due to the adoption of AI or for related reasons, whether actual or perceived, governments or other
regulatory authorities may intervene to slow the rate of adoption of AI, restrict its use, or take other actions that
increase the cost of developing, deploying, or commercializing AI systems. Even in the absence of any legal or
regulatory requirements, we may from time to time voluntarily elect to take actions intended to ameliorate the
impact of such displacement. Any such actions would represent additional costs and expenditures for which we
may not receive a corresponding commercial benefit, and there can be no assurance that any such actions
would be effective in reducing displacement-related harms or in mitigating the associated reputational,
regulatory, or political risks.
Increasingly restrictive AI regulation in the United States and other western jurisdictions could enable
competitors operating in less regulated environments to innovate, scale, and deploy AI technologies more
rapidly, potentially allowing such competitors to become more advanced and pose greater competitive or
strategic threats over time. In particular, increasing strategic competition between the United States and China
in AI development may lead to divergent regulatory approaches, with the potential for the United States to
impose restrictions on AI companies’ interactions with Chinese entities or markets, and for China to impose
reciprocal measures that limit access to or demand for U.S.-origin AI models, platforms, and applications.

considerations, public sentiment, and geopolitical dynamics, we will not be able to fully anticipate how existing
laws will be interpreted or enforced, how new legal frameworks will evolve, or whether regulatory regimes
across jurisdictions will converge or diverge over time. Compliance with new or changing requirements may
require substantial investment in research and development, compliance systems, operational processes, or
localized offerings, and we may need to adjust or limit our activities in certain jurisdictions to address
conflicting or inconsistent legal obligations. In addition, regulatory actions affecting our customers or partners,
including restrictions on their ability to develop, deploy, or commercialize AI-enabled models, platforms, or
applications, could indirectly reduce demand for our models, platform, and applications. Any failure, or
perceived failure, to comply with applicable laws and regulations, or any significant increase in the cost or
complexity of compliance, could result in litigation, enforcement actions, penalties, reputational harm, delayed
or reduced adoption of our offerings, or other adverse effects on our business, financial condition, and results of
operations.

possess or could develop forms of sentience or moral status may lead to regulatory requirements, public
pressure, or advocacy efforts that could constrain how we develop, train, deploy, or modify our models, increase
our costs, or affect our reputation, regardless of the ultimate resolution of these philosophical and scientific
questions. In addition, given our focus on developing frontier AI, and the way we approach model sentience and
moral status, we may face heightened scrutiny or pressure in connection with these debates and could elect to
adopt policies, safeguards, or limitations regarding model development, deployment, or modification that go
beyond existing legal requirements, which could constrain our operations, increase costs, or limit the
commercial potential of our models, platform, and applications. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks,
our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.

For example, in February 2026, in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be
used for mass domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President of the United States stated
that he had directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology. At the same time, the
Secretary of War directed the Department of War to designate us as a “supply-chain risk to national security”
and stated that “effective immediately, no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United
States military may conduct any commercial activity” with us. On March 4, 2026, the Department of War sent
us two letters—one pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 3252 and the other pursuant to Section 4713 of the Federal
Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act (“FASCSA”)—asserting that our models, platform, and applications
present a supply-chain risk. These actions referenced above are defined herein as “Challenged Actions.” We
vigorously challenged these Challenged Actions in
Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al.
(N.D. Cal.) and

nthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al.
(D.C. Cir.). After first obtaining an order from the United States
District Court for the Northern District of California that preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s
directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant
agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on
August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California
that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The court ruled that the Challenged Actions were
retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the First Amendment to the United States
Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment to the United States
Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions, particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. §
3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to
law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment largely in our favor.

stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a supply-chain risk pending review on the merits.
On September 25, 2026, in a 2-1 split decision, the D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals denied our petition for review,
ruling that the Department of War’s Section 4713 supply-chain risk designation was proper, and that our rights
under the First Amendment and Due Process Clause of the Fifth Amendment were not violated. We filed a
petition for rehearing en banc asking the full D.C. Circuit to review the panel’s decision. We cannot predict the
ultimate outcome of these lawsuits.

The bidding process for government contracts can be highly competitive, expensive, and time-consuming, often
requiring significant upfront time and expense without any assurance that these efforts will generate revenue.
Government agencies often undertake a significant evaluation process that results in a lengthy sales cycle. Some
contracts with government agencies are structured in phases or include options, where each phase is subject to
satisfaction of certain conditions and where the exercise of options is discretionary. As a result, the actual scope
of work performed pursuant to any such contracts, in addition to related contract revenue, could be less than
total contract value. In addition, product purchases by such organizations are frequently subject to budget
constraints, multiple approvals, and unanticipated administrative, processing, and other delays. All of these
factors can add further risk to business conducted with these customers and could lead to lower revenue results
than originally anticipated.

Our reliance on a limited number of CSPs and suppliers, some of which have strategic and
investment relationships with us and are our customers, creates complex dynamics that could
give rise to conflicts of interest and adversely affect our access to compute.
We
rely on a limited number of CSPs—Amazon.com, Inc. (together with its affiliates, “Amazon”), Google, and
Microsoft Corporation (“Microsoft”)—and suppliers, such as Broadcom, for compute and critical components of
our compute infrastructure. These relationships are governed by contractual arrangements that, while
providing us with significant committed compute, also create dependencies and potential vulnerabilities. These
CSPs may experience service outages, security incidents, or capacity constraints that affect our operations. The
terms of our arrangements, including pricing, compute commitments, and service levels, are subject to
negotiation upon renewal, and we may be unable to secure renewals on terms as favorable as our current
arrangements. Migrating workloads to alternative providers would be costly, time-consuming, and
operationally complex, and may not be feasible within timeframes that would avoid material disruption to our
model development roadmap or our ability to serve customers. The engineering investment required to
maintain the performance of our unified compute platform across new hardware environments means that any
such migration could degrade our compute efficiency, increasing the compute and infrastructure costs required
to support a given level of business activity during and following any such migration period.
Our relationships with these CSPs are multifaceted and complex. Amazon, Google, and Microsoft, through their
respective affiliates, have made significant equity investments in our company. At the same time, they may have
made, and may in the future make, equity investments in, provide financing to, or otherwise support companies
whose models, platforms, or applications compete with ours. These CSPs are also our customers, purchasing
our intelligence service for internal use or for their own products and services. Their purchasing decisions may
be influenced by their own competing offerings, which could affect their demand for our intelligence service.
Additionally, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft are among the largest technology companies in the world, each
with substantial AI research and development programs, AI-powered models, platforms, and applications that
compete with ours, and strategic interests that may not be fully aligned with our own. Amazon, Google, and
Microsoft each offer AI services and develop and deploy competing AI models through their respective cloud
platforms. We make certain of our models available through these cloud platforms, and our distribution
relationships with Amazon, Google, and Microsoft generate revenue for us, but they also create dependencies,
give them visibility into our pricing and commercial terms across the platforms they operate, and may influence
their incentives regarding pricing, compute allocation, service quality, sales prioritization, and compensation
structures. To the extent these CSPs promote, integrate, prioritize, or provide customer access to our models,
platform, and applications on terms that are less favorable than those applicable to their own competing
offerings or to the offerings of other companies, including with respect to pricing, commercial terms, product
placement, integration, or access to compute or sales incentives, our competitive position, customer adoption,
and business results could be adversely affected.

We are pursuing initiatives to develop our own data center infrastructure, which involves
significant capital commitments, operational complexities, and execution risks that could
adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
To help reduce our dependence on CSPs, address constraints on available compute, and secure access to
compute at the scale necessary for frontier model development, we are pursuing initiatives to develop our own
dedicated on-premise data center infrastructure. These efforts include long-term leases and partnerships with
third-party partners to procure the underlying real estate, power, and data center facilities while we lease
capacity in those facilities and contract with specialized third-party operators for ongoing facility management.

commencing upon AI infrastructure equipment becoming “ready for service” at the applicable data center
facility. The 2026 Lease Arrangement is non-cancelable by the parties to such agreement during the applicable
lease period except in the case of a default. In addition,

75

infrastructure initiatives requires us to recruit personnel with relevant experience and manage complex multi-
year deployment timelines and relationships with developers, contractors, and service providers.
As we continue to build out our own compute and infrastructure and further vertically integrate across the
compute supply chain, these multi-party structures will become more prevalent and will expose us to a
structural timing and liquidity risk in our payment obligations that differs from our historical compute
arrangements. Historically, we have generally obtained compute from a limited number of CSPs under
arrangements in which our compute and infrastructure expenses are paid as compute becomes available to us.
In the future, we expect we will increasingly enter into separate arrangements with a greater number of
different counterparties, each responsible for discrete services or inputs across the compute supply chain.
Under many of these arrangements, we may be obligated to pay a counterparty once it performs its discrete
obligation, even if delays or failures by others prevent us from assembling those discrete services or inputs into
usable compute we can deploy to generate revenue. In addition, counterparties may deliver their services or
inputs later than scheduled, or may fail to deliver them at all, and any such delay or non-delivery by a single
counterparty could postpone or prevent our deployment of the associated compute. As a result, we could incur
significant cash outflows without obtaining usable compute on a timely basis, which could adversely affect our
liquidity, financial condition, and results of operations.
Certain of our data center infrastructure arrangements involve complex multi-party structures in which chips
are procured from or through our CSPs, leased to us by third-party financing entities, installed in data center
facilities procured by or through other third-party partners, and operated by yet another set of third-party
service providers. The complexity of these arrangements increases execution risk, as delays or failures by any
participant in the chain could affect the availability or performance of the resulting compute.
In addition, to meet the substantial energy demands of large-scale AI workloads, we have entered into, and may
in the future enter into, arrangements involving dedicated power generation assets and/or the development,
operation, or control of power stations or other energy infrastructure. Such arrangements expose us to new
operational, regulatory, and environmental liabilities, and require expertise and capabilities that differ from our
core competencies. Successfully executing on these power infrastructure projects requires us to recruit
personnel with relevant experience and manage complex multi-year deployment timelines and relationships
with developers, contractors, service providers, and regulators, including aligning project completion schedules
with the data centers such projects are expected to serve in order to avoid timing delays that constrain our
ability to utilize this compute and to generate revenue and recoup costs from such investments.
Deployment of our data center and power infrastructure projects involves execution risks, including delays due
to permitting issues, change in law, force majeure, lack of network connectivity between facilities, supply chain
disruptions, labor shortages, or contractor performance; cost overruns due to equipment pricing changes,
design modifications, or unanticipated requirements; and technical risks that facilities may not perform as
specified or achieve expected reliability or efficiency levels. Certain of our arrangements are also subject to
conditions precedent that must be satisfied before construction can commence, and completion guarantees that
may terminate upon a lender foreclosure before construction is complete, leaving us without contractual
recourse to compel completion. Certain of these arrangements also depend on the continued performance of
credit support provided by a third party that is also a competitor, the loss or impairment of which could
jeopardize the underlying arrangements. Such credit support provided to third-party data center developers or
hardware providers, from which we derive no direct contractual rights or obligations, may also affect the
availability and cost of data center capacity and hardware generally. Additionally, new tariffs or import fees
enacted after the effective date of certain arrangements may be passed through to us as additional costs. Any
delay in or limitation on the amount of compute delivered to us could adversely affect our business.
The capital-intensive and long-term nature of leasing and equipping data center capacity creates financial risk,
as large upfront investments and long-term payment commitments must be made months before facilities
become fully operational. If our compute requirements or technology needs change, we may find ourselves with
leased or dedicated infrastructure that is poorly suited to our actual needs, and technological changes in AI
hardware or training methodologies could render such infrastructure less efficient than newer alternatives.
Unlike CSP arrangements where compute can be adjusted relatively dynamically, long-term leases, reserved
compute, and dedicated infrastructure investments are much less flexible and create long-term financial
obligations regardless of whether the capacity continues to meet our needs. For example, certain of our
dedicated power and data center infrastructure arrangements have initial terms of 20 years with annual
76
Table of Contents
escalators and include take-or-pay compute payment obligations and uncapped fuel cost pass-throughs that
apply for the duration of the term regardless of actual utilization.
Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and
are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP
arrangements is generally paid as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our
compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments,
including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute
becoming operational. Our existing commitments are substantial, and we expect our capital expenditures to
increase significantly as we continue to expand our compute and infrastructure build-out. See the section titled
“Management’s Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and
Capital Resources” for more information. As a result, we expect these investments to result in significant net
cash used in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future, and our net cash used in these
activities may increase regardless of whether our financial performance improves. The magnitude and timing of
these investments are inherently uncertain and may change materially over short periods, including as a result
of decisions to accelerate or expand our build-out, and such changes could rapidly and significantly alter our
expected results of operations and cash flows for a given period. If our cash flows from operations and available
capital are insufficient to fund these investments, we may be required to raise additional capital on unfavorable
terms or to reduce, defer, or forgo planned investments, any of which could adversely affect our business,
financial condition, and results of operations.

financial condition, and results of operations.

managing, and scaling a direct sales force. We have dedicated and plan to continue to dedicate significant
resources to sales and marketing programs and to expand our sales and marketing capabilities to target
potential customers and achieve broader market adoption of our models, platform, and applications, but there
is no guarantee that we will be successful in attracting and maintaining additional customers. Moreover,
identifying, recruiting, training, and managing sales personnel requires significant time, expense, and attention,
including from our senior management and other key personnel, as there is significant competition for sales
personnel with the skills and technical knowledge that we require, including the ability to understand and
communicate complex and evolving AI use cases, regulatory considerations, customer risk sensitivities, and
rapidly changing product capabilities. These challenges are particularly acute for international expansion,

geographic markets which we target, and an aligned mission-oriented culture. If we are unable to successfully
manage the foregoing risks, our prospects, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be
adversely affected.

We have a limited history selling consumption-based access and subscriptions to our models, platform, and

In addition, our strategy and customer mix expose us to competitive and execution risks as the AI market
continues to evolve. We have organized our research priorities, our product roadmap, and our go-to-market and
Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, and much of the diffusion of Claude to date has been organic—
driven by individual users, including software developers and prosumers, who adopt Claude and often serve as
internal champions for its broader adoption within their organizations—rather than by a large direct sales
organization. This approach has allowed us to scale with a smaller team relative to other large enterprise
technology companies, but it assumes that our applications and distribution will be sufficient to deliver the
capabilities of our models to customers and that individual adoption will continue to translate into
organizational adoption and expansion. Companies with stronger consumer-facing businesses, larger consumer
user bases, more established brands, broader distribution, or deeper customer relationships may choose to
increase their focus on enterprise customers or enterprise use cases and could leverage their scale, resources,
and market presence to compete more effectively with us. In particular, if such competitors capture the
individual users from whom our enterprise adoption often originates, whether through their consumer
applications, by integrating AI functionality into products those users already use, or otherwise, our pipeline of
enterprise opportunities could be reduced in ways that a direct sales organization of our current scale may not
be able to offset. Building a substantially larger sales organization, or shifting investment toward consumer and
application-layer products to compete for those users, would require significant time and resources beyond our
current plans and would involve the trade-offs described in the section titled “—We face intense competition,
and if we are unable to compete effectively, our business, financial condition, and results of operations could be
adversely affected.” Because we have a limited operating history with our current business model and go-to-
market strategy, we have less experience predicting customer adoption, expansion, and retention patterns, and
customers may be slower than expected to adopt our models, platform, and applications or expand usage. Any
failure to successfully scale our operations or effectively execute on and refine our go-to-market strategy could
adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Sales to enterprise customers involve complexities and risks that could adversely affect our
business, financial condition, and results of operations.
We derive a large portion of our revenue from sales to enterprise customers. Our ability to attract, retain, and
expand relationships with enterprise customers depends in significant part on our ability to meet their
generally heightened operational, technical, security, reliability, and compliance requirements. Enterprises
typically expect high levels of system uptime, performance consistency, data security, auditability, internal
controls, and scalability, as well as robust support and service levels. These requirements may be heightened for
our agentic offerings, where enterprise customers may require detailed logs of each action taken by an
autonomous agent within their environment, including the agent’s reasoning, tool invocations, and interactions
with external systems. Any inability on our part to provide such logs at the level of granularity customers
require could limit adoption of our agentic offerings by enterprises or result in customer attrition. If we are
unable to deliver models, platforms, and applications that satisfy these enterprise-grade requirements, or if we
experience outages, performance degradation, security incidents, or other operational failures, our ability to
retain and expand with enterprise customers could be adversely affected. In particular, as we deploy our Virtual

Collaborators, like Claude Code and Claude Cowork, within enterprise environments, these systems will require
broad permissions and deep integrations with customers’ internal tools, data, and workflows in order to operate

increases the potential consequences of any security incident, unauthorized action, or system error, and

they are unable to satisfy themselves regarding the security, reliability, and controllability of such systems.
Our sales efforts targeted at enterprise customers also involve risks and challenges that may not be present, or
that are present to a lesser extent, with sales to individuals or smaller organizations. These customers typically
have longer decision-making cycles, require greater security, functionality, and scalability, expect a broader
range of services, demand that providers take on a larger share of risks, require higher levels of customer
service and support, and expect greater payment flexibility from vendors. We are often required to spend
significant time and resources to familiarize potential customers with the value proposition of our models,
platform, and applications, and this process can take substantially longer with enterprise customers.
Enterprises may also require extensive customization, integration support, and vendor evaluations and demand
more features than we currently offer or than we can deliver within their expected timeframes, including
enterprise-grade functionality such as audit logs, compliance features, security controls, and monitoring tools,
which may require us to make additional investments in product development or services capabilities, before
committing to a purchase. As a result of these factors, sales opportunities with enterprises require us to devote
greater sales and administrative support and professional services resources to each such enterprise customer,
which increases our costs, lengthens our sales cycle, and diverts our sales and customer service resources to a
smaller number of enterprise customers. We may spend substantial time, effort, and money in our sales efforts
without successfully producing any sales. In addition, many enterprise customers procure and deploy our
models, platform, and applications through third-party CSP marketplaces, which can introduce additional
complexity into the sales and deployment process, including reliance on the CSPs’ procurement, security, and
billing workflows and coordination with multiple counterparties. As a result, our ability to attract, retain, and
expand relationships with enterprise customers may also depend in part on factors outside of our direct control,
including the policies, priorities, and operational requirements of such CSPs.
A number of factors influence the length and variability of our sales cycle. The need to educate potential
customers about the uses and benefits of our models, platform, and applications, the discretionary nature of
purchasing and budget cycles, competitive evaluation and purchasing approval processes, procurement
requirements, legal review of contract terms, and internal budget authorization procedures all contribute to
sales cycle variability. The length of our sales cycle, from identification of the opportunity to deal closure, may
vary significantly from customer to customer. Sales to enterprises typically take longer to complete than sales to
individuals or smaller organizations.
A meaningful portion of our revenue is attributable to a relatively small number of such enterprise customer
relationships, which increases the variability of our financial results. Our revenue in any given quarter could be
substantially affected if these customers decide to significantly reduce their spend.
Enterprises may have deep existing relationships with our competitors for models, platforms, and applications
we do not offer, or relationships with others in the ecosystem, which may delay our sales process or cause us to
not succeed with such enterprises.
Enterprise customers are particularly sensitive to our ability to maintain the uptime of our models, platform,
and applications, and any degradation in uptime could adversely affect our ability to retain and expand with our
enterprise customers. Sustaining the uptime, performance, and scale that enterprise customers expect can place
additional demands on our overall compute, and any failure of our capacity management systems to direct

will increase as we expand our business and pursue new customers. Many enterprises have complex internal

particularly with respect to our enterprise customers.

our existing customer base. If we are unable to effectively provide support and integration efforts that enable

usage, fail to renew at expected levels, or reduce their spend, which could materially slow our revenue growth.

power during periods of peak demand, whether in connection with or outside of natural disasters or other
catastrophic events, could interrupt or degrade the provision of our services in the ordinary course of our
business. See the sections titled “—Constraints on the critical inputs supporting compute could limit our ability
to secure adequate compute.” and “—Our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be
adversely affected by war, terrorism, natural disasters, public health crises, political crises, or other unexpected

applications could decline and our brand, business, financial condition, and results of operations could be
adversely affected.

We will incur increased costs and demands upon management as a result of complying with
the laws and regulations affecting public companies, which may adversely affect our
business, financial condition, and results of operations.
As a public company, we will incur greater legal, accounting, and other expenses than we incurred as a private
company. For example, we are subject to the reporting requirements of the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, as
amended (“Exchange Act”), the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 (“Sarbanes-Oxley Act”), the Dodd-Frank Wall
Street Reform and Consumer Protection Act, the rules and regulations of the SEC, and the listing standards of
the Nasdaq Global Select Market. The Exchange Act requires, among other things, that we file annual,
quarterly, and current reports with respect to our business and results of operations. Compliance with these
requirements will increase our legal, accounting, and financial compliance costs, and increase demand on our
systems, making some activities more time-consuming and costly. In addition, changing laws, regulations, and
standards relating to reporting obligations and corporate governance disclosure are creating uncertainty for
public companies, which could result in continued uncertainty regarding compliance matters and higher costs.
We expect these rules and regulations to make it more expensive for us to obtain director and officer liability
insurance, and we may be required to accept reduced policy limits and coverage or incur substantially higher
costs to maintain the same or similar coverage. As a result, it may be more difficult for us to attract and retain
qualified individuals to serve on our board of directors or as our executive officers.
As a public company, we expect to incur significant expenses and devote substantial management effort toward
ensuring compliance with the auditor attestation requirements of Section 404 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act. In
that regard, we will need to hire additional accounting and financial staff with appropriate public company
experience and technical accounting knowledge. In addition, as a public company, we may be subject to
stockholder activism, which can lead to substantial costs, distract management, and impact the manner in
which we operate our business in ways we cannot currently anticipate.
As a result of disclosure of information in this prospectus and in our public filings with the SEC as required of a
public company, our business and financial condition will become more visible, which we believe may result in
threatened or actual litigation, including by competitors and other third parties. If such claims are successful,
our business, financial condition, and results of operations may be adversely affected, and even if the claims do
not result in litigation or are resolved in our favor, these claims, and the time and resources necessary to resolve
them, may divert the resources of our management and our board of directors, and adversely affect our
business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Further, many members of our management team have limited experience managing a publicly traded
company, interacting with public company investors, and complying with the increasingly complex laws and
regulations pertaining to public companies. Our management team may not successfully or efficiently manage
our transition to being a public company subject to significant regulatory oversight and reporting obligations
under the federal securities laws and the continuous scrutiny of securities analysts and investors. These new
obligations and constituents will require significant attention from our management and may divert their
attention away from the day-to-day management of our business, which may adversely affect our business,
financial condition, and results of operations.

Risks Related to Privacy, Cybersecurity, and Intellectual Property
The application of certain copyright law doctrines and contractual interpretations of open-
source licenses to modern AI model training are uncertain.
The application of certain copyright law doctrines and contractual interpretations of open-source licenses to
modern AI model training has not been authoritatively resolved by U.S. and non-U.S. courts as of this date. We
have a good faith belief that we own or possess all sufficient legal rights and/or defenses to the training data
used in or with our AI models, platform, and applications, which is based in part on our belief that our use or
acquisition of the training data used in or with our AI models, platform, and applications constitutes “fair use”
of such training data under copyright law doctrine. In addition, copyright laws in some jurisdictions outside the
United States generally do not recognize fair use, and our reliance on analogous exceptions is subject to
evolving conditions and to adverse or unsettled judicial interpretation in those jurisdictions. If a court of law
disagrees with our belief that our use or acquisition of such training data constitutes fair use or otherwise
concludes that it violates copyright law, for example, by adopting the reasoning in Bartz (as defined below),
including without limitation in currently active litigation against us or another company in our industry, our
business may be adversely affected. In particular, adverse rulings in litigation involving other AI developers,
regardless of the specific facts, data practices, or legal theories at issue in those cases, could establish legal
precedents or interpretations of copyright law that apply broadly across the industry and limit our ability to
train, develop, or deploy AI models, even if our own data procurement and usage practices differ. Such
outcomes could restrict access to certain categories of training data, narrow the scope of available legal
defenses, or impose new licensing, compliance, or operational requirements across the AI industry. For
example, if we cannot rely on the fair use doctrine to access copyrighted work for training our models, we may
be required to pay significant fees to obtain a license to such training data or our ability to further develop our
87
Table of Contents
models, platform, and applications and distribute models trained on such data at issue could be adversely
affected. In addition, an adverse ruling against us or another company in our industry could result in injunctive
relief that restricts our ability to use or distribute models trained on the data at issue or could require us to
retrain affected models from scratch at substantial cost. If we are unable to manage the foregoing risks, our
business, financial condition, and results of operations could be adversely affected.
We are subject to complex and evolving laws, regulations, and other legal obligations related
to privacy and data protection, and any actual or perceived failure to comply with such
obligations could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
We are subject to a range of laws and regulations in the EU, the United States, and other jurisdictions, and
other legal obligations relating to privacy, data protection, and the collection, use, transfer, storage, and other
processing of data. These laws, regulations, and other legal obligations vary across jurisdictions, and include
comprehensive frameworks such as the General Data Protection Regulation 2016/679 (“GDPR”), laws that
impose sector-specific obligations, and those that impose specific requirements or restrictions on the handling
of particular types of data, such as personal data that is considered sensitive. These obligations are not
harmonized, continue to evolve in scope, present technical and operational complexities and challenges, and
may conflict or impose overlapping or inconsistent obligations. Further, these laws and regulations, as well as
other laws and regulations not originally enacted to address privacy or data protection, continue to evolve as
they are applied to new technologies, including AI, and may be interpreted or enforced in ways that are
inconsistent, unclear, novel, or subject to significant regulatory discretion. Additionally, plaintiffs, class action
counsel, state Attorneys’ General, and other claimants continue to pursue claims against artificial intelligence
companies relating to data handling, privacy, and cybersecurity; similar disputes could arise against us and they
could take the form of privacy, cybersecurity, breach of contract, tort, or other claims. New or evolving laws,
regulations, regulatory interpretations, claims, and novel or inconsistent application of existing laws and
regulations to us, or our evolving contractual or other legal obligations, including those that arise as we seek to
enter into new markets or product offerings, may require us to modify our models, platform, and applications,
policies, and practices, delay or limit the development or deployment of certain features, increase compliance
and litigation costs, and result in fines or penalties.
Our compliance obligations and expenditures, and our exposure thereunder, may vary depending on both how
customers access and use our models, platform, and applications, including through our first-party offerings or
third-party distribution channels, and on the nature of data processed in connection with those offerings. For
example, our costs and regulatory exposure may vary based on the demands we receive from individuals,
regulators, and other parties seeking to exercise rights under privacy or data protection laws. We may be subject
to additional obligations, restrictions, or exposure in connection with the processing of data that is considered
sensitive under applicable laws. In connection with the development, deployment, and improvement of our
services, including model training, improvement, and inference, we have faced, and may face in the future,
operational errors or claims or assertions that our use or processing of data, such as personal, sensitive, or
confidential data, is inconsistent with our obligations.
Failure to secure data against risks to its confidentiality, integrity, or availability may result in legal obligations,

As we continue to develop and deploy new features, including those incorporating AI, our systems are exposed
to additional or evolving security risks, including those arising from emerging or imperfectly understood AI-
specific threat vectors. Such AI-specific threats include prompt injection attacks that manipulate model
behavior through malicious inputs, attempts to replicate or reverse engineer our proprietary models through
systematic API queries, adversarial inputs designed to cause model failures or misclassifications, malicious
corruption of training data that could compromise model integrity, and vulnerabilities in continuous
integration and deployment pipelines that could allow insiders or other actors to inject malicious code that is
subsequently propagated or amplified through AI-assisted development workflows. Such attacks may be
difficult to detect, may not be addressed by traditional cybersecurity defenses, and may require specialized
expertise, techniques, and infrastructure to mitigate. Further, features that rely on AI may be particularly
susceptible to unanticipated vulnerabilities as both our understanding and the broader market’s understanding
of AI-related security risks and mitigation techniques continue to develop. Our efforts to mitigate the foregoing
risks may result in false positives and our mistakenly limiting or blocking certain users from accessing our
technology, which could result in potential litigation or regulatory action.
In addition, our agentic offerings interact with external tools, APIs, databases, code repositories, and other
third-party systems, creating cybersecurity attack surfaces that are distinct from those applicable to traditional
AI models. An adversary could manipulate the content of an external data source, API response, document, or
web page processed by an agent to cause the agent to take harmful or unauthorized actions based on that
manipulated input. An attacker could also attempt to compromise an active agent session and redirect the agent
to perform malicious actions using the customer’s authenticated credentials and permissions. Because our
agentic offerings are designed to take autonomous actions with real-world consequences, including executing
code, modifying files, sending communications, and completing transactions, a successful exploitation of these
agentic attack surfaces could result in data exfiltration, unauthorized transactions, code injection, or other
adverse effects, potentially across multiple customer deployments simultaneously. Traditional cybersecurity
defenses, including firewalls, input validation, and access controls, may not be fully effective against these novel
threat vectors, and the security community’s understanding of agentic-specific attack surfaces is still
developing.

result in service disruptions, degraded performance, unintended or harmful outputs, or the unauthorized

networks, systems, and data of our customers. In addition, incidents impacting our customers may be caused by

Cyberattacks, including cyberattacks directed at our networks, our customers’ networks, or the networks of

unauthorized access to our systems or those of our customers, partners, or vendors.
Failures in our internal systems or controls, security breaches, failures to comply with our privacy or data
protection commitments, or other incidents, whether resulting from malicious activity, human error, or system
limitations, could adversely affect our reputation, brand, and business and impair our ability to attract and
retain customers. Our offices and the data centers that host our infrastructure, many of which are operated by
third parties, are also exposed to physical threats as well as failures by the operators of those facilities. A
physical intrusion could damage equipment, interrupt our services, or provide a path to our systems and data,
including our model weights, that bypasses our network defenses.
Although we have dedicated significant resources designed to identify and address these security risks, we
cannot guarantee that our security measures will be effective or that our recovery protocols, backup, and other
systems will be sufficient. Even where we detect an incident, our response may prove inadequate, including if
we misjudge its severity, respond too slowly, or fail to fully remediate the underlying cause. In addition,
incidents that appear minor when they occur may later prove significant when considered together with other
incidents or with information learned afterward, and a series of related incidents, none of which is material on
its own, could prove material in the aggregate. We continue to devote significant resources to protect against
security breaches and other incidents, and we may need to devote significant resources in the future to mitigate
and address problems caused by breaches and other incidents, which may divert resources from the growth and
expansion of our business.
Any actual or perceived security breach or other incident experienced by us or third parties with whom we do
business, particularly our CSPs, could damage our reputation and brand, cause our business to suffer, require
us to expend significant capital and other resources, cause us to incur increasing costs, including costs to deploy
additional personnel and protection technologies, train employees, and engage third-party experts and
consultants, expose us to litigation or regulatory action, cause us to violate applicable privacy, data protection,
security, and other laws and regulations, subject us to adverse publicity and a loss of confidence in our security
measures, and cause us to incur significant fines, penalties, and other liability exposure, which could adversely
affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. We have taken steps to limit our liability for
certain incidents, for example through warranty disclaimers and limitations of liability in our terms of service,
but those contractual protections may not be upheld, or may not apply to certain claims, or may otherwise be
insufficient to limit our liability exposure under applicable law.
In the EU, we face increasingly stringent regulatory reporting obligations for cybersecurity and AI-related
incidents. Under the GDPR, we must notify the competent regulators about incidents that involve personal data
and are likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of individuals. Similarly, the EU Network and
Information Security Directive 2022/2555 (“NIS2”) requires us to notify the competent authorities of any
significant cybersecurity incident through a staged process. In addition, the EU AI Act requires providers of
general-purpose AI models with systemic risk to keep track of, document, and report serious incidents without
undue delay to the AI Office and competent authorities. Going forward, providers and deployers of high-risk AI
systems, as defined under the EU AI Act, will also have to report serious incidents or malfunctions without
undue delay in certain circumstances.
In the United States, companies are increasingly subject to analogous incident reporting obligations, including
under federal and state data breach notification laws, such as the New York Stop Hacks and Improve Electronic
Data Security (SHIELD) Act. In addition, certain U.S. states have adopted incident reporting laws specific to
frontier model providers, such as the New York Responsible AI Safety and Education Act (RAISE Act) and the
California Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act. These frameworks create heightened compliance
and liability exposure in case of delayed, incomplete, or inaccurate incident disclosures.

We employ automated data collection across the web and use other methods to collect data for
training our AI models, and such activities may subject us to liability or limit our ability to

We collect and use various data sources to train our AI models, including publicly available information from
the internet, datasets licensed or commissioned from third parties, and synthetic data generated by our own
models. We use such data across the stages of model development, including pre-training and post-training. To
collect publicly available information, we utilize web scraping or web crawling techniques, book scanning, and
other methods. While we take steps designed to ensure that our activities comply with applicable law,
applicable robots.txt notices, and relevant technical measures such as paywalls or logins, our efforts may not
always be successful. Further, we may not be able to verify whether information collected using such techniques
is protected under privacy, copyright, or other intellectual property laws in certain cases, and our use of any
such protected information may subject us to additional liability for intellectual property infringement or
privacy violations. More broadly, inadequate documentation of training data sources, provenance, or chain of
custody could create legal exposure, complicate our ability to respond to regulatory inquiries or litigation
discovery requests, or raise concerns during due diligence by investors, partners, or potential acquirers that
could adversely affect our strategic transactions or business relationships.
Our data collection activities have in the past resulted, are presently the subject of, and may in the future result
in litigation or other actions filed or instituted against us, alleging that our scraping, web crawling, and other
techniques to collect data violate the law. For example, Reddit, Inc. has filed suit against us, captioned
Reddit,

We incorporate open-source software in our models, platform, and applications, which may
subject us to litigation or other requirements, each of which may adversely affect our

A portion of the technologies we use in our models, platform, and applications incorporates open-source
software, and we may incorporate open-source software in our models, platform, and applications in the future.
From time to time, companies that use third-party open-source software have faced claims challenging the use
of such open-source software and their compliance with the terms of the applicable open-source license. We
may be subject to suits by parties claiming ownership of what we believe to be open-source software or claiming
non-compliance with the applicable open-source licensing terms. Some open-source licenses require end-users
who distribute or make available across a network software that includes open-source software to make
available all or part of such software (which may include valuable proprietary code), at no cost, or license such
software under the terms of the particular open-source license. While we employ practices designed to help
ensure our compliance with the licenses of third-party open-source software and protect our valuable
proprietary source code, we may inadvertently use third-party open-source software in a manner that exposes
us to claims of non-compliance with the applicable terms of such license, including claims for infringement of
intellectual property rights or for breach of contract. These risks may be heightened by our use of our own AI
tools, including Claude Code, in our software development processes, as AI-generated code could incorporate or
reproduce open-source software such that the associated license obligations, including copyleft requirements to
disclose or license proprietary source code, apply to us without our knowledge. Similar concerns regarding AI-
generated code could also lead enterprise customers to limit their use of our products. Further, there is an
increasing number of open-source software license types, almost none of which have been tested in a court of
law, resulting in a dearth of judicial guidance regarding the proper legal interpretation of such license types. If a
third party makes a claim against us alleging that we have not complied with the conditions of the applicable
open-source license, we could incur significant legal expenses defending against such allegations, expend
substantial time and resources to re-engineer some or all of our software, and could be subject to significant
damages, enjoined from the sale of our models, platform, and applications that contained the open-source
software, and required to comply with the conditions of the open-source license, which may include the public
release of certain portions of our proprietary source code, each of which may have an adverse impact on our
business, financial condition, and results of operations.
In addition to risks related to license requirements, use of open-source software can lead to greater risks than
use of third-party commercial software because open-source licensors generally do not provide warranties or
other contractual protections regarding misappropriation, misuse, infringement, ownership, misattribution, or
other violations, the quality of the code, or the origin of the open-source software. Many of the risks associated
with the use of open-source software cannot be eliminated and may adversely affect our business, financial
condition, and results of operations. For instance, open-source software is developed by programmers beyond
our control and may have security vulnerabilities, defects, or errors of which we may not be aware. Even if we
become aware of any such vulnerabilities, defects, or errors, it may take a significant amount of time for either
us or the relevant programmers to address such vulnerabilities, defects, or errors. Such a delay may negatively
impact our models, platform, and applications, including by adversely affecting the market’s perception of our
models, platform, and applications, impairing the functionality of our models, platform, and applications, or
delaying the launch of new features or functionality on our models, platform, and applications, any of which
may adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Risks Related to Legal and Regulatory Matters
We are subject to claims, lawsuits, investigations, executive and administrative orders and
directives, other regulatory actions, and various actions and proceedings, and face potential
liability, expenses for legal claims, and harm to our business.
We are subject to claims, lawsuits, arbitration proceedings, government inquiries and investigations, executive
and administrative orders and directives, and other legal, regulatory, and administrative actions and
proceedings, including those involving intellectual property disputes, compliance with regulatory requirements,
government approvals and authorizations, labor and employment, anti-discrimination, commercial disputes,
competition, privacy, consumer protection, customer complaints, advertising, and other matters relating to our
technology, models, platform, and applications, and we may become subject to additional types of claims,
lawsuits, arbitration proceedings, government inquiries and investigations, executive and administrative orders
and directives, and other legal, regulatory, and administrative actions and proceedings as our business grows
and as we deploy new technologies, models, platforms, and applications. In particular, as our models, platform,
and applications increasingly include agentic AI systems capable of taking autonomous actions with real-world
consequences, we may face novel legal theories of liability, including intellectual property infringement,
product liability, agency, and negligence claims, that have not been tested in the context of autonomous AI
systems and for which the scope of our potential exposure is uncertain.
In addition, as we expand our
healthcare and life sciences offerings, regulators may conclude that certain of our products, or our customers’
use of them, are subject to healthcare regulation or to other laws governing healthcare and health information,
which could require us to obtain authorizations, modify or restrict our offerings, or incur significant compliance
costs. Errors or other undesirable outputs from our models in these contexts could contribute to patient harm,
compromised research, or regulatory failures by our customers, and could expose us to claims from customers,
patients, and other third parties, as well as to regulatory inquiries and enforcement actions.
We are also subject to antitrust and competition law risk arising from our public advocacy regarding AI safety
and the responsible pace of AI development and from our participation in industry groups, safety
collaborations, and standard-setting initiatives. Communications, advocacy, or collaboration among companies
that develop frontier AI models, or conduct alleged to reflect coordination among such companies, may be
characterized as concerted action subject to the antitrust and competition laws, including Section 1 of the
Sherman Act and analogous state and non-U.S. laws, even where undertaken for safety purposes, conducted
publicly, or intended as advocacy for governmental action or industry standards. In September 2026, a putative
class action was filed against us and other developers of frontier AI models in the U.S. District Court for the
Northern District of California, alleging that we and the other defendants agreed to restrain competition by
slowing the pace at which we develop and improve our respective AI models, in purported violation of Section 1
of the Sherman Act. The complaint seeks treble damages, injunctive relief, and other relief on behalf of a
purported class of purchasers of the defendants’ paid consumer subscriptions. We disagree with the claims and
intend to defend the matter vigorously, but the outcome of this and any similar proceeding is inherently
uncertain.
Antitrust litigation can be complex, protracted, disruptive, and expensive, and an adverse outcome could result
in treble damages and injunctive relief. We could also become subject to additional private litigation or to
investigations or enforcement actions by the U.S. Department of Justice, the FTC, state attorneys general, or
non-U.S. competition authorities. We have proposed public efforts to work with the U.S. government and other
developers of frontier AI models to establish safety standards, including with respect to the pace of capability
development, and have suggested that such collaboration may warrant a narrow exemption or safe harbor from
antitrust laws. These proposals have drawn public opposition from political leaders, some of whom have
characterized such efforts as anticompetitive regardless of the purpose of such exemption or safe harbor. There
is no assurance that any such exemption or safe harbor will be adopted. Our advocacy for such an exemption,
and any safety commitments we pursue with other developers of frontier AI in its absence, could subject us to
additional regulatory, litigation, and other risks. These risks may cause us to limit or modify our public
advocacy, our participation in industry safety and standard-setting initiatives, and our communications with

Our models, platform, and applications are subject to U.S. export controls, and our current or future models,

license. However, some exports may require us to obtain authorization from the cognizant government agency.

extend to additional models or capabilities. In addition, future updates to our safeguards or other remedial

timeline or at all. The restrictions imposed in June 2026 and potential restrictions in the future may also limit
our ability to recruit talent, to fully utilize our existing workforce, to continue to improve our models, and to

A portion of our customers authorize us to bill their credit card accounts through our third-party payment
processing partners for our paid subscriptions. We have experienced, and expect to continue to experience,

unauthorized payment credentials, which has resulted, and may in the future result, in losses, including
payment processing fees, chargeback fees, and fines and penalties imposed by our payment processors or card
networks, for which we may not be reimbursed. We maintain fraud-detection and identity-verification
measures, but these measures have not identified, and may not identify, all such activity. Further, our
customers provide us with credit card billing information online, and we do not verify the physical identity of
cardholders or conduct additional verification beyond what we collect online, which increases our risk of
exposure to fraudulent activity.

Risks Related to Tax and Accounting Matters
Changes in tax laws or regulations could be enacted, or existing tax laws or regulations could
be applied to us or our customers in a manner that could increase the costs of our models,
platform, and applications and adversely affect our business.
We operate in multiple jurisdictions and are subject to tax laws and regulations of U.S. federal, state, and local
and non-U.S. governments. Income, sales, use, or other tax laws, statutes, rules, regulations, or ordinances
could be enacted or amended at any time (possibly with retroactive effect) and could be applied solely or
disproportionately to models, platforms, and applications provided over the internet. These enactments or
amendments could reduce our sales activity due to the inherent cost increase the taxes would represent and
ultimately harm our results of operations and cash flows. Further, the application of U.S. federal, state, local,
and non-U.S. tax laws to services provided electronically is unclear and continuously evolving. Existing tax
laws, statutes, rules, regulations, or ordinances could be interpreted or applied adversely to us, possibly with
retroactive effect, which could require us or our customers to pay additional tax amounts, as well as fines or
penalties, and interest for past amounts. If we are unsuccessful in collecting such taxes due from our customers,
we would be held liable for such costs, thereby adversely affecting our results of operations and harming our
business.
As we expand the scale of our non-U.S. business activities, any changes in the U.S. or non-U.S. taxation of such
activities may increase our worldwide effective tax rate and harm our business, financial condition, and results
of operations. We may be subject to taxation in several jurisdictions around the world with increasingly
complex tax laws, the application of which can be uncertain. In addition, our hiring of personnel and
engagement of third-party employer-of-record providers in non-U.S. jurisdictions, as well as our data center
and other infrastructure activities outside the United States, have created, and may in the future create,
permanent establishments or other taxable presence in those jurisdictions, which could subject us to additional
income, withholding, and indirect taxes, as well as interest, penalties, and additional compliance obligations. In
advance of forming and obtaining approvals for local operating entities, we have entered into, and expect to
enter into additional letters of intent, leases, and other agreements relating to our international compute and
infrastructure activities through interim contracting arrangements with existing entities, and we may be unable
to transfer these arrangements to local entities on a timely basis or at all. Any prolonged reliance on these
interim arrangements, or any failure to migrate them to local entities, could increase our exposure to
permanent establishment or other taxable-presence determinations and could result in non-recoverable value-
added or similar indirect taxes, which could be material in certain jurisdictions.
Although we have not been
required to pay income taxes, other than in immaterial amounts in certain jurisdictions to date,
