Our ability to use our net operating loss carryforwards and certain other tax attributes may
be limited.
We have incurred substantial net operating losses (“NOLs”) during our history. In general, under Sections 382
and 383 of the Internal Revenue Code of 1986, as amended (the “Code”), a corporation that undergoes an
“ownership change” is subject to annual limitations on its ability to utilize its pre-change U.S. federal
NOL
carryforwards and certain other tax attributes, including tax credit carryforwards, to offset its future taxable
income or tax liabilities. For these purposes, an ownership change generally occurs if the percentage of a
corporation’s stock (by value) owned by one or more “5-percent shareholders” increases by more than 50
percentage points over a rolling three-year period. We have experienced ownership changes in the past, and we
may experience ownership changes in the future, including as a result of this offering or subsequent shifts in
our stock ownership, some of which may be outside our control. NOLs and other tax attributes of companies we
have acquired are, and of companies we may acquire may be, subject to similar limitations. Similar provisions
of state tax law and the tax laws of non-U.S. jurisdictions may also limit our ability to utilize state and non-U.S.
NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes. In addition, certain states, including California, have suspended or
otherwise limited the use of NOL carryforwards and other tax attributes, which could accelerate or permanently
increase our state income tax liabilities. Separately, under current law, U.S. federal NOLs arising in taxable
years beginning after December 31, 2017 may be used to offset only 80% of taxable income in any year, whether
or not an ownership change occurs. As a result of the foregoing, even if we attain profitability, we may be unable
to use all or a material portion of our NOLs and other tax attributes, which could adversely affect our future
cash flows and results of operations.
Our corporate structure and intercompany arrangements are subject to the tax laws of
multiple jurisdictions, and we could be required to pay additional taxes, which could
adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
As we continue to expand our non-U.S. operations, we are, and may increasingly be, required to report taxable
income in various jurisdictions around the world based on our business activities in those jurisdictions. Our
corporate structure and associated transfer pricing policies reflect the functions, risks, and assets of the entities
involved in our intercompany transactions. However, our tax position is subject to various risks, including

existing tax laws and policies by taxing authorities or courts, any of which could increase our overall tax
obligations.
Our intercompany transactions are subject to complex transfer pricing rules administered by tax authorities in

Risks Related to our Governance Structure
Our capital stock structure features certain provisions that are novel or otherwise not
common among other corporations with multiple-class structures, and may effectively
eliminate the ability of holders of our Class A common stock to influence important decisions,
including a change in control.
We have a novel capital and corporate governance structure that has no direct public company precedent. We
are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law. As a PBC, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of
our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose
identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation. In addition, the LTBT possesses certain
rights that are designed to help ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly balances our goals as
a PBC. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to
elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our
board of directors. See the section titled “Our Governance Structure and Its Goals—Long-Term Benefit Trust—
Election and Removal of Directors” for more information. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent
body of five financially disinterested Trustees, and our Class T common stock has no economic rights. As a
result, the LTBT may have interests that differ from yours, and it may exercise its power in a way with which
108
Table of Contents
you disagree or in a way that may be adverse to your interests. Immediately prior to the completion of this
offering, we will also issue a single share of Class F common stock, a special class of our common stock, to the
Founder LLC. Our Class F common stock will be entitled to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of
the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to
matters submitted to stockholders generally, including the election of our directors other than the Class T
directors. Upon the completion of this offering, we will also authorize a special class of our common stock, Class
E common stock, which we will issue to our employees, excluding our co-founders. Our Class E common stock
will be entitled to vote only on certain limited matters and will not have any economic rights. Under this
governance structure, we expect that the LTBT and the Founder LLC will collectively have the ability to elect all
members of our board of directors, and the Founder LLC will have the ability to determine the outcome of all
matters submitted to a vote of our stockholders generally for the foreseeable future. Accordingly, holders of our
Class A common stock generally will not be able to affect the outcome of any matter submitted to a vote of our
stockholders or the election of our directors, regardless of how they vote, unless a majority of the Continuing
Founders (as defined below) cannot agree on how our Class F common stock will be voted (in which case our
Class F common stock will generally be voted proportionately with the votes of our Class A common stock cast
on the matter).
Our governance structure is likely to have the effect of limiting the likelihood of an unsolicited merger proposal,
unsolicited tender offer, or proxy contest for the removal of directors. As a result, our governance structure may
make it more difficult to replace our directors and management and may have the effect of depriving our
stockholders of an opportunity to sell their shares at a premium over prevailing market prices.
We cannot predict whether our structure will result in lower demand for our Class A common stock, increased
volatility, adverse publicity, or other adverse consequences. In particular, the absence of judicial precedent
interpreting this structure increases the risk and unpredictability of governance-related litigation, and courts
may interpret the obligations inherent in our structure in ways that we might not anticipate.
Our capital structure will concentrate voting power with the LTBT and the Founder LLC for
the foreseeable future and will result in the LTBT and the Founder LLC having voting power
that is not derived from or proportionate to economic interests in our company.
Our Class T common stock will generally entitle the LTBT to elect and remove the Class T directors, who
together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common
stock will remain outstanding indefinitely, subject to the right of our board of directors and the Trustees or
specified majorities of our Class A common stock, Class E common stock, and Class F common stock to amend
or terminate the terms of the LTBT or the rights of our Class T common stock or to redeem our Class T common
stock (such time as no share of Class T common stock is outstanding, the “Class T Sunset Time”).
The Class T
common stock may also be transferred without restriction upon the receipt of the same approvals required to
amend, terminate, or redeem it. We intentionally structured the Class T common stock in this manner to
preserve long-term flexibility if circumstances change. If the Class T common stock were transferred to a person
or entity that is not affiliated with the LTBT or is not otherwise required to consider the Company Purpose, for
so long as we remain a PBC, all of our directors, regardless of how they are elected, would continue to be
obligated to act in accordance with Delaware law and our certificate of incorporation, bylaws, and other
governing documents as then in effect, including those provisions relating to our public benefit purpose.
The
Trust Agreement (as defined below) limits Trustee compensation to a reasonable cash amount fixed annually by
the Trustees. Trustee compensation will not vary with or be conditioned upon the profits or any action or
inaction of our company. The policies of the LTBT prohibit a Trustee from directly purchasing or holding any of
our securities.
Our Class F common stock will entitle the Founder LLC to an aggregate number of votes that equals 50.1% of
the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as of the applicable record date with respect to

redemption thereof agreed to by a Supermajority (as defined below) of the Continuing Founders or upon the

The voting power of the LTBT and the Founder LLC are not derived from or proportionate to economic

stock by our individual co-founders. For additional information about the circumstances in which our Class T

Our governance structure and the adoption of our amended and restated certificate of

We operate as a Delaware public benefit corporation. As a public benefit corporation, we
cannot provide any assurance that we will achieve our Company Purpose.
As a PBC, we are intended to produce a public benefit or benefits and to operate in a responsible and
sustainable manner, balancing our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially
affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of
incorporation. We cannot assure you that we will achieve our Company Purpose or that the expected positive
impact from being a PBC will be realized, which could adversely affect our reputation, business, financial
condition, and results of operations. As a PBC, we are required, under Section 366 of the Delaware General
Corporation Law (“DGCL”) and pursuant to our amended and restated bylaws, to disclose to stockholders a
report at least biennially on our overall performance in promoting the public benefit identified in our amended
and restated certificate of incorporation and the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct and
on our assessment of our success in achieving our Company Purpose and in promoting those interests. If we are
not timely or are unable to provide this report, or if the report is not viewed favorably by parties doing business
with us, regulators, others reviewing our credentials, or other stakeholders, including holders of our Class A
common stock, our reputation as a PBC may be adversely affected.
Our focus on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our
directors to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those
stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose, may conflict
with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business performance, which may
negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock.
We have made, and may in the future make, decisions that we believe balance the pecuniary interests of our
stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose set forth
in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, even if such decisions may negatively impact the
short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business, financial condition, and results of operations or the
short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our Class A common stock. This may impact the value of our
Class A common stock and make owning our Class A common stock less appealing to investors who are focused
on returns. Our decisions and actions in pursuit of long-term success may not result in the long-term benefits
we expect, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations, as well as
the market price of our Class A common stock. Such decisions and actions may include changes to our models,
platform, and applications; limitations on certain uses of our models, platform, and applications; moderating
the pace of the development of our models for safety-related reasons; adjustments to the timing of new
offerings; changes in how we deliver customer support; investments in our relationships with partners and
employees; investments in and introductions of new models, platforms, and applications; investments in social
impact initiatives consistent with our public benefit objectives; and changes in our approach to working with
local or national jurisdictions on laws and regulations governing our business.
Our policies, including those on usage, currently prohibit, or may be revised in the future to prohibit, certain
usage or other actions, which may have adverse commercial consequences to us. For example, our usage policy
prohibits the use of our models, platform, and applications to develop or operate fully autonomous weapons or
to conduct mass surveillance, including mass domestic surveillance, and we have declined to permit such uses
based on our Company Purpose, notwithstanding the revenue those or similar uses could generate. Maintaining
these limitations has had, and may continue to have, adverse commercial and financial consequences. We have
also restricted or delayed the availability of certain capabilities for safety reasons. For example, we initially
released our Mythos model only as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing rather than making it
broadly available to the public. Similarly, we have chosen not to develop certain commercially attractive
offerings, such as image and video generation models, in order to direct our compute toward our research and
safety priorities. Our public advocacy, and the decisions we make to moderate the pace of AI development,
delay or restrict the release of models or features, or forgo commercial opportunities for safety-related reasons,
may not maximize stockholder value, could have a negative impact on the value of our Class A common stock,
and could result in litigation. Each of these decisions reflects our directors’ balancing of the pecuniary interests
of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose.

Table of Contents
While we believe these decisions are consistent with the Company Purpose, as a result of these decisions, we
may forgo revenue, customers, or growth opportunities that a corporation managed solely to maximize
stockholder value might pursue.
Further, while directors of traditional corporations typically have a fiduciary duty to focus on maximizing
stockholder value, directors of a PBC have a duty to consider not only the stockholders’ financial interests but
also the company’s specific public benefit purpose and the best interests of those stakeholders materially
affected by the company’s actions. Thus, our directors are not merely permitted, but obligated, to consider our
Company Purpose and the interests of other stakeholders. Under Delaware law, directors are shielded from
liability for breach of these obligations if they make informed and disinterested decisions that serve a rational
purpose. In the event of a conflict among the interests of our stockholders, our Company Purpose or the
interests of our other stakeholders, our directors must only make informed and disinterested decisions that
serve a rational purpose; thus, we cannot guarantee that such a conflict would be resolved in favor of our
stockholders’ monetary interests, which could adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of
operations and cause the market price of our Class A common stock to decline. In addition, there is very limited
judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to PBCs under Delaware law, particularly
for companies with significant scale or visibility, or with a scope of PBC purpose similar to ours. As a result, the
scope of directors’ obligations, the standards by which their decisions may be reviewed, and the nature and
availability of stockholder remedies in connection with alleged failures to responsibly balance these interests
remain uncertain. Future judicial interpretations of these provisions could be more expansive than we currently
anticipate and could result in increased litigation risk, greater scrutiny of board decision-making, or outcomes
that differ from our expectations.
Additionally, as a PBC, we are less vulnerable to an unsolicited takeover effort than a traditional company
would be and, therefore, your ability to realize your investment through an acquisition may be limited. We may
also not be an attractive target for activists or hedge fund investors because new directors must consider and
give appropriate weight to the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially
affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose, and stockholders may be able to enforce this obligation
through litigation. Further, by requiring that our board of directors consider additional stakeholders and our
Company Purpose, and not just maximizing stockholder value, Delaware law could make it easier for our board
of directors to reject a hostile bid, even where the acceptance of such a bid would provide the greatest short-
term financial yield to investors.
In addition, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources toward our public benefit initiatives,
which may include contributions to nonprofit organizations, research institutions, underserved communities,
and other third parties that may not otherwise have access to frontier AI capabilities. These initiatives, which
include the Initial Public Benefit Issuance and the future Public Benefit Issuances, have been, and may continue
to be, substantial in scale, and we expect to significantly grow these efforts over time. The benefits of such
expenditures may be difficult or impossible to measure in financial terms and may not result in any direct or
measurable benefit to our business or our stockholders. The amount of resources directed toward these
initiatives may, in any given period, reduce our revenue, increase our expenses, and could otherwise affect our
results of operations.
As a Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation
concerning our board of directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary
interests, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct and our Company
Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our business, financial
condition, and results of operations.
Section 367 of the DGCL provides that stockholders of a Delaware PBC with shares listed on a national
securities exchange may only file an action to enforce the statutory balancing requirement imposed on the
board of directors by the DGCL if they, individually or collectively, own the lesser of at least two percent of the
corporation’s outstanding shares or shares of the corporation with a market value of at least $2,000,000 as of
the date the action is instituted and, in the case of a derivative action, such stockholders satisfy any other
conditions applicable to filing a derivative action. This potential liability for enforcement of the statutory
balancing requirement does not exist for traditional corporations. Therefore, we may be subject to the
possibility of increased litigation, which would require the attention of our management, and, as a result, may
adversely affect our management’s ability to effectively execute our strategy. There is limited judicial precedent
112
Table of Contents
for this type of balancing litigation, which may create uncertainty around the scope of our directors’ obligations
or the remedies available to stockholders. Additionally, any such litigation may be costly, which may adversely
affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations.
Our amended and restated bylaws will designate a state or federal court located within the
State of Delaware as the exclusive forum for substantially all disputes between us and our
stockholders, and also provide that the federal district courts will be the exclusive forum for
resolving any complaint asserting a cause of action arising under the Securities Act of 1933, as
amended, each of which may limit our stockholders’ ability to choose the judicial forum for
disputes with us or our directors, officers, stockholders, or employees.
Our amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to the completion of this
offering, will provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the Court of
Chancery of the State of Delaware (or, if the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware does not have
jurisdiction, another State court in Delaware or the federal district court for the District of Delaware) will, to the
fullest extent permitted by law, be the sole and exclusive forum for (i) any derivative action or proceeding
brought on our behalf, (ii) any action asserting a claim of breach of a fiduciary duty owed by any of our current
or former directors, stockholders, or officers or other employees to us or our stockholders, (iii) any action
arising pursuant to any provision of the DGCL, or as to which the DGCL confers jurisdiction upon the Court of
Chancery of the State of Delaware, (iv) any action arising pursuant to or to interpret, apply, enforce or
determine the validity of our amended and restated certificate of incorporation, or our amended and restated
bylaws, or (v) any action asserting a claim governed by the internal affairs doctrine, except for, in all cases, any
claim as to which such court determines that there is an indispensable party not subject to the jurisdiction of
such court (and the indispensable party does not consent to the personal jurisdiction of such court within 10
days following such determination).
Section 22 of the Securities Act of 1933, as amended (the “Securities Act”), establishes concurrent jurisdiction
for federal and state courts over Securities Act claims. Accordingly, both state and federal courts have
jurisdiction to hear such claims. To prevent having to litigate claims in multiple jurisdictions and the threat of
inconsistent or contrary rulings by different courts, among other considerations, our amended and restated
bylaws will also provide that, unless we consent in writing to the selection of an alternative forum, the federal
district courts of the United States will, to the fullest extent permitted by applicable law, be the sole and
exclusive forum for resolving any complaint asserting a cause or causes of action arising under the Securities
Act against any person in connection with any offering of our securities, including, without limitation, any
auditor, underwriter, expert, control person, or other defendant. Unless we consent in writing to the selection of
an alternative forum, the United States District Court for the District of Delaware will, to the fullest extent
permitted by applicable law, be the sole and exclusive forum for the resolution of any derivative action or
proceeding brought to enforce any duty or liability created by the Exchange Act or the rules or regulations
thereunder. All other claims arising under the Exchange Act may be brought in any federal court of competent
jurisdiction.
Any person or entity purchasing, holding, or otherwise acquiring any interest in any of our securities shall be
deemed to have notice of and consented to the foregoing bylaw provisions. Although we believe these exclusive
forum provisions benefit us by providing increased consistency in the application of Delaware law and federal
securities laws in the types of lawsuits to which each applies, the exclusive forum provisions may limit a
stockholder’s ability to bring a claim in a judicial forum of its choosing for disputes with us or our current or
former directors, officers, stockholders, or other employees, which may discourage lawsuits with respect to such
claims against us and our current and former directors, officers, stockholders, or other employees. Our
stockholders will not be deemed to have waived our compliance with the federal securities laws and the rules
and regulations thereunder as a result of our exclusive forum provisions.

Although our Class N common stock is not entitled to vote, it is entitled to economic rights equivalent to those
of our Class A common stock, including the right to participate ratably with our Class A common stock in any
dividends we may declare and in distributions upon a liquidation, dissolution, or winding-up. As a result, the
shares of Class N common stock issued in connection with the completion of this offering as a result of the
Preferred Stock Conversion and Convertible Notes Conversion will dilute the economic interests, including any
dividends and any proceeds available for distribution to stockholders, of the holders of our Class A common
stock, and such shares are included together with our Class A common stock in determining net tangible book
value per share. See the section titled “Dilution.”
The shares of Class N common stock will automatically convert into an equal number of shares of Class A
common stock upon a transfer effected through: (i) a registered offering or an open market sale of such shares
or (ii) a transfer to an unaffiliated third party, subject to certain limitations described in the section titled
“Description of Capital Stock.” While held as Class N common stock, these shares are non-voting and therefore
do not impact the voting power of the holders of our Class A common stock. Upon the conversion of shares of
Class N common stock into Class A common stock, however, the resulting shares of Class A common stock will
be entitled to one vote per share and the issuance of such shares will dilute the voting power of the existing
holders of our Class A common stock. Any shares of Class N common stock that we issue in the future would
have the same effect, diluting the economic interests of the holders of our Class A common stock while
outstanding, as well as diluting their voting power upon conversion into Class A common stock.
Future issuances of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock will not dilute the
voting power of our Class F common stock.
Future issuances of our Class A common stock, including upon conversion of our Class N common stock, and
our Class N common stock will not dilute the voting power of our Class F common stock because our Class F
common stock is entitled to a fixed 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as
of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally. For example, if we
were to issue 1,000,000 additional shares of Class A common stock, our Class F common stock would
automatically be entitled to an incremental number of votes sufficient to cause the aggregate voting power of
our Class F common stock to equal 50.1% of the total voting power of our outstanding shares of capital stock as
of the applicable record date with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally, or approximately
1,004,008 additional votes. Any future issuances of additional shares of Class A common stock, including upon
conversion of our Class N common stock, and Class N common stock will not be subject to approval by our
stockholders except as required by the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market.
Future sales of our Class A common stock in the public market could cause the market price of
our Class A common stock to decline.

aforementioned third parties and by us.
Certain estimates in this prospectus regarding global knowledge workers’ wages, which we refer to as the
annual economic value represented by global knowledge workers, are our own, derived from third-party data.
Based on wage data for U.S. workers by occupation classification from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics in
2025, we calculate the total salary for the subset of workers that we believe to represent knowledge workers.
Based on International Labor Organization data for global labor income as a percentage of global GDP, and
based on 2025 global GDP, we estimate a 2025 global wages figure. We calculate the ratio of total U.S. wages in
2025 to the 2025 global wages figure, and apply that ratio to the total U.S. knowledge workers’ wages figure to
arrive at an estimate of global knowledge workers’ wages.

Dividend Policy
We have never declared or paid any cash dividends on our capital stock. We currently intend to retain all

be made at the discretion of our board of directors, subject to applicable laws, and will depend on a number of

terms of the A&R Credit Agreement place certain limitations on the amount of cash dividends we can pay, even

Dilution
If you invest in our Class A common stock in this offering, your ownership interest will be diluted to the extent
of the difference between the initial public offering price per share of our Class A common stock and the pro
forma as adjusted net tangible book value per share of our Class A common stock and Class N common stock
immediately after this offering. Net tangible book value dilution per share to new investors represents the
difference between the amount per share paid by purchasers of shares of our Class A common stock in this
offering and the pro forma as adjusted net tangible book value per share of our Class A common stock and Class
N common stock immediately after completion of this offering.
Net tangible book value per share is determined by dividing our total tangible assets less our total liabilities and
redeemable convertible preferred stock by the number of shares of our Class A common stock and Class N
common stock outstanding; because our Class T common stock, Class F common stock, and Class E common
stock have no economic rights, they are excluded from the per share calculation.

The following discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations should be read in
conjunction with the section titled “Summary Consolidated Financial and Other Data” and the consolidated
financial statements and related notes thereto included elsewhere in this prospectus. This discussion contains
forward-looking statements that involve risks and uncertainties. Factors that could cause or contribute to
such differences include those identified below and those discussed elsewhere in this prospectus, particularly
in the sections titled “Risk Factors” and “Special Note Regarding Forward-looking Statements.” Financial
data as of and for the years ended December 31, 2023, 2024, and 2025 have been derived from our audited
consolidated financial statements appearing at the end of this prospectus. Our historical results are not
necessarily indicative of the results that may be expected for any period in the future.
Overview
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define
AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is
the responsible development and maintenance of
advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity
. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and
culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the
core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier AI and shape
the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier AI, Claude, is delivered to customers
through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest
enterprise adoption
of any
technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of
2023 to $
for the three months
ended
September 30, 2026.
Our
Financial Model
Our financial model is built on four primary drivers that define the trajectory of our results:
•
Adoption of Claude
.
The advancing intelligence and capabilities of each successive version of a
Claude model drive the diffusion of Claude across the global economy. As new customers adopt Claude
and existing customers expand their usage into new workflows, our revenue grows.
•
Compute Efficiency
.
We are focused on increasing the intelligence produced and revenue generated
per dollar of compute invested and have delivered significant efficiency improvements.
•
Operating Efficiency
.
Our high talent density, efficient go-to-market, and how extensively our
teams leverage Claude in their work help to drive improved operating margin, Adjusted Operating
Margin, and revenue per employee.
•
Compute Investments
.
Investing in compute is critical to support our long-term growth, and we
intend to continue making substantial investments in compute.
The drivers of our financial model materialize on different timelines. The adoption of Claude and associated
revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency have each increased rapidly over time. Compute is
procured and committed in advance and the expense is incurred as it is brought online and added to our
fungible pool, often in large, discrete steps. The fungible pool can support all workloads dynamically, including
research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. As a result, there is a lag
between when investment is committed and when the full revenue associated with such investment is realized.
This dynamic has produced a financial model in which our operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin
for the nine months ended September 30, 2026 have expanded significantly year over year. As significant
incremental compute is brought online in future periods, the associated expense will be recognized in advance
of the full revenue that the compute will ultimately support, and we expect operating margin and Adjusted
Operating Margin may compress in those periods. At our current stage, this cycle is an inherent aspect of our
134
Table of Contents
business and will cause operating margins to fluctuate from period to period, at times meaningfully, even if the
underlying economics of the business continue to improve.
In addition, the majority of our compute is contracted under multi-year commitments that we typically procure
12 to 18 months in advance of availability. When customer demand or research needs exceed this long-term
capacity, we procure short-term compute, which typically carries a higher cost per unit of compute. We expect
our use of short-term compute to increase in the near term and to in turn compress our operating margin and
Adjusted Operating Margin as a result.
Adoption of Claude
Each successive version of a Claude model is designed to advance the frontier with capabilities that customers
value most, including coding, agentic workflows, computer use, and complex reasoning, which unlock new
categories of use and drive compounding demand from new and existing customers. Claude’s intelligence is a
primary driver of its diffusion and our revenue growth: because Claude leads at the AI frontier, customers
rapidly adopt it, quickly see real value, and organically expand their use. We complement this intelligence-led
growth with direct go-to-market and Applied AI teams and extend our reach through native availability across
all three major cloud platforms—AWS, GCP, and Azure—and through partnerships with SIs,
consultants, and
data platforms
.
We deliver this intelligence through an integrated approach. Our Claude model family is the foundation, with
model classes optimized for different points along the capability-cost-speed curve. On top of our models, Claude
Platform gives developers access to the primitives we use ourselves, which they can use to build their own AI
solutions. We have also built first-party applications on Claude Platform for customers that prefer a ready-to-
deploy option. We believe the value of this integrated approach is reflected in the increasing number of
customers that use both Claude Platform and our first-party applications.
For the three months ended
September 30, 2026, over 50% of our customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis used
Claude Platform and at least one of our first-party applications,
up from approximately 30% for the three
months ended December 31, 2025.
As more customers adopt Claude and expand their usage, we have rapidly grown our base of customers that
generate meaningful revenue. We had more than 11,900 customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a
TTM basis as of September 30, 2026, up from more than 950 as of September 30, 2025.
In addition, as
customers further embed Claude into their most critical workflows and growth initiatives, many rapidly expand
their deployments into higher revenue tiers. As of September 30, 2026, we had more than 1,900
customers with
$1 million or more of revenue on a TTM basis and approximately 250 customers
with $10 million or more of
reve
nue on a
TT
M
b
asis
.
135
Table of Contents
This
custo
mer
momentum is driven by significant usage expansion as customers realize the value of deploying
Claude across their organizations. The value that Claude delivers to customers has helped drive our Net
Revenue
Retention of approximately 900%
as of September 30, 2026.
The growth in our business reflects the degree to which enterprises are embedding Claude directly into their
business-critical workflows. Despite these trends, adoption across the global economy remains nascent. As
Claude’s capabilities continue to advance, we believe the addressable opportunity will expand, and Claude will
continue its rapid diffusion across more enterprises.
Compute Efficiency
Compute is the most significant operating cost in our business, and compute efficiency is a critical determinant
of our operating efficiency and revenue. Our research-driven algorithmic improvements in training and
inference optimization and
multi-chip compute architecture
have combined to dramatically increase our
compute efficiency as our revenue has scaled. The result is that we are able to continue increasing the
intelligence our research can produce and the revenue our business can generate per dollar of compute
investment.
We define compute efficiency as maximizing the intelligence produced and revenue generated per dollar of
compute invested. Three pillars drive our compute efficiency:
•
Training Efficiency
.
Our researchers regularly innovate compute multipliers. Increasingly, Claude
itself assists in the research and engineering that produce each successive version of our models, which
is a recursive dynamic we refer to as “closing the loop,” with successive versions of our models
accelerating the development of the next and compounding these gains across model generations.
•
Inference Efficiency
.
Our researchers have delivered meaningful compute multipliers for inference
—
reducing the compute required to serve a given level of model performance
—while our engineering
teams have driven significant optimizations in how efficiently that compute is utilized in production.
This allows us to provide greater value for customers and generate greater revenue from our compute
base over time, which is critical as we have consistently operated in a compute-constrained
environment where customer demand exceeds available compute.

Compute Investments
Investing in compute is a prerequisite for long-term growth. We invest in compute for research, model
development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our commercial traction, research progress, and
the scale of the opportunity ahead give us the conviction to continue investing aggressively in compute. An
increasing portion of these investments relates to building out our own compute and infrastructure and
vertically integrating across the compute supply chain to secure long-term compute at the scale required for
frontier model development. These investments take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments,
including lease obligations, that we incur well in advance of the related compute becoming operational and
generating revenue. As a result, we expect this build-out to change the cash flow profile of our business and to
be a significant use of net cash in operating and investing activities for the foreseeable future. See the section
titled “—Liquidity and Capital Resources” for more information.
In addition, as our compute needs have grown substantially, we are shifting from sourcing compute solely
through fixed-term cloud agreements to a hybrid model that also includes leasing chips directly and hosting
them in dedicated facilities operated on our behalf. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic
Direct, which helps to address our scaling compute requirements and we believe will provide long-term
economic advantages. Anthropic Direct represents a more flexible use of capital by allowing us to separate our
commitments for data center capacity from our commitments for the compute infrastructure deployed inside
them. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs,
this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments
until our specific compute needs are more certain.
As of and subsequent to September 30, 2026, we have entered into purchase commitments and lease
agreements, including short-term commitments, as well as leases not yet commenced, with an aggregate

compute we procure during periods of high demand with more cost-effective, long-term compute as our
dedicated infrastructure comes online.

How We Generate Revenue
At the foundation of our business is our family of four Claude model classes—Mythos (including Fable), Opus,
Sonnet, and Haiku—
each optimized for a different point on the capability-cost-speed curve. Our frontier
models allow customers to match the right model to each use case. Customers typically use higher-capability
models for complex reasoning, coding, and agentic workflows where greater model intelligence is required.
Customers also frequently adopt our full range of models,
routing individual tasks to the models that are most
optimized to meet their needs along the capability-cost-speed curve
. The model a customer uses and the volume
of usage are the primary drivers of customer spend. We establish a direct contractual relationship with the
customer and offer customers the flexibility to purchase directly from us or through CSP marketplaces, and
many customers utilize both channels.
Pay-for-intelligence, our consumption-based revenue model, is our primary revenue model and currently
represents the substantial majority of our total revenue. Under this model, customers pay for usage, which is
metered in tokens and priced according to the model selected. Our pay-for-intelligence revenue is primarily
generated from customers building applications incorporating Claude or utilizing our first-party applications.
In addition, we offer certain of our applications on a subscription basis, serving both enterprises and
prosumers. Under this model, customers pay a subscription fee for a specified level of usage and capabilities
during the subscription term, which is generally 12 months or less.
Depending on the model, platform, or applications chosen by our customers, they enter into pay-for-
intelligence pricing, subscription-based pricing, or both. For example, when subscribers approach or exhaust
the usage capacity included in their tier, they may
utilize
a higher subscription tier or purchase more
intelligence directly, creating a seamless bridge from subscription to incremental pay-for-intelligence revenue.
A growing number of enterprise customers agree to non-cancelable annual or multi-year contracts with
minimum spend commitments in exchange for a committed price list. These contracts result primarily in
consumption-based revenue.
Consumption-based revenue increased from $288 million, or 75% of total revenue, for the year ended
December 31, 2024, to $3.8 billion, or 83% of total revenue, for the year ended December 31, 2025, to
$13.1
billion
,
or
80%
of total revenue, for the six months ended June 30, 2026
. Subscription-based revenue increased
from $98 million, or 25% of total revenue, to $789 million, or 17% of total revenue, to
$3.2 billion
,
or
20%
of
total revenue, over the same periods. The higher increase in consumption-based revenue reflects the growth in
customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis. For 2023, our revenue of $41 million was
substantially all consumption-based, reflecting our early operations. We expect consumption-based revenue to
continue to represent the substantial majority of total revenue for the foreseeable future.
Our recent growth may reflect early-stage adoption dynamics, the nascency of the AI market, and rapid initial
customer expansion that may not be sustainable over time. We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over
time, and it may decline significantly and more rapidly than we anticipate as our revenue base increases and as
the market matures.

Our Customers and Approach to Claude Diffusion
Our Customers
We serve enterprises of all sizes and across industries, in nearly every region of the world. Organizations that
use Claude range from the world’s largest enterprises to AI-native startups, research institutions, and mission-
driven organizations working on some of the world’s most consequential problems. Customers realize value
from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in
their products. As enterprise customers push Claude into increasingly complex workflows, we engage with them
to understand their evolving requirements, which helps shape our product roadmap. This feedback loop
deepens customer relationships with each release and makes Claude more capable for all customers.
Software developers have been core to our strategy: they are simultaneously the architects of applications built
on our platform, and they encode their workflows and institutional knowledge into Claude-powered agents.
Developers have been our earliest adopters and often most discerning users: they apply models to unanticipated
use cases quickly and surface the edge cases that sharpen each successive version of a Claude model. Claude
Code is now embedded in software development workflows across major organizations, with these relationships
often beginning with individual engineers who recognized the value of autonomous coding agents and
accelerated adoption across their enterprises
.
The same intelligence and capabilities we deliver to enterprises are also valuable to prosumers in their personal
endeavors. These users provide strategic value as a top-of-funnel engine for our enterprise business—
individuals who utilize Claude for their personal work and then champion it inside their organizations.
We are seeing broad-based growth across customer use cases, from software development to financial analysis
,
content creation, and complex knowledge work. Claude is extensible: regardless of entry point, enterprises
quickly discover that frontier AI applies to a wide and expanding range of tasks across their organizations. As a
result, what sometimes begins as a single use case frequently expands into broader adoption spanning coding,
legal analysis, financial modeling, customer operations, and other knowledge-intensive work.
Our Approach to Claude Diffusion
A core driver of Claude’s diffusion is its intelligence—as Claude’s capabilities advance, value to customers
expands, and that value drives greater adoption. Ensuring the accessibility of such intelligence is also critical,
and we do that in the following ways: through our composable platform and applications that meet customers
where they are, through our go-to-market and Applied AI teams directly, and through partnerships that extend
our reach at scale.
Intelligence-Led Growth.
Our platform and applications are the primary mechanism through which Claude’s
intelligence can reach users. As users begin building, brainstorming, and problem-solving with Claude, they
quickly come to rely on it as a trusted partner in their work. As Claude becomes part of how people work, they
experience firsthand what frontier AI makes possible, and such individual adoption reshapes how entire
organizations operate. This pattern repeats across organizations: prosumers become internal champions, teams
expand their use of Claude, and what begins as a single workflow grows into something that impacts how an
entire organization operates. This pattern has been core to our revenue growth.
Direct Teams.
This organic adoption is complemented and enhanced through our direct go-to-market teams
who help scale Claude to organizations with complex workflows and business processes. By the time our direct
teams engage a customer, Claude is often already in use. Our go-to-market teams use this organic momentum
to build executive sponsorship and drive enterprise-wide adoption.
Applied AI Teams.
Our Applied AI teams embed more deeply with select customers, building solutions that
make it easier for organizations to benefit from Claude’s intelligence. They work with enterprises to design and
deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to the
customer’s own requirements. This work drives deeper adoption within individual customers and generates the
feedback and information from users that help to shape our platform and product roadmap.
140
Table of Contents
Cloud Partnerships.
Claude is accessible on all three major cloud platforms, AWS, GCP, and Azure, allowing
enterprises to deploy Claude within the infrastructure, security perimeters, and commitment structures they
already operate. These CSPs extend our reach through their large combined field teams that are empowered to
sell our platform and applications, accelerating market adoption at a scale we believe would be difficult for any
single organization to directly replicate. We have a joint go-to-market approach with these CSPs through which
we establish direct contractual relationships with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure
allows us to foster stronger commercial alignment with these CSPs, avoid channel conflict, set pricing, and
realize the financial benefits of ongoing compute efficiency improvements.
Ecosystem Partnerships
. Major global SIs have built dedicated Claude practices with teams trained to deploy
our platform and applications. Go-to-market alliances with leading data platforms embed Claude into data
infrastructure that enterprises already operate, facilitating adoption of Claude within existing workflows and
making it easier for enterprises to realize value from Claude.
Ode with Anthropic.
We recently launched an AI services company in partnership with leading private equity
firms to bring Claude’s capabilities to mid-sized companies across sectors, building solutions on the Claude
Platform and supporting customers over the long term. Ode with Anthropic will partner closely with our
Applied AI and go-to-market teams.
Together, these approaches have led to a structurally efficient approach to facilitating the diffusion of Claude in
the economy, with our sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses representing
19%
of revenue for the six
months ended June 30, 2026.
Key Factors Affecting Our Performance
Remaining at the Frontier of AI
We believe enterprises consistently choose the most capable and trustworthy AI systems, making our position
at the frontier an important driver of our success. Our ability to rapidly grow our revenue is partially dependent
on our continued delivery of more intelligent and capable models. Our experience is that as we deliver models
with meaningfully improved capabilities that deliver higher intelligence per dollar spent, customers find new
applications for AI across their businesses, accelerating adoption and revenue growth.
This can be seen in the trajectory of our model family adoption. Successive versions of our most intelligent
generally available model have delivered meaningfully greater intelligence and capabilities. With each release,
we have seen most customers
utilize
the latest version of our models, reinforcing the direct relationship
between frontier model quality and revenue generation. As we deliver more capable models, customers have
expanded their usage into new use cases and increased their spending accordingly.
We expect our ability to deliver innovation in intelligence and capability at the frontier to remain a key driver of
revenue growth in future periods, and maintaining a leading position requires continued investment in research
and compute, top technical talent, and access to capital sufficient to support our growth trajectory.
Securing Sufficient Compute and Optimizing its Utilization
Our ability to continue advancing intelligence at the frontier depends on securing sufficient compute for
research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our ability to leverage
heterogeneous compute
helps us to secure compute at sufficient scale and optimal price-performance
. If any of
our chip partners are unable to deliver committed compute or experience delays, or if we need to procure
incremental compute, we benefit from having a range of partners as opposed to being overly reliant on any one
partner. The availability, timing, and cost of compute are subject to factors largely outside our control,
including the concentration of chip and memory manufacturing among a limited number of suppliers and
geographies, constraints on the availability of power and data center capacity, and evolving export controls. We
have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded
the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs on which we rely for compute are also strategic
investors in us, are our customers, and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These multifaceted
relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest or competitive dynamics that adversely affect our access to
compute, its cost, or the prioritization of our workloads.

As our compute needs have grown substantially, we are shifting from sourcing compute solely through fixed-
term cloud agreements to a hybrid model that also includes leasing chips directly and hosting them in dedicated
facilities operated on our behalf. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic Direct, which helps
to address our scaling compute requirements and provides potential long-term economic advantages of direct
hosting. Anthropic Direct provides us with a more flexible use of capital by allowing us to separate our
commitments for data center capacity from our commitments for the AI accelerators deployed inside them.
Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this
approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our
specific compute needs are more certain.
Optimizing the utilization of our compute is equally important to our success in satisfying customer demand.
We continuously direct compute to its highest-value use case, balancing the need to advance research and
model development with the need to serve our customers and support internal usage of Claude. We rely on
compute efficiencies, such as the discovery of compute multipliers, to get the most out of the compute that we
procure. Our ability to effectively direct compute and drive compute efficiencies will be an important
determinant of both our pace of innovation and our financial results over time.
Attracting and Retaining Technical Talent
Advancing the frontier and maximizing the return on our compute investment require that we attract, hire, and
retain top technical talent. Talent attraction and retention start with our seven co-founders, all of whom have
remained with the company. We believe our culture and mission alignment enable us to hire and retain the
talent required to continuously push the frontier of AI forward in a safe and responsible way. We expect our
ability to continue attracting and retaining top technical talent to remain a key determinant of our pace of
innovation and our financial results in future periods.
Our Continued Access to Capital
We must make significant investments in compute for research, model development, serving customers, and
internal usage of Claude. Our compute requires substantial upfront commitments and ongoing payments as the
compute becomes available to us. Our compute commitments will continue to grow as we scale our business.
Our ability to secure sufficient compute is directly linked to our ability to access capital on favorable terms, such
as through equity or debt financing or cash flow from operations.
In order to maintain our access to capital, we must continue to demonstrate that we are able to invest that
capital in a highly productive way. The best measures of our progress are Claude’s intelligence and capability,
and customer adoption of Claude. Our ability to convert compute investment into frontier model performance,
and then increase customer adoption, will be a key determinant of our access to capital.
Our ability to sustain access to capital depends in part on demonstrating a credible trajectory toward
profitability. Our revenue growth, compute efficiency, and operating efficiency have significantly improved our
operating margin and Adjusted Operating Margin, but we plan to keep investing heavily, which will adversely
impact our results of operations. Our compute commitments are substantial and generally must be satisfied
regardless of our revenue or utilization, while our access to additional capital depends on a number of
conditions, many of which are outside our control, including market conditions and investor demand. In
addition, a portion of our compute and infrastructure build-out has been funded or supported by capital or
credit support provided or facilitated by certain of our CSPs and chip partners. Our ability to reduce this
reliance over time is a function in part of our ability to obtain financing from independent sources on our own
credit.

Our financial performance depends on the pace and breadth at which AI, and in particular Claude, is adopted
across the global economy. While Claude’s capabilities already address a wide range of enterprise use cases, we
believe that enterprise adoption remains nascent. We believe that our ability to capture this opportunity and
drive revenue growth in future periods will depend on three dynamics:

Customer Usage Patterns
Our revenue is influenced by customer usage patterns, which are impacted by the frequency and capability of
new model version releases, as well as seasonal trends, each of which can create variability in our results from
period to period. The continuous and overlapping cadence of new model version releases is inherent to
remaining at the frontier of AI development. For example, model versions released in the six months ended
September 30, 2026
accounted for over 80% of our revenue for the three
months ended September 30, 2026.
As we have released successive versions of Claude models, we have continued to see revenue growth as new
capabilities unlock additional use cases, prompting new customers to adopt Claude and existing customers to
expand their usage.
Our customer usage patterns have also typically exhibited seasonality, particularly around holiday and vacation
periods in the summer and winter, when certain workflows slow down and overall customer activity declines.
For example, developer commits and feature launches are typically slower during the code freezes that many
companies schedule over holidays. Consistent with this pattern, for the two weeks ended January 2, 2026, total
customer spend declined by approximately 20% compared to the prior two weeks ended December 19, 2025.
However, our historical growth rates may mask the impact of seasonal trends on our results. These dynamics
are inherent aspects of a pay-for-intelligence revenue model and may be important determinants of our
financial results in future periods.
Because of these seasonal patterns, our results of operations have varied, and are expected to continue to vary,
from period to period, and our results for any one period may not be indicative of our results for any future
period. As our revenue growth rate declines over time, we expect seasonal effects to become more apparent in,
and to have a greater effect on, our period-to-period results, and to make it more difficult to forecast our results
of operations.

expenses, which currently consist primarily of charitable donations under our donation matching program,
have not historically been significant. For the year ended December 31, 2025, expenses related to our donation
matching program were $541 million, representing approximately 4% of our total operating expenses. However,
we expect the cadence and magnitude of resources directed toward our public benefit initiatives to increase in
future periods and remain a factor affecting our results of operations.
Components of Results of Operations
Revenue
We generate revenue as customers use Claude through our platform and applications, including Claude Code,
Claude Cowork, and vertical solutions for key industries. Claude is powered by our proprietary Claude model
family, a set of frontier models, each with varying levels of capability, cost, and speed. E
nterprise customers
access our intelligence service directly from us or through CSP marketplaces, where we maintain direct
contractual relationships with our customers.
Depending on the model, platform, or applications chosen by our customers, they enter into pay-for-
intelligence pricing, subscription-based pricing, or both. A growing number of enterprise customers agree to
annual or multi-year contracts with minimum spend commitments.
Revenue is recognized when customers use our intelligence service, based on the quantity of tokens consumed.
Subscriptions are generally prepaid on a monthly or annual basis, and are subject to usage limits that reset over
short periods, which results in revenue being recognized on a ratable basis over the subscription period, which
is generally 12 months or less.
We expect our revenue growth rate to decline over time and to fluctuate from period to period. R
evenue growth
in any period may be affected by customer usage patterns, customer adoption, the deployment of our models,
platform, and applications
, the pricing of our offerings,
the timing and success of new model and product
releases
,
measures we decide to implement to safely deploy new capabilities
,
our ability to continue meeting
customer requirements, and other factors affecting demand for our models, platform, and applications,
including those described in the section titled “Risk Factors—We are at an early stage of our rev
enue growth, we
145
Table of Contents
have experienced rapid growth in recent periods, and our historical growth rates are not indicative of future
performance or our ability to sustain or forecast future revenue growth.”
In addition, our revenue has included, and we expect will continue to include, amounts from customers that we
subsequently determine are using our models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or
commercial terms. We believe this dynamic is common in our industry. Because detection, investigation, and
enforcement take time, we recognize revenue from such customers when the related services are provided,
before restricting or terminating their access. Based on our detection and review process, we estimate that
revenue from such customers represented approximately 5% to 7% of our revenue for the nine months ended
September 30, 2026. This estimate requires judgment and may change as our detection methodologies evolve
and we identify previously undetected usage. We expect the percentage of revenue from customers using our
models, platform, and applications in violation of our usage policy or commercial terms to decline in future
periods as we have enhanced our detection and enforcement efforts, in particular in August and September
2026; however, the timing and magnitude of any resulting adverse effect on our revenue and revenue growth
are uncertain.
Operating
Expenses
Compute and Infrastructure
Compute and infrastructure expenses primarily consist of costs attributable to operating our technology
infrastructure, which supports the full range of workloads for our models, including research, model
development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. These costs primarily consist of compute fees
paid to CSPs under committed and on-demand arrangements, including storage, networking, and connectivity,
and related support costs, infrastructure costs associated with serving customer workloads through partner
channels, colocation facility costs, equipment leases and committed power costs associated with our data center
operations, and third-party application infrastructure software costs directly related to our compute operations.
Beginning in 2026, as our obligations commence under compute and infrastructure leases, these expenses also
include operating lease costs, amortization of finance lease assets, variable lease costs, and depreciation and
amortization on owned servers, networking equipment, and related data center assets. See Note 8 to our
consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus for a functional presentation of our
operating expenses, including cost of revenue, and a description of the workloads underlying the compute and
infrastructure expenses within each functional caption. Within that functional presentation, substantially all of
the cost of revenue consists of compute and infrastructure expenses associated with customer-serving
workloads. Additionally, cost of revenue includes certain personnel-related costs and allocated overhead costs.
Customers adopt and retain our technology based on whether our models are at the frontier of AI capability and
maintaining that frontier position is essential to revenue generation. Each model release represents continuous
intelligence improvements, making ongoing model development a critical factor in revenue generation. We
operate an iterative cycle in which compute deployed to model development yields more capable and efficient
models.
Those efficiency gains free compute to serve additional customer workloads. In turn, serving our
customers at scale generates feedback
that informs research and model development. In this cycle, customer-
serving activity and model development are each a direct input that informs the other, and we therefore view
compute and infrastructure costs as critical to our ability to generate revenue within a short time of incurring
such costs.
We expect compute and infrastructure expenses to increase in absolute dollars and remain
our largest
operating expense for the foreseeable future as additional committed compute becomes available to us under
multi-year arrangements with CSPs, and as we continue to invest in additional compute. These expenses are
paid and recognized as compute becomes available to us, rather than when committed, and are generally fixed
in the near term given the majority of our compute
is
contracted under multi-year commitments that we
typically
procure
12 to 18 months in advance of
availability
. We deploy this committed compute as a single,
shared resource across all workloads, and thus plan, incur, and assess it on a total basis rather than by
individual workload. As a result, compute and infrastructure expenses as a percentage of revenue will depend
primarily on how our revenue scales relative to our total committed compute cost base. In addition, as part of
our public benefit initiatives, we intend to direct a meaningful portion of our resources, which may include
compute, toward ensuring that the benefits of frontier AI are broadly accessible, and we expect to significantly
scale these efforts over time.
146
Table of Contents
Personnel
Personnel expenses primarily consist of stock-based compensation, including expense related to stock options,
RSUs, and restricted stock awards (“RSAs”), cash compensation, including base salaries and bonuses, employee
benefits, including health and welfare benefits, and employer payroll taxes.
We expect personnel expenses to increase in absolute dollars as we continue to expand our headcount to
support the growth of our business. We also expect to incur additional stock-based compensation expense in
connection with this offering, including for certain RSUs for which the performance condition will be satisfied
upon the effectiveness of the registration statement of which this prospectus forms a part. We expect that
personnel expenses may fluctuate as a percentage of revenue depending on the timing and magnitude of stock-
based compensation expense, and the pace of hiring across our organization.
Bartz settlement
Bartz
settlement consists of the charge we recorded in 2025 to settle the Bartz litigation
. See Note 13 to our
consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus for additional information.
Sales, Marketing, and Partnerships
Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses primarily consist of fees paid to channel partners and marketing
and advertising costs, including media and public relations spend.
We expect sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses to increase in absolute dollars as we continue to invest
in activities to drive continued adoption and expanded usage of our models. We expect that sales, marketing,
and partnerships expenses may fluctuate as a percentage of revenue depending on the timing of and spend on
marketing campaigns and changes in the terms of our channel partner distribution arrangements and the cost
to deliver our intelligence service.
Other Operating and Administrative
O
ther operating and administrative expenses primarily consist of charitable donations expense related to o
ur
donation matching program, vendor costs related to data quality and performance evaluation services,
information technology and cloud software costs, payment processing and platform fees, facility and occupancy
costs, non-income taxes, professional services costs, bad debt expense, and depreciation and amortization
related to non-data center assets.
We expect that other operating and administrative expenses will increase in absolute dollars as our business
grows and as a result of operating as a public company, including expenses related to compliance with SEC
rules and regulations, the listing standards of the Nasdaq Global Select Market, additional costs for directors’
and officers’ liability insurance, and professional services. We also expect other operating and administrative
expenses to fluctuate as a percentage of our revenue over time as our business grows, in part as we significantly
scale our public benefit initiatives, including expanded programs to make Claude accessible to underserved
communities, increased charitable donation matching, contributions to philanthropic vehicles or foundations
we may establish or support in the future, and other efforts aligned with our mission.
Interest Income
Interest income consists of interest earned on our cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments which
primarily consist of debt securities, including U.S. Treasury and agency securities, corporate debt, and
commercial paper.
Change in Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
Change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs consists of gains and losses as a result
of recording our convertible promissory notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE liabilities at fair value at the end
of each reporting period. Because these instruments are marked to market, increases in our enterprise
valuation drive increases in this expense. We will continue to recognize changes in the fair value of our
147
Table of Contents
convertible notes until they are converted into equity, repaid, or otherwise settled. For more information, see
Note 4 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus.
Other Income (Expense), Net
Other income (expense), net consists primarily of the change in fair value of strategic investments and financial
instruments, the change in fair value of certain derivative instruments in connection with an acquisition of a
privately-held
company in December 2025, interest expense from finance leases, and foreign currency exchange
gains and losses. For more information on the acquisition, see Note 15 to our consolidated financial statements
included elsewhere in this prospectus.
Provision for Income Taxes
The provision for income taxes primarily consists of income taxes in certain federal, state, local, and foreign
jurisdictions in which we conduct business. Our effective tax rates will vary depending on the impact of the
valuation allowance and nondeductible fair value adjustments to derivatives, as well as the relative proportion
of foreign income to domestic income, generation of tax credits, changes in the valuation of our deferred tax
assets and liabilities, and changes in tax laws.

$249 million and $96 million, respectively, for the year ended December 31, 2024 compared to the year ended
December 31, 2023. The increase was primarily driven by growth in new customers and reflected the broader
commercial availability of our AI platform following the launch of the Claude 3 family of Opus, Sonnet, and
Haiku models in 2024, which expanded the range of supported use cases and drove adoption. The number of
customers with $100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis grew from approximately 20 as of December 31,
2023 to approximately 200 as of December 31, 2024. Total revenue from these customers grew from
approximately $37 million to $220 million and represented approximately 90% and 57% of total revenue for
the years ended December 31, 2023 and 2024, respectively.

Non-GAAP Financial Measures
To supplement our consolidated financial statements prepared and presented in accordance with GAAP, we use
certain non-GAAP financial measures, as described below, to facilitate analysis of our operating performance
and for internal planning and forecasting purposes.
We use Adjusted Operating Income (Loss), Adjusted Operating Margin, and Adjusted Net Income (Loss) to
evaluate our operating performance, formulate business plans, prepare budgets and forecasts, and make
strategic decisions, including those relating to operating expenses and the allocation of internal resources. By
excluding certain items that management believes are not directly reflective of the ongoing operating
performance of our business, we believe these non-GAAP financial measures provide investors, analysts, and
others with meaningful insight and enhance their overall understanding of our business and financial
performance by providing a more consistent and comparable overview of our financial performance across
periods.
Other companies in our industry, including those with similar business models, may define or calculate
similarly titled measures in different ways, which may limit the usefulness of these measures for direct
comparison. In addition, other companies may not publish these or similar metrics. Further, these metrics have
certain limitations in that they do not include the impact of certain expenses that are reflected on our
consolidated statements of operations. Thus, our non-GAAP financial measures should not be viewed in
isolation or as a replacement for the most directly comparable measures prepared in accordance with GAAP.
We encourage investors and others to review our business, financial condition, and results of operations in their
entirety, not to rely on any single financial measure, and to view our non-GAAP financial measures in
conjunction with their respective most directly comparable financial measures calculated in accordance with
GAAP, as well as our consolidated financial statements and accompanying notes included elsewhere in this
prospectus.
Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) and Adjusted Operating Margin
We define Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) as operating loss excluding (i) stock-based compensation expense,
(ii) non-cash charitable contributions, and (iii) the Bartz settlement. We define Adjusted Operating Margin as
Adjusted Operating Income (Loss) divided by revenue.
