Quarterly Trends
Revenue
Revenue increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, from
$376 million
for the
three months
ended March 31, 2025
to
$11.6 billion
for the
three months ended June 30, 2026
. The increases in each quarter
were driven by successive model and product releases that drove higher usage, expansion, and broader
adoption across our offerings, with both consumption-based and subscription-based revenue contributing.
Growth in customers generating meaningful revenue contributed across the periods: customers with $100,000
or more of revenue on a TTM basis grew from
approximately
400
as of
March 31, 2025
to more than
6,000
as
of
June 30, 2026
.
Operating Expenses
Compute and Infrastructure
Compute and infrastructure expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, from
$944
million
for the
three months ended March 31, 2025
to
$5.6 billion
for the
three months ended June 30, 2026
,
driven by the delivery of committed compute under our multi-year CSP arrangements. Because we typically
procure compute 12 to 18 months in advance of availability, these expenses are generally fixed in the near term
and increased as committed compute became available to us rather than in response to in-period demand.
159
Table of Contents
Compute and infrastructure expenses as a percentage of revenue decreased from
251%
to
48%
over the same
period, as revenue growth outpaced the growth of our committed compute cost base.
Personnel
Personnel expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, driven by headcount growth and
the associated increases in compensation, including stock-based compensation.
Bartz settlement
In the three months ended September 30, 2025, we recorded a
$1.5 billion
charge to settle the Bartz litigation.
See Note 13 to our consolidated financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus.
Sales, Marketing, and Partnerships
Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, with the
most significant increases observed in the
three months ended March 31, 2026
and
June 30, 2026
. The
increases were primarily driven by fees paid to channel partners, reflecting the growth of our business, and
increased marketing and advertising expenses, reflecting higher media spend to support product launches.
Other Operating and Administrative
Other operating and administrative expenses increased over the quarters presented
, other than in the three
months ended March 31, 2026, which reflected lower donation matching program charges than in the three
months ended December 31, 2025.
The overall increase reflected vendor costs related to data quality and
performance evaluation services, information technology and cloud software costs, payment processing and
platform fees, and professional services costs as our business scaled. The increase in the three months ended
December 31, 2025
was primarily driven by non-cash charges related to our donation matching program.
Operating Income (Loss)
Our
operating loss
widened in the three months ended June 30, 2025, primarily driven by the delivery of
additional committed compute under our CSP arrangements, the associated expenses of which grew faster than
our revenue in the period, and in the three months ended September 30, 2025, which included the Bartz
settlement. Our operating loss narrowed in the three months ended December 31, 2025 and March 31, 2026,
and we generated operating income of
$1.0 billion
for the
three months ended June 30, 2026
, as revenue
growth outpaced the growth in total operating expenses.
We expect our operating results to continue to
fluctuate from quarter to quarter, particularly as the amount of incremental compute we receive, and the
associated expenses we incur, may vary from period to period.
Interest Income
Interest income increased sequentially in each of the quarters presented, from
$51 million
for the three months
ended March 31, 2025 to
$762 million
for the
three months ended June 30, 2026
, primarily driven by higher
average cash and cash equivalents and short-term investments balances.
Change in Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
Changes in the fair value of our convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs resulted in expense in each
of the quarters presented, primarily driven by increases in the fair value of our outstanding convertible
promissory notes resulting from increases in our enterprise valuation during each period. The expense was
largest in the
three months ended June 30, 2026
, reflecting the increase in our enterprise valuation in
connection with our Series H financing. We will continue to recognize changes in fair value until these
instruments are converted into equity, repaid, or otherwise settled. See Note 4 and Note 9 to our consolidated
financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus.

Liquidity and Capital Resources
Since inception, we have financed our operations, corporate investments, and capital expenditures primarily
through proceeds from the issuance of convertible promissory notes, redeemable convertible preferred stock,
cash generated from sales, and SAFEs. To date, we have financed our compute and infrastructure primarily
under arrangements with our CSPs, as well as through proceeds from the financing activities described above
and cash generated from operations. As of June 30, 2026, we had cash and cash equivalents of
$112.4 billion
,
$19.3 billion
of short-term investments, and
$3.2 billion
available under the Credit Facility, as described below.
Cash and cash equivalents consist of cash held in checking and interest-bearing accounts, money market funds,
and other highly liquid investments with original maturities of three months or less from the date of purchase.
We have generated losses from our operations, as reflected in our accumulated deficit of
$132.9 billion
, which
includes
$113.2 billion
related to changes in the fair value of our convertible notes driven by increases in our
enterprise valuation and derivative liabilities since 2023, including
$72.4 billion
during the six months ended
June 30, 2026
. Additionally, we have generated negative cash flows from operating and investing activities in
2023, 2024, and 2025, driven by ongoing expenditures to support business growth including investments to
secure access to more compute and infrastructure capacity. We continue to invest in our own data center
infrastructure and enter into compute and infrastructure capacity arrangements to support anticipated demand
for our intelligence service.
Given the long lead times between contracting for, purchasing, or leasing compute
and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure these arrangements well in advance of
anticipated demand. To secure certain data center development projects, which require significant capital
commitments in advance of deployment, we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on
arrangements with financing sources or partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the
development of data center capacity that is expected to host such partner’s chips or computing infrastructure.
Our ability to expand compute and infrastructure capacity through these arrangements in the future may
depend on the continued willingness and ability of a limited number of CSPs, partners, and financing sources to
enter into and perform under such arrangements. In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the
delivery of the equipment or infrastructure. We anticipate making significant and increased investments for the
foreseeable future, including for owned or leased compute and infrastructure in advance of delivery. These
investments help ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our position at the
frontier of AI.
Our increasing efforts to build out our compute and infrastructure require substantial capital expenditures and
are changing the cash flow profile of our business. Whereas the compute purchased through our CSP
arrangements is generally paid as the compute becomes available to us, we expect an increasing portion of our
compute and infrastructure investment to take the form of capital expenditures and other commitments,
including lease obligations, that require significant upfront payments well in advance of the related compute
becoming operational. We expect our capital expenditures to increase significantly as we expand our build-out,
and we expect these investments to result in significant net cash used in operating and investing activities for
the foreseeable future. Our net cash used in these activities may increase regardless of whether our financial
performance improves. The magnitude and timing of these investments are inherently uncertain and may
change materially over short periods, including as a result of decisions to accelerate or expand our build-out,
and such changes could rapidly and significantly affect our cash flows for a given period.
In addition, these
investments are subject to known trends and uncertainties that could adversely affect our results of operations.
The compute and chips necessary for frontier model development are available from a limited number of
suppliers and geographies and are subject to intense competition, supply constraints, and evolving export
controls, and we have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for
compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs and chip partners on which we
rely provide us capital or credit support, serve as our infrastructure vendors, and develop and offer AI models
162
Table of Contents
and services that compete with ours. These relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest that affect our
access to compute, its cost, the prioritization of our workloads, or the terms on which such capital or credit
support is provided. For a discussion of these and other risks, see the section titled “Risk Factors.”
We believe our existing available cash and cash equivalents, together with cash generated from sales and
amounts available under our A&R
Credit Facility
(as defined below), will be sufficient to support working
capital, operating and finance lease payments, and capital expenditure requirements for at least the next 12
months from the date of this prospectus. However, our future capital requirements will depend on many
factors, including our revenue growth, the timing and extent of our investments in compute and infrastructure
capacity, including additional or expanded CSP, equipment lease, and data center arrangements, the success
and expansion of our sales, marketing, and business development strategies, any potential future investment in
complementary businesses, products, technologies, assets, and talent, risks associated with the AI industry, and
other factors described under “Key Factors Affecting Our Performance.” As a result of these and other factors,
we may be required to seek additional financing sooner than we currently anticipate. Even if we determine that
additional financing is required, we may not be able to raise it on terms acceptable to us or at all. Any such
financing, if completed, may be costly, dilutive, or lead to restrictions on how we operate our business. If we are
unable to raise additional capital when required, or if we cannot expand our operations or otherwise capitalize
on our business opportunities because we lack sufficient capital, our business, financial condition, results of
operations, and cash flows would be adversely affected.
Over the longer term, we expect to have significant cash requirements as we continue to invest in our business,
primarily for compute and infrastructure, including our data center infrastructure build-out, as well as for
general operating needs. We expect to fund these long-term cash requirements through a combination of cash
flows from operations, proceeds from equity financings, including the net proceeds from this offering, proceeds
from debt financings and potential future indebtedness, and financing arrangements with our partners,
including under our note purchase agreements and our equipment lease and data center arrangements. Our
ability to meet these requirements over the long term depends on our ability to grow our revenue and generate
cash flows from operations and to access additional capital on acceptable terms. If sufficient funds are not
available, we may be required to reduce, defer, or forgo planned investments, which could adversely affect our
business, competitive position, and results of operations.
Revolving Credit Agreement
In May 2025, we entered into a Credit Agreement (as amended from time to time prior to the A&R Credit
Agreement (as defined below), the “Credit Agreement”) with certain lenders from time to time party thereto
and Morgan Stanley Senior Funding, Inc., as administrative agent and collateral agent for the lenders, which
initially provided for a $2.5 billion senior secured revolving credit facility with a $400 million letter of credit
sublimit (the “Initial Credit Facility”). In September 2025, we amended the Initial Credit Facility to increase the
aggregate revolving commitments to $2.75 billion and in November 2025, we further amended the Initial Credit
Facility to increase the aggregate revolving commitments to $3.25 billion (the Initial Credit Facility, as
amended, the “Credit Facility”).
As of
June 30, 2026
, we had no borrowings drawn under the Credit Facility and
$78 million
of standby letters of credit outstanding
. As of
June 30, 2026
, we were in compliance with all
covenants under the Credit Agreement.
In September 2026, we entered into an Amended and Restated Credit Agreement (the “A&R Credit
Agreement”), which amended and restated the Credit Agreement to provide for a $15 billion senior secured
revolving credit facility with the full amount thereof available for letters of credit (the “A&R Credit Facility”).
The A&R Credit Facility will mature on September 4, 2031, subject to earlier springing maturity if more than
$500 million in aggregate scheduled cash principal payments on certain of our indebtedness are required
within the 91-day period preceding the date on which any such scheduled principal payment is due, and we do
not have sufficient liquidity to make all such payments then due and remain in pro forma compliance with our
financial covenant, subject to certain other exceptions and conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement.
The proceeds of the A&R Credit Facility may be used for working capital, general corporate purposes, and other
lawful purposes. We may request borrowings in U.S. dollars or certain other agreed currencies, subject to the
terms of the A&R Credit Agreement.
We may borrow, repay, and reborrow amounts under the A&R Credit Facility from time to time. We are
required to pay commitment fees on the unused portion of the A&R Credit Facility and fees in connection with
163
Table of Contents
letters of credit. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release Date (as defined below), such commitment
fees will vary depending on our credit ratings, as set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. Our obligations under
the A&R Credit Facility are required to be guaranteed by certain of our material subsidiaries and secured by
substantially all of our assets and the assets of such subsidiary guarantors, subject to certain exceptions and
exclusions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. The A&R Credit Agreement further provides that, on and
after the date we have obtained an Investment Grade Rating (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement) from at
least two out of three of Moody’s, S&P, and Fitch, at our election, all guarantees and security interests securing
the obligations under the A&R Credit Facility will be released, discharged, and terminated, subject to certain
conditions set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement (such date, the “Guarantee and Collateral Release Date”).
Borrowings under the A&R Credit Facility bear interest at rates based on either the Alternate Base Rate (as
defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), Term SOFR Rate (as defined in the A&R Credit Agreement), or other
applicable benchmark rates in the case of foreign currencies, plus an applicable margin. From and after the
Guarantee and Collateral Release Date, such applicable margin will vary depending on our credit ratings, as
more fully set forth in the A&R Credit Agreement. In addition, the A&R Credit Agreement includes customary
affirmative and negative covenants, including, but not limited to, restrictions on additional indebtedness, liens,
asset sales, investments, mergers, and restricted payments. On and after the Guarantee and Collateral Release
Date, the negative covenants limiting asset sales, investments, restricted payments, and affiliate transactions
will cease to apply and the negative covenants restricting additional indebtedness and liens will be modified in
certain respects, including to permit additional indebtedness, subject to a cap on certain indebtedness that is
secured by assets that do not secure the A&R Credit Facility or that is incurred or guaranteed by restricted
subsidiaries that are not guarantors under the A&R Credit Facility. The A&R Credit Agreement includes a
financial covenant requiring that we maintain l
iquidity
of at least $5.0 billion as of the last day of each fiscal
quarter, beginning with the fiscal quarter ending December 31, 2026. The A&R Credit Agreement also includes
customary events of default, which, if triggered, could result in the acceleration of amounts due under the A&R
Credit Facility and termination of the commitments thereunder.
AMD Agreement
In July 2026, we entered into a hardware supply framework agreement (the “Hardware Supply Agreement”)
with Advanced Micro Devices, Inc. (“AMD”) to
purchase, lease, or access
AMD-based Helios rack-scale systems
featuring AMD Instinct™ MI450 series GPUs. Pursuant to the terms of the Hardware Supply Agreement, AMD
has provided a commitment to purchase up to $5.0 billion of our Class N common stock, which becomes
available for us to draw on in increments following the achievement of specified AMD GPU delivery and
deployment milestones. Based on the deployment schedule contemplated by the Hardware Supply Agreement,
we expect the first of such milestones to be achieved in 2027. Following the completion of this offering, any
purchases of our Class N common stock will be made at a price per share equal to the volume-weighted average
price of our Class A common stock over the 30 trading days immediately preceding the applicable closing date
of such purchase, and we must make any draw request within 12 months following the final delivery and
deployment of AMD GPU capacity under the Hardware Supply Agreement.

Operating Activities
Net cash used in operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2025 decreased by $3.1 billion compared
to the year ended December 31, 2024.
The decrease was primarily driven by a decrease in prepaid hosting
services reflecting the consumption during 2025 of hosting capacity that had been prepaid in prior periods and
an increase in accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities due to increased CSP costs and
the timing of related payments. The decrease was partially offset by higher cash payments, including a payment
related
to the Bartz settlement
, higher cash compensation costs from headcount growth, and an increase in
accounts receivable.
Net cash used in operating activities for the year ended December 31, 2024 increased by $4.1 billion compared
to the year ended December 31, 2023. The increase was primarily driven by an increase in prepaid hosting
services due to business expansion requiring additional hosting capacity.

provided by
operating activities was
$3.9 billion
for the

as compared to

for the

. Our operating cash

and services, employee compensation, operating leases, and interest payments. The increase in operating cash
flow was primarily driven by an improvement in net loss adjusted for non-cash items
, and changes in working
capital, primarily reflecting the timing of payments to vendors and cash receipts from customers. Working
capital at any point in time is subject to many variables, including the timing of billings and cash collections,
vendor payment terms, and the timing of invoice receipt and payment
.

higher capital expenditures related to servers, networking and infrastructure equipment, and purchases of

Quantitative and Qualitative Disclosures about Market Risk
We are exposed to market risks in the ordinary course of our business. Market risk represents the risk of loss
that may impact our financial position due to adverse changes in financial market prices and rates. Our market
risk exposure is primarily the result of fluctuations in interest rates and foreign currency exchange rates.
Interest Rate Risk
As of
June 30, 2026
, we had
$112.4 billion
of cash and cash equivalents and
$19.3 billion
of short-term
investments in a variety of securities, including money market funds, U.S. Treasury and agency securities,
corporate debt securities, and commercial paper. In addition, we had
$2.5 billion
of restricted cash primarily
due to amounts held as collateral for our lease and other obligations. Our cash, cash equivalents, and short-
term investments are held for working capital purposes, and we do not enter into investments for trading or
speculative purposes. Due to the relatively short-term nature of our investment portfolio, a hypothetical 100
basis point increase or decrease in interest rates would not have had a material effect on the fair value of our
investment portfolio as of
June 30, 2026
.
Foreign Currency Exchange Risk
We transact business globally in multiple currencies, with the vast majority of our revenue denominated in U.S.
dollars and, to a lesser extent, other currencies such as euros and British pounds. Our international revenue, as
well as costs and expenses denominated in foreign currencies, and intercompany transactions with our foreign
subsidiaries, expose us to the risk of fluctuations in foreign currency exchange rates against the U.S. dollar. A
hypothetical 10% change in foreign currency exchange rates applicable to our business would not have a
material impact on our consolidated financial statements as of
June 30, 2026
. We have not entered into
derivative or hedging transactions, but we may enter into such arrangements in the future if our exposure to
foreign currency becomes more significant.
Critical Accounting Estimates
Our discussion and analysis of our financial condition and results of operations are based upon our financial
statements, which have been prepared in accordance with GAAP. GAAP requires us to make certain estimates
and judgments that affect the amounts reported in our financial statements. We base our estimates on historical
experience, anticipated future trends, and other assumptions we believe to be reasonable under the
circumstances. Because these accounting policies require significant judgment, our actual results may differ
materially from our estimates.
We believe that of our significant accounting policies, which are described in Note 1 to our consolidated
financial statements included elsewhere in this prospectus, the following accounting policies involve a greater
degree of judgment and complexity. Accordingly, these are the policies we believe are the most critical to aid in
fully understanding and evaluating our consolidated financial condition, results of operations, and cash flows.
Stock-Based Compensation
We measure compensation expense for all stock-based payment awards, including stock options and RSUs,
granted to employees, directors, and other service providers, based on the estimated fair value of the awards on
the date of grant. The most significant input in determining the fair value of a stock option is the estimated fair
173
Table of Contents
value of our common stock. The estimated fair value of our common stock is also used to measure the grant
date fair value of RSUs and RSAs, including those subject to performance-based vesting conditions.
Stock Options
We estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees, consultants, officers, and directors using the
Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model on the date of grant. The fair value of stock options that are
expected to vest is recognized as compensation expense on a straight-line basis over the requisite service
period. Forfeitures are accounted for when they occur.
The Black-Scholes-Merton model considers several variables and assumptions in estimating the fair value of
stock-based awards. These variables include:
▪
Fair Value of Common Stock. Because our common stock is not yet publicly traded, we must estimate
the fair value of our common stock. Our board of directors considers numerous objective and
subjective factors to determine the fair value of our common stock as discussed in the section titled “—
Common Stock Valuations” below.
▪
Expected Volatility. Since we have no trading history of our common stock, the expected volatility of
our underlying common stock is estimated by taking the weighted-average historical volatility of a
group of comparable publicly traded companies over a period equal to the expected life of the options.
•
Expected Term. Expected term represents the period over which we anticipate stock-based awards to
be outstanding. We estimate the expected term based on the options’ vesting term and contractual
terms, such that the expected life is equal to the average of the stock-based award’s weighted-average
vesting period and its contractual term.
•
Risk-free Rate. The expected risk-free rate assumption is based on the U.S. Treasury instruments
whose term is consistent with the expected term of the stock options.
•
Expected Dividend Yield.
The expected dividend yield is zero, as we have never declared or paid any
dividends and have no current plans to do so.

, there was ap

Common Stock Valuations
Prior to our initial public offering, given the absence of a public trading market of our Class A common stock,
and in accordance with the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants Accounting and Valuation Guide,
Valuation of Privately-Held Company Equity Securities Issued as Compensation
, our board of directors
exercised reasonable judgment and considered numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the best
estimate of the fair value of our common stock, including:
•
contemporaneous third-party valuations of our common stock;
•
the prices paid for common or redeemable convertible preferred stock sold to third-party investors by
us and prices paid in secondary transactions, including any tender offers;
•
the rights, preferences, and privileges of our redeemable convertible preferred stock relative to those of
our common stock;
•
actual and forecasted operating and financial performance;
•
our stage of development;
•
the industry outlook;
•
the lack of marketability of our common stock;
•
the likelihood of achieving a liquidity event, such as an initial public offering or a sale of our company,
given prevailing market conditions;
•
the history and nature of our business, industry trends, and competitive environment; and
•
general economic outlook, including economic growth, inflation and unemployment, interest rate
environment, and global economic trends.
Our board of directors determined the fair value of our common stock by first determining the enterprise value
of our business and then allocating the value among the various classes of our securities to derive a per share
value of our common stock. The enterprise value of our business was primarily estimated by reference to the
closest round of equity financing to the date of the valuation.
In allocating the enterprise value of our business among the various classes of stock prior to this offering, we
used a hybrid method based on a contingent claims analysis (“CCA”) and a common stock equivalent (“CSE”)
method. The CCA is based on the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model, which models each class of stock
as a call option with a unique claim on our assets. The CSE method presumes that all shares of redeemable
convertible preferred stock convert into common stock based upon their conversion terms and other differences
in the rights and preferences of the shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock are ignored.
After the allocation of enterprise value to the various classes of stock, a discount for lack of marketability
(“DLOM”) is applied to arrive at a fair value of the common stock. A DLOM is meant to account for the lack of
opportunity to sell a private company stock that is not traded on public exchanges. In making the final
determination of common stock value, consideration is also given to the recent sales and/or expected sales of
common stock.
Application of these approaches involves the use of estimates, judgment, and assumptions that are complex and
subjective, such as those regarding our expected future revenue, expenses, and future cash flows, discount
175
Table of Contents
rates, market multiples, the selection of comparable companies, and the probability of possible future events.
Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions or the relationships between those assumptions
impact our valuations as of each valuation date and may have a material impact on the valuation of our
common stock.
Following this offering, it will not be necessary to determine the fair value of our common stock, as the shares of
our common stock will be traded in the public market.
Fair Value of Convertible Notes, Derivative Liabilities, and SAFEs
We elected to account for our convertible notes at fair value pursuant to Accounting Standards Codification
(“ASC”) Topic
825, Financial Instruments
. The convertible notes are recognized at their estimated fair value on
our consolidated balance sheet, and changes in fair value are recorded in change in fair value of convertible
notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in our consolidated statement of operations. We elected the fair value
option to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately accounting for the
liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation model.
In connection with the 2023 and 2024 note purchase agreements with both Amazon and Google, we recognized
derivative liabilities representing obligations to issue future convertible notes pursuant to the terms of those
agreements. The derivative liabilities were measured at estimated fair value, with changes in fair value recorded
in change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of
operations.
The estimated fair value of the convertible promissory notes is determined using a hybrid approach comprising
a CCA and a CSE method. The analysis estimates the fair value of the convertible promissory notes using a
scenario-based analysis that considers the probability-weighted present value of the instruments across the
range of possible outcomes available to the note holders, including conversion into redeemable convertible
preferred stock, Class N common stock, cash repayment at maturity, and cash settlement at a premium upon a
change of control. The scenarios included consider the probability-weighted value of the instruments in the
CCA and CSE framework.
The application of this methodology involves the use of complex and subjective estimates, judgments, and
assumptions, including the probability and timing of each settlement scenario such as a qualified equity
financing, initial public offering, direct listing, or change of control; the estimated fair value of our equity
securities into which the notes may convert; the applicable conversion prices, which vary by note series and are
contingent on factors such as elapsed time since issuance and contractual caps and percentage discounts; and
the ownership thresholds and rollover provisions that determine the extent to which principal balances convert
into equity versus being reissued as rollover notes. In particular, the ownership cap and rollover mechanism—
whereby conversion is capped at specified ownership thresholds and any unconverted principal balance is re-
issued as a non-interest bearing rollover note that remains subject to fair value measurement—requires
significant judgment in estimating what proportion of each note financing will convert versus roll over, because
this determination depends on the size and structure of future equity financings that are inherently uncertain.
Changes in any or all of these estimates and assumptions, or the relationships between those assumptions,
impact our valuations as of each measurement date and may have a material impact on the amounts recognized
in our consolidated statement of operations.
The fair value option election described above also applied to the SAFEs that we issued during the year ended
December 31, 2023. The SAFEs were measured at estimated fair value using the same scenario-based
framework, with the monetary settlement amount fixed at inception and the number of equity shares received
upon conversion being variable; consistent with the convertible notes, changes in fair value were recorded in
change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statement of
operations. All SAFEs were converted into redeemable convertible preferred stock during the years ended
December 31, 2023 and 2024, and no SAFEs remained outstanding as of December 31, 2024 or 2025. No
SAFEs were outstanding at any point during the six months ended June 30, 2026. Accordingly, the primary
ongoing estimation exposure under the fair value option relates to the convertible notes and rollover notes
described above.

Leases
We lease facilities and equipment, including compute and infrastructure capacity, under operating and finance
leases. We determine whether an arrangement is or contains a lease at inception and evaluate the classification
of our leases at lease commencement and, as necessary, upon modification. Accounting for leases requires
significant judgment, including determining whether an arrangement is or contains a lease, and significant
estimates, including the expected lease term, the fair value of the leased property, and our incremental
borrowing rate.
Given the size and duration of our lease portfolio, changes in our estimate of the fair value of the underlying
leased asset, the expected lease term, or the determination of our incremental borrowing rate could result in a
different lease classification or a materially different measurement of our right-of-use assets and lease
liabilities.
Income Taxes
We account for income taxes using the asset and liability method, recognizing deferred tax assets and liabilities
for temporary differences between the financial reporting and tax bases of assets and liabilities, as well as for
net operating loss and credit carryforwards, measured at enacted tax rates applicable in the years of expected
reversals. We establish valuation allowances when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to amounts more-
likely-than-not expected to be realized, based on the weighting of positive and negative evidence.
Assessing the realizability of our deferred tax assets is an area of significant management judgment. We
evaluate our deferred tax assets for recoverability based on historical taxable income, projected future taxable
income, reversal patterns of existing temporary differences, and available tax planning strategies. As an AI
company operating in a rapidly evolving market with significant ongoing investment in compute and
infrastructure, our projections of future taxable income are inherently uncertain. Should our assessment of the
recoverability of deferred tax assets change, our income tax provision would be adjusted in that period, which
could materially impact our results of operations.
We account for uncertain tax positions in accordance with
ASC Topic 740, Income Taxes
. Tax benefits from
uncertain positions are recognized when it is more likely than not that the position will be sustained on
examination based on its technical merits, measured at the amount that is more likely than not to be realized
upon settlement. These assessments require judgment, particularly with respect to the qualification and
documentation of research and development tax credits, where supporting evidence may be subject to differing
interpretations. The actual outcome of these matters may differ materially from our current estimates. We
recognize interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits within our provision for income taxes.
Loss Contingencies
We are involved in legal claims, proceedings, and other regulatory and administrative matters that arise in the
ordinary course of business, certain of which may include speculative claims for substantial or indeterminate
amounts of damages.
We routinely assess each significant matter and its potential financial exposure. We record a liability when we
believe it is both probable that a loss has been incurred and the amount can be reasonably estimated, and we
disclose matters for which a loss is reasonably possible and the loss or range of loss can be estimated. These
assessments require significant judgment in determining both the likelihood and estimated amount of potential
losses. We base our accruals on the best information available at the time, taking into account the specific facts
and circumstances of each matter, the merits of our defenses, and the impact of negotiations, settlements,
regulatory proceedings, rulings, and advice of legal counsel. Our estimates are subject to change as additional
information becomes available and as matters develop, and we have in prior periods revised our assessments
based on updated information.

Business
Overview
For the first time in history, intelligence is something humans can build. The cognitive capability to reason,
analyze, synthesize, decide, and create is producible at scale and accessible on demand. We believe this
abundance of AI will rapidly transform every sector of the global economy in ways greater than the impact of
industrialization, electricity, semiconductors, and the internet. AI that truly delivers on its potential—with the
risks well managed—could significantly accelerate global growth and dramatically improve quality of life for
people around the world.
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the breakthroughs that define
AI. We are first and foremost a research lab—our mission is
the responsible development and maintenance of
advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity
. This mission directs our focus—along with our talent and
culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy, it is one of the
core advantages that set us apart. These advantages enable us to continuously advance frontier AI and shape
the standards for its safe and responsible development. Our frontier AI, Claude, is delivered to customers
through our models, platform, and applications. Claude has experienced the fastest enterprise adoption of any
technology in history, as demonstrated by revenue growing from $0 at commercial launch in the first quarter of
2023 to
$
for the three months ended September 30, 2026.
This rapid and growing adoption generates
two self-reinforcing dynamics—an improvement loop that advances Claude and an investment loop that helps
fund our continued research in
frontier
AI.
We believe the diffusion of AI through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history
to improve how humans live and work, and this process is just beginning. In our view, the world has only begun
to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is
used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier. Claude’s
capabilities have evolved significantly in recent years, and we expect they will continue advancing rapidly. This
will lead not only to an expanding addressable market, but also to an expanding scope of impact on the world.
We aim to ensure that impact is as positive as possible.

Our Core Advantages
Mission & Focus.
All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to
concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid
conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier AI while
mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together.
Talent & Culture.
Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including
researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a
low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier AI capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. We
believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
Frontier & Safety Research.
We believe that sustained, focused research at the frontier of intelligence is
required to build the most capable and safest AI systems. Our frontier capabilities and safety research are
deeply integrated and directly shape model design, training, and deployment, helping us produce systems that
are more reliable, steerable, and well-suited for real-world deployment, particularly in demanding enterprise
environments. We translate our research leadership into innovation velocity, and have consistently released
better models, platform capabilities, and applications. Each version of a Claude model assists in building the
next, helping to compress development timelines and produce compounding improvements in the speed at
which we innovate. We refer to this recursive dynamic as “closing the loop,” and we believe it is one of the most
significant structural advantages in frontier A
I
and
can greatly accelerate the rate at which capabilities advance.
We believe that model capabilities must be advanced together with safety, alignment, and security practices,
particularly as the speed of AI development accelerates. We assess the risks of each model during development
and before and after release, and take the steps we believe are appropriate to balance model capabilities with
safety, alignment, and security, even where doing so may moderate the rate at which we release new
capabilities. We view decisions of this kind as deliberate tradeoffs that we make because they serve the
Company Purpose, the long-term interests of our mission, and our customers’ demand for safe and aligned
models.
Our Approach to Compute
. We manage compute as a single, fungible pool
from multiple strategic partners,
and
we dynamically direct available compute between workloads based on where the marginal unit is expected to be
most productive at any given time. We believe that this approach to compute enables us to deliver superior
models, serve more customers, and achieve greater productivity from our compute investment. This compute

Enterprise Strategy.
Our enterprise strategy is built on the belief that frontier AI is most valuable in real-world
settings, as deployment across enterprises is where economic impact is greatest and where the improvement
loops from customer feedback are richest. Accordingly, we have organized our research priorities, our product
roadmap, and our go-to-market and Applied AI teams around enterprise use cases, which range from routine
knowledge work to the most complex problems. The customer feedback we gather directs our research focus
and makes Claude more capable over time. This broadens where Claude can be deployed and further expands
enterprise adoption, which helps ensure that the benefits of our AI reach people and organizations at scale.

Enterprise Adoption of Claude
The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the

Our customer base as of September 30, 2026 includes:

More than 11,900

Unlike a static product that serves a single use case, Claude is frontier AI with rapidly advancing capabilities.
We build at three layers of the stack: the models themselves, the platform for building on those models, and the
applications that place Claude directly in the hands of our users. An advance at any layer compounds across all
three layers, accelerating the pace at which we can deliver more capable intelligence. We believe the value of
this integrated approach is reflected in the increasing number of customers that use both Claude Platform and
our first-party applications. For the three months ended September 30, 2026, over 50% of our customers with
$100,000 or more of revenue on a TTM basis used Claude Platform and at least one of our first-party
applications, up from approximately 30% for the three months ended December 31, 2025.
Today, enterprises rely on Claude to reason, plan, and execute across complex workflows with a level of
trustworthiness and judgment that we believe was not previously available from earlier generations of AI.
Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and
embedded intelligence in their products. As Claude’s capabilities grow, our customers benefit and often
broaden their adoption of Claude in new workflows. This expanding role reflects a broader shift in how Claude
is used inside the enterprise, from a tool that responds to discrete prompts to what we call a Virtual
Collaborator: an AI system that works alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional
levels.
We drive the diffusion of Claude primarily by making it accessible across multiple product surfaces. For
example:
•
Claude Platform, our comprehensive agentic development environment, provides customers with
direct access to the primitives to build, deploy, and scale their own applications that leverage Claude’s
capabilities within their own products and workflows.
•
Claude Code, our coding agent, works alongside human software developers on end-to-end software
development: writing, planning, editing, testing, debugging, and committing code across production-
scale codebases.
•
Claude Cowork, our knowledge work agent, has computer use capability that enables it to work with
professionals on end-to-end business tasks: autonomously researching, drafting, analyzing,
synthesizing, and executing other knowledge work.
Much of the diffusion of Claude has been organic. We amplify this with our go-to-market and Applied AI teams,
which extend our reach by meeting customers where they are through distribution partnerships that place
Claude inside customers’ existing technology stacks. For example, Claude is accessible on all three major cloud
platforms—AWS, GCP, and Azure. We have a joint go-to-market approach with these CSPs through which we
establish direct contractual relationships with our customers while paying a fee to each CSP. This structure
allows us to foster stronger commercial alignment with these CSPs, avoid channel conflict, set pricing, and
realize the financial benefits of ongoing compute efficiency improvements. Ecosystem partnerships also expand
our reach, allowing customers to adopt Claude through SIs, such as Accenture, Deloitte, KPMG, and PwC,
consultants, and data platforms, such as Salesforce and Snowflake. We recently launched Ode with Anthropic,
an AI services company, in partnership with leading private equity firms to bring Claude’s capabilities to mid-
sized companies across sectors, building solutions on the Claude Platform and supporting customers over the
long term.

Claude is Accelerating Our Ability to Close the Loop
Claude itself has become one of the most powerful drivers of our progress—each new version of a Claude model
directly accelerates development of the next. Many aspects of the research, training, and testing of subsequent
model generations now involve Claude, including running experiments, generating and processing training
data, automating evaluations and safety audits, and writing and reviewing code. We refer to this recursive
dynamic as “closing the loop.” A direct expression of this dynamic is our accelerating pace of producing
compute multipliers. More capable models help our researchers discover these improvements faster; in turn,
more powerful compute multipliers enable us to train even more capable models and deploy them more
efficiently.
A clear example of our ability to close the loop is the deployment of Claude Code, our agentic coding product,
across our engineering organization. As our models have advanced, we have seen significant improvement in
Claude’s capability on more challenging, open-ended engineering problems that lack a clear specification and
have historically depended on experienced human judgment.
Claude’s success rate on these problems reached
approximately 90% in September 2026, up approximately 50 percentage points in nine months, based on our
internal benchmarks.

AI is Transforming Intelligence
We believe that Powerful AI, a highly capable and impactful form of frontier AI characterized by the following
key attributes, will become widely available within a few years:
•
cognitive capabilities matching or exceeding those of top human experts across most professional and
scientific disciplines;
•
the ability to navigate all interfaces available to a human working virtually, including text, audio, video,
and direct computer control;
•
the ability to reason through complex tasks autonomously over extended periods—lasting hours, days,
or weeks—and seek clarification and feedback when needed;
•
the ability to coordinate across multiple instances and collaborate with both humans and other AI
systems; and
•
the ability to interface with the physical world by digitally controlling laboratory equipment, robotic
systems, and other machines through digital connections.
If Powerful AI is directed at solving humanity’s hardest problems and the risks are managed responsibly, the
potential is extraordinary. The possibilities include compressing decades of scientific progress into years;
accelerating drug discovery, disease detection, and the delivery of personalized therapy; providing individually
tailored education and expert financial and legal advice; advancing power grids and battery design for greater
efficiency and reliability; and extending to the developing world capabilities that took wealthy nations
generations to build.
Scaling Laws and the Predictability of Progress
The intelligence and capabilities of AI systems have advanced dramatically. Tasks that were beyond the reach of
AI systems just a few years ago, such as complex mathematical reasoning, designing scientific experiments, and
executing substantial portions of software development, are now routinely performed by AI.
These advances have followed empirical “Scaling Laws,” the finding that AI model performance improves
predictably with increases in model size, training data, and compute. The foundational paper,
Scaling Laws for
Neural Language Models
, whose lead authors (including Dario Amodei, Jared Kaplan, Sam McCandlish, and
Tom Brown) later co-founded Anthropic, was critical in establishing these relationships and helped guide the
wave of modern LLMs.
We expect AI capabilities—across language, reasoning, mathematics, coding, scientific analysis, and an
expanding range of agentic tasks and knowledge work—to continue advancing for many years. As a result, we
believe this will drive demand for AI that outstrips supply for the foreseeable future, limited principally by the
availability of compute. We believe that the majority of this demand will be concentrated at the frontier: our
experience has been that enterprises gravitate to our most capable models across a wide variety of workloads,

The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior
While the potential benefits of AI are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society
in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if the technology is not developed and deployed
responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using AI’s capabilities to
discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse,
including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. AI deployed at scale also has the potential
to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm
society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned AI systems could corrupt institutional decision-
making or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their
users and operators. We believe that frontier AI companies must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure
the responsible diffusion of this technology. We also believe that safety, alignment, and ethical behavior
resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and
demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting an AI partner for mission-critical
workloads.
Our Core Advantages
We have five core advantages that define our position at the frontier: our mission and focus, our talent and
culture, our frontier and safety research, our approach to compute, and our enterprise strategy.
Mission and Focus
Anthropic was founded in 2021 by a team of researchers responsible for many of the consequential
breakthroughs that define frontier AI.
They share a conviction that safety must be a foundational principle for
building Powerful AI. We have a corporate structure consistent with that objective, incorporating as a Delaware
PBC and implementing the
LTBT with an
explicit mandate to advance our mission. Further, we publish safety
methodologies, model evaluations, and our Responsible Scaling Policy because we believe transparency is a
prerequisite for trust, and trust is a prerequisite for the responsible deployment of frontier AI at scale.
Every employee at Anthropic works towards the same mission, and that mission guides every decision—from
model architectures, to product strategy, to partnership terms, and to how we direct research and compute. We
do not pursue projects based on commercial opportunity or research novelty alone; our efforts must advance
our mission. When difficult tradeoffs arise between commercial gain and safety or trust, we have a clear answer.
For example, in April 2026, we initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview
through Project Glasswing, available to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making
it broadly available at launch due to its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We believe this
187

clarity of mission reduces friction, accelerates decision-making, and fosters a culture where safety and
capability are pursued in tandem.
Talent and Culture
Talent is one of our most important advantages, because technology, capital, product, and distribution all flow
from superior talent. Talent density matters more than talent mass. Brilliant people are inspired and motivated
when surrounded by equally brilliant colleagues, creating an environment that attracts more exceptional
people. This talent can leverage Claude to maximize each individual’s impact.
We believe we have assembled the deepest concentration of AI research talent in the world, including many of
the researchers who pioneered the techniques that underlie modern LLMs. Our founding team originated
several foundational advances in AI, including Scaling Laws, GPT-2 and GPT-3, RLHF, and mechanistic
interpretability. Our conviction that safety and capability must advance together helps us attract and retain
world-class talent, including researchers and engineers. For example, we have experienced
approximately 1%
regrettable attrition of our employee base overall in the TTM period ended September 30, 2026.
We maintain a commitment to open internal collaboration and truth seeking, which is underpinned by our low-
ego, high-impact, and mission-aligned culture. Researchers share results openly, and colleagues critique and
redirect in real time. When multiple teams pursue parallel approaches, the norm is to rigorously evaluate which
approach is demonstrating stronger and more aligned results. This collaborative dynamic is difficult to replicate
because it requires both the foundation of trust we have built from the earliest days of our organization and a
relentless commitment to preserving such trust. That trust manifests in ways that are uncommon at our scale:
teams that consistently pull in the same direction rather than at cross-purposes.
We believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.
Frontier and Safety Research
Our frontier model leadership is a direct product of our talent density. We believe our researchers have
consistently pushed the boundaries of intelligence, capability, and reliability further than bigger teams or those
with larger budgets. Claude is widely recognized for its performance on real-world tasks across industries,
including coding, medicine, law, science, and mathematics.
Our approach to research provides key advantages to our business:
•
Our Model Research and Compute Performance Are Co-designed from the Start
. Architectural
decisions are made with compute efficiency in mind from day one. Our model architecture and
inference infrastructure are designed in a single unified process. AI researchers and inference
infrastructure engineers share planning cycles, reporting lines, and performance targets. This approach
enables us to develop model versions that are both more capable and more efficient compared to prior
versions.
•
Our Pre-training Process Is Engineered for Capital Efficiency
. We focus on a clear pipeline for
developing model improvements to architecture, training methodology, and data. These are tested at a
smaller scale before they consume significant compute. The bar for inclusion in a frontier training run
is high and strictly evidence-based: we require demonstration that a given improvement holds as
models increase in size, not merely that it performs well at reduced scale. Frontier training runs are
planned, scheduled capital deployments with known inputs and rigorous inclusion criteria. The result
is a repeatable process for converting research investment into capability gains, while managing the
risks inherent to frontier training runs.
•
Our Post-training Investment Is Purpose-Built for Agentic Capabilities
. Post-training has grown from
a finishing step into a major research investment, reflecting the market shift from assistants to agents.
This is where our models hone their ability to write code, use tools, follow instructions, and operate
software on a user’s behalf. We train against complete, realistic tasks whose complexity reflects real
professional work.

Table of Contents
•
Our Safety Research Is a Commercial Benefit
. As models take on agentic roles with access to critical
business systems, trust and reliability are paramount. And as capabilities increase, the ability to
operate safely becomes one of the key determining factors for commercial viability. Models that are
well-aligned are better at following a user’s instructions—for example, they avoid taking potentially
destructive actions without fully understanding user intent. They are also more robust against attacks
such as prompt injection, where malicious actors attempt to hijack the model by feeding it illicit
instructions. Our work on alignment, interpretability research, safeguards, and red-teaming, as well as
the use of external reviewers who can assess our safety practices, helps us create safer, more reliable
models, and therefore positions us to meet our customers’ rigorous requirements. Safety and capability
research are integrated, which enables us to deliver the trust and performance required for enterprise
workflows.
Our Approach to Compute
Our approach to compute starts with training models that are designed to be more capable and run more
efficiently on any given type of compute.
Our ability to build more capable models and serve them more efficiently reflects the compounding returns of
an iterative cycle between our pre-training, post-training, and inference research, all of which is enabled by our
fungible compute pool. Pre- and post-training research produces proprietary compute multipliers that make
our models more capable. Research and inference engineering drive sustained reductions in the compute
required to serve those models.
In addition to enabling more capable and efficient models, our multi-chip compute architecture across AWS
Trainium, Google TPUs, NVIDIA GPUs, and AMD GPUs allows us to orchestrate workloads to optimize for
price and performance. We have years of experience effectively training and running our models across
multiple chip families, which we believe is differentiated and difficult to replicate. This foundation, paired with
Claude’s increasing understanding of chip and model architectures, allows us to onboard new chip platforms in
a fraction of the time this once required.
Our compute pool is fungible by design. We have made substantial engineering investments to build the
internal orchestration, scheduling, and capacity management systems that allow accelerator capacity,
regardless of provider, chip architecture, or physical location, to be directed across workloads. The same
infrastructure that serves customer workloads is also directed to research, model development
, a
nd internal
usage of Claude. These systems manage the underlying hardware as a unified capacity pool, monitor utilization
and demand across that pool, and direct compute to wherever it is expected to be most productive at any given
time.
Our multi-chip compute approach provides us with substantially greater chip access than relying on one
platform and enables us to opportunistically capture the price-performance benefits of each chip family and
generation
. Securing this access requires significant advance commitment. Given the long lead times between
contracting for compute and that compute becoming available to serve workloads, we secure compute well in
advance of anticipated demand.
In some cases, we may also make payments in advance of the delivery of the
equipment or infrastructure.
We anticipate making significant investments for the foreseeable future, including
in compute and infrastructure, to ensure we have the technological resources to maintain and expand our
position at the frontier of AI.
Enterprise Strategy
Our enterprise strategy aligns with our mission. We build our most capable models for the problems that
demand the highest intelligence. That same intelligence is also applied efficiently to everyday work—calibrating
effort to the difficulty of each task and routing workloads to the models within our model family that are best
suited for them. As a result, our customers around the world are adopting Claude across a broad range of work,
from routine knowledge tasks to their most important problems. Today, Claude is deployed for knowledge work
across major industries, including financial services, insurance, healthcare, life sciences, law, education, retail
and commerce, telecommunications, professional services, technology, and cybersecurity. Beyond practical
enterprise challenges, Claude is also being applied to pressing global problems in scientific research, drug
discovery, education, and climate analysis.

We have built our models, platform, and applications for usefulness in production environments instead of
benchmark performance. This distinction matters, as many AI systems prove difficult to implement and fail to
deliver the expected value in complex enterprise environments, where governance and security concerns
remain among the top barriers to adoption.
Our applications, such as Claude Code and Claude Cowork, multiply the impact of employees. Over time, our
applications have become more capable and are now frequently being used to conduct long-running
autonomous work alongside employees. Organizations also integrate Claude as the intelligence that powers and
transforms internal business processes. In addition, our Claude Platform is used as the foundation for
enterprises building AI-native products.
As enterprise customers integrate Claude into increasingly complex workflows, they surface the use cases and
requirements that shape our roadmap. They also provide feedback that allows us to continuously improve our
models, platform, and applications as well as develop new solutions to advance their AI adoption.
With each model and product advancement, Claude is able to address more valuable use cases, deepening its
impact for existing customers while lowering the adoption threshold for new ones. When a model crosses the
capability, reliability, and trust threshold required for a category of work, adoption in that category generally
moves quickly from experimentation into production. Coding was the first such category: within roughly a year,
Claude progressed from suggesting individual lines of code to operating fleets of agents working autonomously
across production codebases. Cybersecurity is following a similar curve, with Claude’s performance on
ExploitBench, a benchmark developed by Carnegie Mellon researchers that evaluates AI models’ ability to
exploit software vulnerabilities, increasing from 40% with Opus 4.8, to 78% with Claude Mythos 5, and to 91%
with Opus 5.5 over a period of approximately four months. Cyberdefenders are now identifying and patching
vulnerabilities at scale. We expect these improvements in model capabilities to unlock additional use cases.
Claude Security and our recently launched OSS Scanner are early examples, providing the ability to scan
codebases on a continuous basis and propose fixes before attackers find vulnerabilities.
Claude as a Virtual Collaborator
We believe we have reached an inflection point where AI systems can function as genuine collaborators in
professional work. They quickly complete substantive tasks that might otherwise occupy a skilled professional
for several hours, a full day, or longer. AI systems are also becoming increasingly capable of performing tasks
that were previously too difficult or costly to complete or surfacing original insights and analyses.
We refer to these AI systems that work alongside humans to perform complex, multi-step work at professional
levels as Virtual Collaborators. Virtual Collaborators carry the access rights,
system connections, and context
that their organizations grant them, which allows them to function more accurately and reliably. They can
navigate and use internal tools and execute workflows that span multiple steps that require sustained
reasoning. Virtual Collaborators are AI designed to be embedded where work gets done, and our aim is to
10
IDC, Worldwide Developer Population Growth Forecast, 2025–2029, doc # US53789825, September 2025.

Table of Contents
continue extending them to knowledge workers globally, a population that is estimated to exceed one billion in
2028.
10
Claude Code
The clearest manifestation of Virtual Collaborators today is Claude Code, our coding agent and the product we
believe has most concretely defined what autonomous AI work looks like. Claude Code shifted the market’s
understanding of what an AI system could do in collaboration with software developers: the model suggests the
next line of code and goes further by planning, writing, testing, and debugging—a process that results in
production-grade code. Within months of its release, autonomous coding became the reference point for
measuring the progress of frontier AI. For enterprise AI use cases, we believe the launch of Claude Code was
comparable in its impact to the introduction of the first widely adopted conversational AI assistants. What
makes Claude Code a Virtual Collaborator is its sustained reasoning, a harness that translates intent into
actions, an execution environment that maintains a persistent state whether on a developer’s machine or in a
sandboxed cloud environment, integration with existing tools and systems, and a user-friendly interface. Its
uses are highly varied and often surprising: for example, NASA engineers used Claude Code to plan and write
navigation commands for the Mars Perseverance rover, resulting in the first AI-planned drive on Mars.
Software developers are powerful advocates for Claude—they understand how systems work, have credibility
evaluating technical tools, and often serve as internal champions for adopting new technologies. Winning their
trust creates a foundation for broader diffusion of Virtual Collaborators across enterprise workforces. We are
already seeing this pattern play out with non-technical teams increasingly adopting Claude Code and Claude
Cowork to manage their own workflows.
Claude Cowork
All digital work is ultimately an expression of code, and Claude’s mastery of it powers Virtual Collaborators
capable of handling complex work far beyond software development. Claude Cowork extends the same agentic
architecture of Claude Code to knowledge workers broadly by translating a user’s intent into completed work,
autonomously reading files, navigating applications, and executing multi-step workflows on a user’s desktop
while the underlying code is abstracted away. By extending beyond Claude Code with applications purpose-built
for specific professions and industry verticals, we accelerate Claude’s diffusion into new categories of knowledge
work and deepen our presence across the enterprise.
As of September 30, 2026, adoption of Claude Cowork,
191
Table of Contents
which we made available as a research preview in January 2026, outpaced the adoption that Claude Code
achieved at the equivalent point following its research preview release in February 2025. In September 2026,
we began merging Claude Cowork and Claude.ai, bringing agentic and conversational work into a unified
application. Users can now move from a simple question to complex, multi-step tasks in the same conversation.
Extending Virtual Collaborators
We believe the trajectory for Virtual Collaborators is clear and accelerating. Each
generation of Claude models
has expanded along multiple dimensions: the depth and rigor of their reasoning, the duration and autonomy of
the work they can sustain, the complexity of tasks they can complete, and the volume of useful output they can
produce.
Capability evaluations and benchmarking have shown substantial improvements across Claude model
versions in the duration and complexity of tasks that can be completed reliably, with more recent model
versions demonstrating particularly significant advances.
We are building towards a world where Claude can be given open-ended tasks lasting hours, days, or weeks,
and then execute them autonomously with the judgment and initiative of a brilliant colleague. Ultimately,
millions of Virtual Collaborators can run in parallel, each working independently on unrelated problems or
collaborating seamlessly to achieve a shared objective. The result is something without historical precedent:
what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a data center, available to every organization and sector of the
economy.

Claude Platform—A Composable System for Building AI Solutions
We seek to bring Claude to every corner of the economy at whatever level of autonomy each task demands, from
a single suggestion to an agent that runs independently for hours. Achieving this goal requires more than a
192
Table of Contents
capable model. The most demanding deployments need intelligence that is reliable, connectable, and
deployable within the specific data environments, regulatory constraints, and workflow patterns of each
organization. Intelligence is one limiting factor, but so are connectors that do not yet exist, governance
frameworks that are not yet written, and orchestration logic that needs to be built from scratch. Our platform
seeks to close these gaps, and we believe the breadth and speed with which we have done so is a primary reason
customers build on Claude.
Our platform provides our customers with direct access to the primitives to build, deploy, and scale AI-native
applications. At the foundation are model capabilities that make Claude’s autonomy possible: native tool use,
computer use for desktop control, memory, and extended thinking. Long context and low-latency model
variants make that action sustainable: for example, an agent could hold an entire codebase, a full data room, or
hours of accumulated task state in working memory and iterate fast enough that autonomy persists rather than
stalls. Above these sit composition primitives such as our Agent Software Development Kit (“SDK”), Claude
Managed Agents, agent skills, multi-agent orchestration, and the Model Context Protocol (“MCP”) for universal
connectivity to enterprise data and tools. Together, these assemble into complex production workflows.
These building blocks are composable and interoperable. The same primitives that power a coding agent also
power a research agent, a financial analyst agent, or a compliance-review agent. While these agents have
different connectors and agent skills, they have the same SDK, protocol, and orchestration framework. That
composability is one of the reasons our customer base spans across industries and why customer expansion can
happen seamlessly across additional use cases without significant integration work.

Diffusion: Intelligence Available Everywhere
Our distribution strategy is built around one objective: getting Claude’s intelligence in the hands of every

Intelligence-Led Growth
. Our platform and applications are the primary mechanism through which Claude’s
intelligence reaches users. As users begin building, brainstorming, and problem-solving with Claude, they

experience firsthand what frontier AI makes possible and expand their usage significantly. This pattern repeats
across organizations: prosumers become internal champions, teams expand their use of Claude, and what
begins as a single workflow grows into something that impacts how an entire organization operates.
Direct Teams
. This organic adoption is complemented and enhanced through our direct go-to-market teams

to build executive sponsorship and drive enterprise-wide adoption.
Applied AI Teams
. Our Applied AI teams embed more deeply with select customers, building solutions that
make it easier for organizations to benefit from Claude’s intelligence. They work with enterprises to design and
deploy custom solutions, specialized workflows, and domain-specific implementations tailored to the
customer’s own requirements. This work drives deeper adoption within individual customers and generates the
feedback and information from users that help to shape our platform and product roadmap. Our direct and
Applied AI teams work together as a hybrid sales and engineering function, organized by geography and then by
industry so that they bring domain expertise to each customer.

.

advantages. First, Amazon, Google, and Microsoft each host Claude natively on their respective cloud

Our Models, Platform, and Applications
We are building at every layer of frontier AI. Our Claude model family provides the underlying intelligence. Our
Claude Platform makes that intelligence available as a set of composable primitives that developers and
enterprises can assemble into their own solutions. Our applications draw on those same primitives, packaged
into products customers can deploy directly. Because we build these layers cohesively, improvements at any
layer compound across the stack and benefit our customers. We believe this integrated approach has made us a
partner of choice for customers transforming their business through AI. Customers can adopt, govern, and scale
our technology immediately, and each new primitive and application we release expands the range of workflows
they can run on Claude.
Our platform unifies frontier intelligence with the harnesses, connectors, governance, and orchestration that
are all required to put that intelligence into production. As customers build on the primitives we provide,
Claude becomes an integral part of their data, workflows, and institutional knowledge, and the relationship
deepens with each integration. We open our platform to all builders because we believe enabling a wide range of
companies to build on Claude generates more innovation and value than we could create on our own.
We build first-party applications to demonstrate where frontier models are heading and to deliver fully
integrated solutions where we have a distinct viewpoint on the workflow. Applications like Claude Code and
Claude Cowork are early examples of what the future of agentic work might look like; they put our latest AI
capabilities directly into the hands of users while accelerating the market’s understanding of AI’s possibilities.
Because our research and product teams work side by side, new model capabilities inform our products and
customer feedback on those products informs our research priorities. This allows us to build products for where
we believe model capabilities are going, not just where they are today. For example, we designed Claude Code
around the agentic coding capabilities we expected our models to achieve, which positioned it to scale rapidly as
those capabilities arrived. We have taken a similar approach with Claude Cowork.
We also design our products to close the gap between what Claude can do and how fully customers use it, which
we believe is important to helping customers realize the value of frontier intelligence. Rather than requiring
customers to learn how the underlying models work, we build products that allow them to interact with Claude
as they would with a colleague, simply and naturally, so they can adopt new capabilities as they become
available. We believe that as we extend the frontier and broaden our application surfaces, customers realize
value faster, embed
Claude more deeply into their operations, and increasingly rely on us as a primary provider
for their AI
transformation
