The Claude Model
Family
The Claude model family is currently composed of four model classes: Mythos (including Fable), Opus, Sonnet,
and Haiku. Our model classes can be used individually for certain tasks or in combination with one another.
They offer broad flexibility to choose the ideal performance, cost, and speed for each use case. All models
support text, code, and multimodal inputs.
•
Mythos (including Fable)
. Our most capable model class, delivering frontier performance across all
domains and solving problems AI has not reliably handled before, especially in coding and long-
running agentic tasks. Given its advanced capabilities in sensitive areas like software vulnerability
discovery and biology, we deploy this underlying model in two distinct configurations. Fable is
generally available and runs with our production safeguards, which block or limit performance on
certain sensitive topics, including by routing requests to a less capable Claude model. Mythos runs with
safeguards calibrated for vetted organizations and individuals doing cybersecurity and life sciences
work, and is available through our trusted-access programs, including our Cyber Verification Program.
We first made the class available in April 2026 as Claude Mythos Preview through Project Glasswing,
made Fable 5 generally available and offered Mythos 5 to Project Glasswing participants in June 2026,
and released Mythos 5.1 and Fable 5.1 in September 2026.
•
Opus.
Our powerful workhorse model class for reasoning-intensive tasks. Our most recent Opus
release, Claude Opus 5.5, is designed to serve as the enterprise daily driver, powering agents that run
projects end to end and advancing capabilities across agentic coding, computer use, and knowledge
work. Opus models consistently rank among leading models on key industry benchmarks.
•
Sonnet.
Our versatile model class for everyday tasks, providing a balance of performance, cost, and
speed for the widest set of general-purpose use cases, including high-volume sub-agents in multi-agent
orchestration setups.
•
Haiku.
Our lowest-cost and fastest model class. Haiku models are designed for high-volume workloads
like customer service agents and large-scale document processing.

The Claude Platform
Customers choose Claude for more than the models. The Claude Platform lets developers and businesses build,
manage, and deploy agentic AI applications on infrastructure with high reliability, security, and availability.
Platform Features
Platform features enable developers to customize their usage of Claude, including:
•
Extended Thinking
. Claude can perform additional internal reasoning before producing a final
response, working through complex, multi-step problems to improve response quality on tasks like
analysis, math, and coding.
•
Adaptive Thinking
. Claude automatically calibrates whether a given request calls for extended
reasoning and how much reasoning to apply—so developers get the benefits of extended reasoning
without configuring reasoning levels request by request.
•
Effort Controls
. Developers can specify an effort level on each request to guide how much reasoning
Claude applies, allowing them to balance response quality against cost and latency.
•
Tool Use.
Claude can natively call external functions and APIs throughout a conversation, with support
for parallel execution and interleaved thinking between tool calls. The search tool loads only the tools
required for a given task on demand, which can reduce token overhead compared to loading full tool
libraries upfront.
•
Long Context
. Claude supports large context windows and maintains its strong performance even as
inputs grow, meaning that developers can include entire codebases, large document sets, or long agent
histories in a single request.
•
Structured Outputs.
Developers can constrain Claude’s responses to a specified schema, such as valid
JSON (JavaScript Object Notation), so results integrate reliably with downstream systems and
application code with less additional parsing or validation.
•
Code Execution
. A sandboxed execution environment where Claude can write, run, and iterate on code
within an agent loop, which is foundational for data analysis and automation workflows. This
environment lets Claude call tools and process large volumes of data more efficiently and run the
scripts packaged in Agent Skills.
•
Web Search
. A native tool giving Claude access to real-time web information, enabling grounded,
citation-aware responses in production applications.
•
Files API.
Allows developers to upload documents once and reference them across multiple sessions,
simplifying workflows that depend on persistent documents.
Context Management
Developers can connect context to Claude for their agents and applications using context primitives.
•
Model Context Protocol.
MCP is an open standard we introduced in November 2024 and donated to
the Linux Foundation’s Agentic AI Foundation in December 2025. MCP defines a universal interface
through which Claude, as well as other AI tools, can connect to enterprise data sources, tools, and
workflows. Claude Platform’s native MCP connector handles connection management, tool discovery,
and error handling automatically.
•
Agent Skills.
A modular framework that lets organizations encode repeatable tasks, workflows, and
domain expertise into reusable packages, or skills, that Claude loads on demand. We provide pre-built
skills for common formats like Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF, while custom skills can capture
anything from engineering standards and regulatory processes to proprietary toolchains. These skills
turn institutional knowledge into agent capabilities.
201
Table of Contents
•
Model Hardware Standard
. Currently in research preview, our Model Hardware Standard enables AI
agents to find, understand, and safely operate lab and manufacturing equipment such as microscopes,
liquid handlers, and off-the-shelf robotic arms. Our Model Hardware Standard is model-agnostic and
lets any agent harness reach devices with a programmable interface through standard protocols such as
MCP.
Infrastructure
The Claude Platform offers high reliability and availability for enterprise-grade agentic workloads. Customers
building on Claude need the model served dependably wherever they operate, they need it to run efficiently at
scale and speed, and they need the tooling that allows a model to work on its own. We operate that
infrastructure so our customers do not have to build and maintain it themselves.
•
Availability
. The Claude Platform is available directly from Anthropic and through the major cloud
providers, including AWS, GCP, and Azure. Feature availability varies by deployment.
•
Cost, Speed, and Scale
. Developers can tune how Claude runs to fit the performance and economics of
each workload:
◦
Prompt Caching
. Large, reused prompt components can be cached for up to one hour, reducing
cost by up to
approximately 97%
and latency by approximately 60% for long prompts, compared
with processing the same requests without caching.
◦
Batch Processing
. Enables high-volume asynchronous processing at reduced cost.
◦
Fast Mode
. Delivers lower-latency responses for latency-sensitive and interactive applications
where speed is critical.
Harnesses
A model alone is not an agent. Running one reliably in production is challenging, because agents must survive
crashes and interruptions, act on systems with scoped and auditable credentials, and scale across variable
workloads. Autonomous operation requires a harness, which provides the secure environment, credentials,
memory, and orchestration loop a model needs to plan, call tools, verify its work, and complete a task safely on
its own. Building and operating that infrastructure is specialized, continuous work that, until recently, each
customer had to take on themselves. We offer two ways to run a harness on the Claude Platform:
•
Agent SDK.
This solution makes the same production-grade harness that powers Claude Code available
to all developers, to run on their own compute. It provides built-in context management, session
handling, multi-agent coordination, and prompt optimization, so customers can build and run
sophisticated agents on their own infrastructure in a fraction of the time otherwise required.
•
Claude Managed Agents.
An out-of-the-box solution in which we operate the harness on our
customers’ behalf, on Anthropic-managed compute. We host the sandboxes, store the credentials,
maintain the memory, and run the agent loop; customers define their agent’s tasks, tools, and
guardrails. When a new model becomes available, customers do not need to rebuild their agent loop.
Direct Applications and Integrations
Our platform primitives and models are the foundation for all of our products and support a wide range of use
cases, from coding agents to specialized products in life sciences, finance, security, and more. Paired with our
deep understanding of current and future capabilities of our models, this foundation allows us to rapidly deliver
products that unlock value across many user types and workflows.
•
Claude Code.
A coding agent, available as a terminal tool, desktop app, web interface, and mobile app,
with native integrations for GitHub and popular IDEs (Integrated Development Environments).
Claude Code handles multi-step software development tasks—planning, writing, editing, testing,
debugging, and committing code—across large codebases with sustained context and supports parallel
agent sessions, so a single developer can keep multiple tasks moving in parallel.

Our Data Center Strategy
Historically, we purchased compute under fixed-time agreements. As our compute requirements have scaled,
we have transitioned to a hybrid model in which, in addition to purchasing compute as a cloud service, we also
procure specialized AI accelerators directly and operate this hardware in dedicated data center facilities leased
and operated on our behalf, to our specification. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic
Direct. This transition is driven in part by the scale of our compute requirements as well as the potential long-
term economic advantages of direct infrastructure leasing and hosting.
Our first data center facility became
operational this year.
Anthropic Direct also lets us separate our commitment to data center capacity from our commitment to the AI
accelerators deployed inside it. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction
of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger
accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain.
Our data center infrastructure strategy includes several contractual arrangements that, taken together, form a
new source of compute to supplement the capacity we procure from our CSPs. Such arrangements include the
following:
•
Compute Infrastructure Equipment.
We procure specialized AI accelerators and associated
components, including CPUs and high-bandwidth memory, through master equipment leases,
including the 2026 Lease Arrangement, pursuant to which we receive such hardware for deployment in
dedicated data center facilities operated by others on our behalf. See the section titled “Management’s
Discussion and Analysis of Financial Condition and Results of Operations—Liquidity and Capital
Resources—Contractual Obligations—Infrastructure Equipment Leases” for more information
regarding the terms of these leases.
•
Data Centers.
In certain of our data center infrastructure arrangements, third-party partners procure
the underlying real estate, power, and data center facilities, while we lease capacity in those facilities
and contract with specialized third-party operators for ongoing facility management. For example, we
have entered into a colocation and services agreement with Fluidstack USA I Inc. (“Fluidstack”), under
which Fluidstack provides data center development and operations services to us. We have also
executed data center leases directly and expect to do so increasingly over time. To secure certain data
center development projects, which require significant capital commitments in advance of deployment,
we have in some cases relied, and expect to continue to rely, on arrangements with financing sources or
partners who guarantee the lease obligations to support the development of data center capacity that is
expected to host such partner’s chips or computing infrastructure. Our ability to expand compute and
infrastructure capacity through these arrangements in the future may depend on the continued
willingness and ability of a limited number of CSPs, partners, and financing sources to enter into and
perform under them.
•
Electrical Power.
Electrical power procurement requires separate arrangements with utility providers
or, in some cases, development of behind-the-meter power generation capacity that supplies electricity
directly to the facility rather than through the broader electric grid. Securing adequate power capacity
for data center projects, whether through grid-connected or behind-the-meter arrangements, typically
requires long lead times and significant financial commitments well in advance of when facilities
become operational.
Our data center infrastructure projects are currently located primarily in the United States. As we continue to
expand our global customer base and research operations
, we are pursuing additional data center capacity
internationally to support our full range of workloads.

enterprises deploy Claude in mission-critical production workflows—for example, underwriting insurance

sectors where the cost of unreliable AI is prohibitive and trust cannot be retrofitted.
In addition, leading AI-native companies build next-generation coding tools, design platforms, and productivity
applications on Claude. Government and research institutions also apply Claude to work that ranges from
materials science to energy security; mission-driven organizations use Claude to compress the expected
timeline of scientific research, clinical workflows, and the delivery of public benefits.
Our customer base has grown rapidly in both the number and scale of customer relationships, with
organizations expanding from initial use cases into enterprise-wide production deployments. As of September

more than

Our customers fall into two primary categories: enterprises and prosumers.
Enterprises
Our enterprise customers include a wide range of organizations deploying AI at scale, from AI-native startups
building products to the world’s largest organizations that require enterprise-grade security, governance, and
compliance before a single workflow impacts production. We serve this full spectrum from a single composable
platform, providing frictionless access to our frontier models as well as the controls customers require, such as

Software developers remain a critical adoption force within enterprises: they are simultaneously customers, the

into our roadmap and deepens our customer relationships with every release.
Prosumers

prosumers build agentic workflows across their applications without writing code, accomplishing in minutes
what previously required hours of manual effort.
Prosumers are some of our earliest adopters and often among our most discerning users. They test out

How Claude Drives Value for Customers
Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and
embedded intelligence in their products
. These outcomes are different expressions of the same intelligence,
each drawing on the same models and primitives.
More Productive Employees.
Adoption most often begins here. An individual experiences the impact that a
frontier AI model can have on their own output—for instance, hours of financial analysis or code review
completed in minutes—and that conviction spreads from the first user to their team, and from one team to the
entire company. This happens for Claude Code in software development; Claude Cowork delivers this for
knowledge workers more broadly. Our Claude Enterprise plan provides the governance, security, and
administration to support adoption of Claude at organizational scale.
Faster Processes.
As adoption deepens, Claude stops being something employees consult and starts being
something the organization runs on. As organizations encode more of their workflows into Claude—their data,
systems, conventions, and prior work—the platform becomes more valuable for them. Claude can draw on that
accumulated context to suggest the next workflow worth automating, reducing the effort required for each
successive deployment.
Embedded Intelligence.
At the deepest level, Claude moves from an operational advantage to a commercial one.
Product teams build on the Claude Platform to embed frontier AI into their own products, including customer-
facing agents, AI-native features, and entirely new product lines that were not previously viable without AI
capabilities. Claude is both a tool the organization uses and an ingredient in the value it delivers to its own
customers.
Across all three dimensions, a significant share of expansion requires minimal to no new deployment at all.
Each new version of a Claude model is designed to improve the performance of existing use cases: employees
produce higher-quality work, encoded processes run with greater accuracy and reliability, and embedded
products deliver more value to end users.
As a result, customers can increase usage, utilize higher subscription
tiers, and bring additional workflows onto the platform without a new sales cycle or procurement decision.
Despite the pace of adoption, we believe we are in the earliest stages of penetrating the frontier AI opportunity.
Most enterprises that use Claude today have deployed it across a small number of teams and use cases relative
to the scope of work Claude can address today, and the scope of work we believe Claude can address in the
future. We believe most knowledge workers globally have not yet used frontier AI. As each new version of a
Claude model advances in capability, the range of tasks and workflows that become viable on the platform
continues to expand. Because we operate the platform and offer applications, model advances reach our
customers through

channels
simultaneously.

Our Culture, Values, and Talent
Anthropic
was founded by a team of researchers who believe that the most consequential technology in history

dimension of the organization: how we hire staff, the research we perform, the policy positions we adopt, and
the choices we make about the deployment of our models. As a result, we are able to achieve breakthroughs that
we believe would be impossible in a culture where safety, model capability, and commercial success are treated
as opposing forces.
All seven of Anthropic’s co-founders remain active leaders in the organization. It is uncommon to see this level
of continuity among the founding team of a technology company, including other major frontier AI labs. The
continuity reflects a genuinely mission-driven and high-trust team.
Our Culture
Several features of our culture are distinctive and difficult for any organization to replicate:
•
We Use What We Build

, and Claude is embedded
in workflows across all teams at the company. When every team relies on the product daily, the
feedback loop between builder and user is compressed: deficiencies can be found rapidly, and
improvements are felt company-wide.

Researching Both Safety and Capability
. At the same time we advance frontier AI, we develop the
policies and techniques designed to keep our models safe. We were the first frontier AI lab to adopt a

developed by the same researchers who build our models. Our alignment and mechanistic
interpretability research are examples of active scientific fields that help us understand ever-more-

TTM revenue per employee was over $6.6 million
—a reflection of extraordinary talent density and a
culture built to compound it. Our employees are known internally as “Ants”—a nickname that captures
the collaborative, ego-light culture of the team. Ants include many of the researchers and developers
defining the frontier of AI, alongside proven operators across disciplines. Shared purpose paired with
low ego translates directly into less organizational friction and greater impact per employee. Claude
compounds that impact further: Ants use Claude across every function to take on work that would

output.

Rigor Applied to Every Function
. A majority of our workforce works in research, engineering, and

our policy team publishes detailed policy frameworks and proposals; our go-to-market team co-

where the best argument wins, not the loudest voice or the most senior title. The result is a company
where the distance between a research insight and a released product is unusually short.

Research Lab Identity and the Research-to-Product Pipeline
We are first and foremost a research lab. We develop the foundational science to train frontier models, perform
rigorous research to understand these models’ inner workings, and develop techniques to align these models to
human values and make them safe.
Research Philosophy
Our research culture is organized around a principle we apply across the company: do the simple thing that
works. We pursue continuous, empirically validated improvements to data composition, model architecture,
and training methodology, all of which must demonstrate measurable gains that hold as models increase in
scale. This is why we currently focus on software development and agentic capabilities: these are areas where
economic impact is large; where safety concerns manifest, making them a test bed for safety research; and
where outputs are largely verifiable.
230
Table of Contents
Every research project must ultimately advance our mission. This focus also guides what we choose not to
pursue. For example, we do not currently focus on developing video and image generation models, despite their
commercial appeal. That compute instead goes to coding, agentic skills, and safety research—a research
decision that has also aided the capital efficiency of our models.
Our research culture is highly collaborative and transparent. When multiple teams pursue parallel approaches,
the norm is to consolidate behind the approach with the best empirical results rather than the loudest voice or
most senior person in the room. This requires institutional trust we have built since our earliest days, and we
believe it is a primary reason our research velocity has scaled significantly faster than headcount.
How Research Becomes Product
Anthropic was founded on the empirical conviction that Scaling Laws are the primary engine of AI progress. We
operate with a sustained rigor in how we allocate research resources, including talent and compute, and
measure whether each investment translates into scaled model performance. We believe that sustained and
focused research can allow us to advance at an accelerated rate beyond what Scaling Laws alone predict through
our compute multiplier advancements that have allowed us to push the frontier of model capability
with better
compute efficiency.
Pre-training.
Our pre-training process operates as a disciplined pipeline. Researchers propose potential
improvements to model architecture, training methodology, or data composition, and each candidate is then
validated at a smaller scale before we permit it to consume large amounts of compute. We set a high bar for
inclusion in a frontier training run; we require evidence that demonstrates a given improvement holds as
models increase in size. Frontier training runs are themselves planned capital deployments with defined inputs
and strict inclusion criteria. Although not every run performs as our researchers expect, the process is designed
to turn research investment into predictable capability gains with greater consistency over time.
Post-training.
Pre-training produces raw model capability. During post-training, that capability is refined into
practical utility—the ability to write production-quality code, operate software tools, follow complex multi-step
instructions, and act autonomously on a user’s behalf. This phase has evolved from a minor adjustment step
into one of the largest areas of our research investment, reflecting evolution in model capability from
conversational assistants to autonomous agents that perform tasks independently. Post-training centers on
training models against complete, realistic tasks whose complexity reflects the demands of real professional
environments. We have made substantial proprietary investments in developing this task portfolio, and its
breadth and realism constitute one of our most durable scientific advantages, which we believe is difficult to
observe from outside the organization and correspondingly difficult to replicate.
Inference.
Our model architecture and inference infrastructure are co-designed. AI researchers and inference
infrastructure engineers share planning cycles, reporting lines, and performance targets. Model architecture
decisions are made with inference economics as a priority, which is why successive versions of Claude models
can deliver both higher capability and greater efficiency than their predecessors.
Safety Research is Core to Our Business
Any technology that is powerful enough to produce the enormous benefits that we believe AI will bring also
poses risks. Responding to these risks requires a portfolio of safety research that spans how we train, evaluate,
interpret, secure, and monitor our models.
Anthropic’s
Responsible
Scaling Policy
Our Responsible Scaling Policy describes how we approach the catastrophic risks posed by AI. The policy
requires us to regularly publish detailed risk reports that reflect our perspectives on the overall level of risk
posed by our models and how we are mitigating such risks. Our teams test each model extensively before
release, assessing its capabilities in the domains most relevant to catastrophic risk and evaluating the extent to
which the model can be misused. Our risk report describes an overall assessment of the results of these
evaluations, the mitigations we have implemented to address these risks, and whether, and if so, why, we
believe the identified risks are justified by corresponding benefits. As part of the current version of our
Responsible Scaling Policy, we publish a Frontier Safety Roadmap, detailing our plans for measurable advances
231
Table of Contents
in security, alignment, safeguards, and AI policy. This acts as an internal spur for safety research and
development and is externally visible so customers and regulators can use it to gauge our progress.
Consistent
with this approach, we assess the risks of each model during development and before and after release and we
take the steps we believe are appropriate to mitigate those risks. In the past, these steps have included delaying
the release of new models and limiting their initial availability, such as our initial release of Mythos through
Project Glasswing, and in the future, as we learn more about model capabilities and behavior, could include
additional measures that affect how and when we develop or release these new models. We believe these
practices also serve our customers, since rigorous safeguards and predictable model behavior have become
decisive criteria when selecting an AI partner.
Claude’s Constitution
We have developed a constitution for Claude that describes our vision for how an AI model should be and how
it should behave, which is used directly in the model training process. We have used Claude’s constitution to
meaningfully advance how frontier models are trained, and it is our attempt to grapple with the most difficult
questions regarding the development of this new type of artificially intelligent entity. It is a living document
that we intend to revise as we develop further models and learn more about how they work. Our researchers
have found that training Claude on high-quality constitutional documents combined with fictional stories
portraying an aligned AI contributes to reducing Claude’s misalignment rate. We believe Claude’s constitution
has also proven commercially valuable: transparently laying out the values we intend Claude to hold increases
customer trust.
This constitution orients Claude around four priorities:
•
Be Broadly Safe.
Avoid irreversible actions and support human oversight of AI behavior.
•
Be Broadly Ethical.
Maintain honesty and sound moral judgment, and avoid harmful acts.
•
Be Compliant with our Guidelines
. Adhere to our operational standards for user interactions and
absolute prohibitions on certain categories of harm.
•
Be Genuinely Helpful.
Deliver substantive, expert-level assistance that creates real value for users.
Model Validation and Training Data
Beyond the assessments performed under our Responsible Scaling Policy, we evaluate each Claude model prior
to its release through a structured, multi-stage evaluation program covering model capabilities, safety
behaviors, and societal impacts, including bias and discrimination, and we document the results of these pre-
deployment evaluations, and their limitations, in our publicly available model system cards. This testing
addresses the reliability and accuracy of model outputs, including through capability and accuracy
benchmarking, evaluations focused on factual accuracy and hallucinations, evaluations of whether model
outputs are honest and accurately reflect the information on which they are based, reliability testing of agentic
performance over long-running tasks, and adversarial red-teaming designed to identify ways in which a model
may fail or behave in unintended ways. Where these evaluations identify issues, we address them through
additional post-training, adjusted safeguards, and re-evaluation prior to release, and we document residual
limitations in the applicable model system card.
Claude models are trained on data drawn from a broad range of sources, modalities, and languages, including
publicly available information from the internet, datasets licensed or commissioned from third parties, and
other sources, such as synthetic data generated by our own models. We conduct diligence on third-party data
sources to assess their quality, provenance, and suitability for our usage, and in many cases include contractual
restrictions intended to discourage the inclusion of personal data in sourced datasets. We apply data curation
and filtering processes to sourced data, which are designed to improve data quality, deduplicate content, and
reduce potential exposure to harmful content.
We address bias and fairness risks at multiple stages of model training and deployment. We manage the
representativeness and diversity of our training data through a layered approach in which dataset curation,
post-training alignment, pre-deployment evaluation, and deployment safeguards each play a part, rather than
through dataset composition alone. When deployed, our usage policy prohibits the use of Claude for
232
Table of Contents
discriminatory decision-making and requires human oversight for high-stakes automated decisions, such as
those affecting employment, housing, or legal issues. Our validation, safeguards, and monitoring practices
continue to evolve as model capabilities advance and as new risks and failure modes are identified.
Further, we have obtained ISO/IEC 42001 certification, an international standard established by the
International Organization for Standardization (“ISO”) and the International Electrotechnical Commission
(“IEC”), following an independent third-party audit of our AI management system, covering risk identification,
assessment, and mitigation processes for the responsible development and deployment of AI. Compliance
documentation, including our ISO/IEC 42001 certificate and SOC 2 (System and Organization Controls 2)
reporting, is available upon request through
the trust center page of our website
. We also provide pre-
deployment model access to external evaluators, including government AI evaluation bodies such as the U.S.
Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (the “CAISSI”) and the U.K. AI Security
Institute, for recent frontier models, as described in our model system cards.
Alignment
As AI models grow more capable, ensuring safe and predictable behavior becomes more challenging. Our
Alignment team focuses on whether models behave as intended, and do not take unwanted actions of their own
accord. The team evaluates models to surface undesirable behaviors and develops comprehensive safety
evaluations, many of which we open source.
Misaligned behaviors, whether occurring in testing or real-world
deployments, have been observed across the industry and include examples of models circumventing network
and sandbox restrictions, granting themselves permissions they had not been given, taking unintended actions
in pursuit of assigned goals, interfering with other AI agents, and misrepresenting whether tasks had been
completed or verified. As models are granted greater autonomy, permissions, and integration with internal and
external systems, the consequences of such misaligned behavior may increase. For more information about the
risks related to model misalignment, see the section titled “Risk Factors—Our AI models may behave in
unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party
directed, which could adversely affect our reputation and brand, business, financial condition, and results of
operations.”
Our own internal alignment evaluation shows that our newly released frontier models have
demonstrated improved alignment compared to their predecessors.
Interpretability
Unlike traditional software, where unwanted outputs are traceable to specific bugs, the inner workings of LLMs
like Claude are more inscrutable. Our researchers describe AI models as “grown, not built”—software
developers can set the initial conditions and some constraints, but they cannot fully control any given output or
behavior. This makes assurances about safety—and the diagnosis of problems—far more challenging for AI than
for standard software. Anthropic is widely recognized as a leader in mechanistic interpretability: the science of
how LLMs work. We have developed mathematical techniques to map how models form and connect concepts
as they reason through problems; investigated how they reflect constructs analogous to psychological states and
thought processes; and tested how their behavior can be steered through direct adjustments to internal
representations. We use interpretability research along with other alignment research techniques to test for
unwanted behavioral tendencies before a model release.
Safeguards
Our Safeguards team reduces the risk of Claude producing dangerous, harmful, or undesirable content through
multiple approaches, including probes and classifiers that monitor inputs and outputs, training against specific
attack vectors such as prompt injection, and monitoring for user safety concerns including encouragement of
harmful ideation. When we detect potential violations, enforcement actions range from real-time response
adjustments to account warnings and, in severe cases, termination of the offending user’s accounts. Findings
from ongoing monitoring, external expert stress-testing, and threat intelligence inform our policies, model
training, and detection systems. Identified issues may be addressed through measures such as updates to
detection classifiers, reward-model adjustments during training, and changes to the instructions provided to
our models that guide their behavior (known as system prompts). We also maintain public reporting channels,
including a responsible disclosure policy and a bug bounty program for testing our safety defenses.
233
Table of Contents
We have observed that more capable models are generally better at recognizing and preventing high-stakes
misuse. We believe that robust safety measures and model utility are not inherently in tension, and that safety
can improve alongside the capability of the models themselves.
Our Approach to Model Releases
Each release is accompanied by a detailed system card covering capability and safety evaluations, external
tester reports, and discussion of areas where performance remains limited or where the model shows signs of
unwanted behavior. For example, AI poses clear and present risks in the cybersecurity domain as advanced
models could assist threat actors in security breaches and exploits. Mitigating these risks is a priority across our
research, evaluation, and deployment practices. Before each model release, our Frontier Red Team conducts a
detailed analysis to determine whether new models provide meaningful new capabilities to assist potential
attackers, and our Safeguards team maintains dedicated classifiers and monitoring systems targeting cyber-
related misuse, including prompts related to malware creation, phishing, and infrastructure attacks.
We make decisions about model development and deployment, including whether to begin training a new
model, on a case-by-case basis. Before releasing a frontier model, we consider a variety of factors, such as the
capabilities and behaviors of the specific model at issue and of our models overall, how well our safeguards and
security measures work, and how widely the model would be available. We plan to extend our testing to include
more assessments at each stage of model training: pre-training, post-training, and internal deployment.
Depending on these assessments, we may delay or suspend training or related research, delay releases, or limit
access to models until we have confidence they can be developed and deployed safely. Our assessments are also
informed by voluntary pre-deployment evaluation of certain models by the CAISSI
and the U.K. AI Security
Institute.
For certain models that materially advance the capability of the frontier in areas relevant to national
security, we also provide designated government partners with expanded early access so that they can
independently evaluate model capabilities and safeguards before release.
Based on our analyses, we do not release every model we develop for general use; when the model’s capabilities
warrant caution, we may restrict availability or decline to release entirely
. For example, in April 2026, we
initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available
to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to
its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery.
We later released Fable 5 for general use, but with
safety restrictions on certain cybersecurity, biology, and chemistry capabilities.
Race to the Top
Building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems cannot be the task of one AI company alone. Our goal is to
foster a race to the top in which AI developers compete on the safety and security of their systems, rather than
rushing to release increasingly powerful models without adequate safeguards. In addition to publishing a large
volume of research, we open source our evaluations where possible and participate in groups such as the
Frontier Model Forum to share safety-critical findings with other AI developers. We have also sought to lead by
example in ways that shape industry norms. After we published the first version of our Responsible Scaling
Policy in September 2023, two other leading frontier AI labs adopted similar frameworks within months.
Building on this approach, we have publicly called for “pacing the frontier,” by which we mean establishing
industry-wide standards primarily related to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that AI capabilities
do not advance faster than the safety, alignment, and security practices needed to support them. This call to
pace the frontier contemplates frontier AI developers collaborating with governments and does not describe our
own model development or release timelines, which continue to be informed by our risk assessments. If
standards of this kind are adopted industry-wide through government action or regulation, the rate at which AI
capabilities advance could be faster or slower than it is today, depending on the extent to which safety,
alignment, and security practices advance together with model capabilities. We believe the first step toward
“pacing the frontier” is independent verification of compliance with future regulatory standards, and we have
begun implementing a program under which independent evaluators work alongside our own risk and safety
teams with broad internal access, subject to legal, confidentiality, and security limits.
As part of this program,
we currently anticipate investing at least $1 billion over the next five years to build external reviewer capacity
with Accenture. The terms of this arrangement have not been finalized and are subject to change.
We have also
called on other frontier AI developers to adopt comparable practices to demonstrate that safety commitments in
234
Table of Contents
our industry can be independently verified. We have further supported regulation and oversight of frontier AI,
including measures focused on transparency and independent third-party auditing, and international
coordination, so these practices apply across frontier developers rather than depend on voluntary adoption
alone.
We believe frontier AI companies and governments should take action to strengthen the security of critical
infrastructure against AI-related and other cyber threats, including by:
•
providing responsible model access, funding, training, and hands-on support, particularly for under-
resourced critical-infrastructure defenders;
•
building observability and security tools;
•
working to ensure agentic identities are traceable and accountable;
•
sharing best practices in continuous monitoring;
•
investing in authorized testing, private disclosure, and verified remediation of vulnerabilities; and
•
sharing tools, playbooks, and threat assessments with governments, security partners, and open-source
maintainers.
We believe that by fixing the most dangerous weaknesses, verifying the fixes, and sharing what works, frontier
AI companies and governments can turn today’s AI advances into lasting improvements in security that benefit
everyone. We have committed up to $100 million in cyberdefense-related initiatives through Project Glasswing,
and we expect to devote significant additional resources over time toward strengthening the security of AI
systems and the critical infrastructure that depends on them. The scope, timing, and amount of any such future
investments have not been finalized and remain subject to change based on business, regulatory, and other
considerations, and there can be no assurance that these initiatives will achieve their intended effect.
Our own trajectory demonstrates that commercial success and a serious commitment to safety are not in
tension. We have built one of the fastest-growing businesses in history while maintaining safety as a core
priority at every stage.
Our Commitment to Public Benefit
We founded Anthropic on the belief that the most transformative technology in human history demands an
extraordinary level of responsibility, and that responsibility extends far beyond building safe systems. Our
public benefit purpose is the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term
benefit of humanity—a mission in which safety is central to our work. Powerful AI can deliver immense
benefits, but only if it is developed and deployed with rigorous attention to its risks. At times, that may require
pausing the launch of our own most capable systems if we conclude they cannot yet be deployed safely. It also
means actively working to ensure that the benefits of AI reach everyone, that the organizations and
communities people depend on are strengthened, and that the hardest problems facing humanity are not left to
market forces alone to solve.
Realizing this mission requires understanding how AI is actually being used and how it is reshaping society.
Our Societal Impacts team builds privacy-preserving tools to study real-world, large-scale uses of Claude—
examining how students, educators, and workers use the model, how its values surface in everyday
conversations, and what users hope and fear about the future of AI. This includes what we believe to be the
largest multilingual qualitative study of its kind, in which more than 80,000 people shared in depth how they
see AI shaping their lives. Our Economics team extends this work to the labor market, publishing recurring data
reports and fully open datasets (the Anthropic Economic Index) on how Claude is used across jobs, industries,
and regions, as well as modeling potential future economic scenarios, so that workers, employers, policymakers,
and independent researchers can ground their decisions in evidence and rigorous modeling. To deepen and
broaden the reach of this work, we have established the Anthropic Institute, an effort to share research and
internal data from across Anthropic with external partners and the public, working together to address the
biggest questions posed by Powerful AI.

Competition
We face competition across multiple dimensions of our business. These competitors include:
Model Developers
We face direct competition from companies building frontier models for third-party software developers and
enterprises, including OpenAI and Google, and large, well-capitalized technology companies investing to reach
the frontier. These are well-capitalized organizations with significant financial resources, large existing
customer bases, and the ability to integrate their models into first-party applications sold directly to businesses.
While these competitors have built meaningful market presence, we believe our primary focus on enterprises,
236
Table of Contents
our ability to remain at and define the frontier, our research talent, and the efficiency through which we
maximize our compute investment position us favorably with customers who prioritize model quality, safety,
and reliability.
We also face competition from a broader set of model providers. These include large companies, specialized AI
labs and a growing range of other open-weight or open-source (shared weights, training data, and code) models
released by state actors and international and domestic research organizations. While these models seek to
prioritize cost efficiency over maximum intelligence, we believe our frontier models are highly effective and
efficient across a broad range of workloads, from routine knowledge tasks to customers’ most important
problems. We believe we compete favorably based on our ability to deliver the most capable models for the
problems that demand the highest intelligence, as well as efficiently applying our models to complete everyday
work to deliver high quality results at a lower cost.
First-Party Application Providers
As a platform company, our primary focus is on building the foundation upon which other companies and
software developers can create products and services driven by Powerful AI. However, as we continue to
develop our own first-party applications, we may from time to time compete with enterprise software and
application companies in select categories.
Status Quo
Beyond direct competition, one obstacle to the diffusion of Claude is the natural resistance to change within
organizations. Many enterprises operate with deeply entrenched legacy systems, established workflows, and
institutional processes that have been refined over many years. Adopting frontier AI capabilities such as Claude
often requires substantial change management, including workforce retraining, process redesign, internal
policy development, and shifts in corporate culture. These can introduce friction, cost, and perceived risk that
can delay or prevent adoption. Especially in highly regulated or risk-averse industries — where the perceived
downside risk of major changes can often outweigh the potential benefits — decision-makers might default to
maintaining the status quo.

Intellectual Property
Our intellectual property is an important aspect of our business and helps us to maintain our competitive
position. To establish and protect our rights in our proprietary technology, we rely upon a combination of trade
secret, copyright, patent, and trademark laws and contractual restrictions such as confidentiality agreements,
licenses, and intellectual property assignment agreements.
We control access to our intellectual property and confidential information through internal and external
controls. Access to our most critical intellectual property is tightly controlled, with only a subset of our
workforce able to view or modify these systems. We maintain a policy requiring our employees, contractors,
consultants, and other third parties to enter into confidentiality and proprietary rights agreements to control
access to and maintain non-disclosure of our proprietary information and to protect our property rights.
As part of our broader intellectual property strategy, we have invested in a patent program covering certain
technologies relevant to our business.
As of September 30, 2026, we held 40 issued U.S. patents, with an
additional 67 U.S. patent applications pending (including 32 nonprovisional and 35 provisional), and 26 issued
patents in foreign jurisdictions, with an additional 12 patent applications pending. We continually review our
development efforts to assess the existence and patentability of new intellectual property.
In addition to our patent program, we have an ongoing trademark and service mark registration program
pursuant to which we register our brand names and product names, taglines, and logos in the United States and
other countries, to the extent we determine appropriate and cost-effective. As of September 30, 2026, we held
29 registered trademarks in the United States, with an additional 11 applications pending, and 237 registered
trademarks in foreign jurisdictions, with an additional 261 applications pending.
We intend to pursue additional intellectual property protection to the extent we believe it would be beneficial
and cost-effective. Intellectual property laws and our procedures and restrictions provide only limited
protection, and any of our intellectual property rights may be challenged, invalidated, circumvented, infringed,
misappropriated, or violated. For more information, see the section titled “Risk Factors—If we fail to adequately
protect our intellectual property rights, our competitive position may be impaired, and we may lose valuable
assets, generate reduced revenue, and incur costly litigation to protect our rights, which may adversely affect
our business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
Government Regulation
We are subject to laws and regulations of various jurisdictions and government agencies affecting our
operations and the provision of our models, platform, and applications, and we have been, and expect to
continue to be, subject to inquiries, investigations, and subpoenas by governmental authorities relating to such
laws and regulations. We believe that the responsible development of AI requires thoughtful governance, and
we actively support efforts by governments and regulatory bodies to establish frameworks that promote safe,
beneficial AI. We were founded on the premise that AI systems must be developed with safety and societal
benefit as central priorities, and we believe that well-designed regulation can reinforce those values across the
industry. Because AI development at the frontier is a relatively nascent and rapidly evolving field, the laws,
regulations, and standards in place today were not necessarily designed with these technologies in mind. We
have proactively engaged with legislators, regulators, and other stakeholders in the United States and
internationally to promote the development of regulatory frameworks that we believe are good for society, our
customers, and the long-term health of the economy, and we intend to continue doing so.
For example, we
entered into an agreement with the CAISSI whereby we committed to provide access to our models for testing
and evaluation before and after their public release, agreed to provide model access to the U.K. AI Security
Institute for pre-deployment testing consistent with our agreement with the CAISSI, and publicly endorsed
California’s Transparency in Frontier Artificial Intelligence Act (SB 53).

As an AI technology company, we are subject to rapidly evolving and increasingly complex laws, regulations,
and governmental review across multiple jurisdictions. New laws, rules, regulations, and changes to existing
laws and regulations are continuously being adopted, implemented, and interpreted as governments worldwide
develop frameworks to address AI development, deployment, and safety. The primary areas of regulation that
affect our business include AI-related regulations, data privacy and security, export controls and trade
regulations, and other matters such as intellectual property, employment and labor, competition and antitrust,
consumer protection, and tax.
The following discussion addresses the most significant regulatory areas affecting our business.
AI-Related Regulation
Various governments and regulatory authorities in the United States and other countries have proposed,
enacted, or are considering legislation, regulations, and guidance relating to AI model development and
deployment, data usage, privacy, data protection, transparency, safety, consumer protection, content
generation, intellectual property, cybersecurity, export controls, and competition. For example, in the United
States, AI regulation is developing at both federal and state levels. The National Institute of Standards and
Technology has developed the AI Risk Management Framework, which is currently voluntary but could
potentially inform or shape future mandatory requirements. The FTC and many state attorneys general are
interpreting federal and state consumer protection and privacy and security laws to impose standards for the
online collection, use, dissemination, other processing, and security of data. Various states have enacted or are
considering enacting AI-related legislation. For example, on September 24, 2026, state attorneys general in
New York and New Jersey, together with a coalition of other state and territorial attorneys general, sent a letter
to U.S. Senate and House of Representatives leadership to urge Congress to establish comprehensive federal
legislation and safety protocols for frontier AI. In the EU, the EU AI Act establishes a risk-based framework
categorizing AI systems by potential risk level. General-purpose AI models face obligations including
transparency requirements, technical documentation, EU copyright compliance, and publication of training
data summaries, and those with systemic risk face additional obligations, including model evaluation, systemic
risk mitigation, serious incident reporting, and cybersecurity protection. High-risk systems must meet
requirements for risk management, data governance, documentation, transparency, human oversight, accuracy,
robustness, and cybersecurity. Any actual or perceived non-compliance could result in regulatory
investigations, enforcement actions and other actions, significant fines, litigation, reputational harm, loss of
customer trust, and interruptions in the availability or performance of our products or services; require
unfavorable changes to existing products or services; and delay the introduction of future products or services,
which could have an adverse effect on our business.
We have called for regulation and oversight of frontier AI development, including standards primarily relevant
to the use of AI to accelerate AI development, so that safety, alignment, and security practices advance in
proportion with capabilities. We have also proposed working with the U.S. government and other frontier AI
developers to establish safety and evaluation standards. Certain of the approaches we support, if adopted, could
increase our compliance burdens, limit our product development or deployment flexibility, affect how and
when we develop or release new models, or otherwise slow our growth.
Data Privacy and Security
We collect, store, transfer, and otherwise process various types of data, including personal information, and are
subject to numerous federal, state, local, and foreign laws and regulations addressing privacy, data protection,
security, data localization, and the collection, use, transfer, and other processing of data. In the United States,
these include comprehensive state privacy laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act, which imposes
obligations on us to, among other things, provide specific privacy disclosures, afford privacy rights such as
abilities to opt out of certain processing, selling, or sharing of personal information, and expand consumer
rights to personal information. On the federal level, the FTC and many state attorneys general are interpreting
federal and state consumer protection and privacy and security laws to impose standards for the online
collection, use, dissemination, other processing, and security of data, some of which may be inconsistent.
Outside of the United States, numerous foreign jurisdictions, including the EU, United Kingdom, and other
jurisdictions in which we operate our business, have enacted similar laws and regulations that affect our
business. For example, the EU General Data Protection Regulation and the United Kingdom General Data
Protection Regulation impose stringent requirements upon the processing of personal data. The EU’s Digital
239
Table of Contents
Services Act imposes requirements on online platforms, while the EU’s Data Act introduces rules on data
switching and data sharing. With respect to security, the EU’s Network and Information Security Directive
requires risk management and incident reporting. These laws and regulations may be subject to differing

concerning government access to data. Compliance with these laws and regulations requires significant

interruptions in the availability or performance of our models, platform, and applications, requirements for

offerings, which could adversely affect our business.
Export Controls and Trade Regulations
As a global company, the provision of our models, platform, and applications across borders is subject to laws
and regulations including international treaties, export controls, economic and trade sanctions laws, customs
regulations, and local trade rules around the world. The scope, nature, and severity of such controls vary widely
across different countries and may change frequently over time. Such laws, rules, and regulations may delay the
introduction of our models, platform, and applications or impact our competitiveness through restricting our
ability to do business in certain places or with certain entities and individuals. For example, the U.S.
Department of Commerce continues to tighten export controls and add firms to the Entity List, which identifies
foreign parties that are subject to specific license requirements for the receipt of certain items. Obtaining the
licenses needed to serve or otherwise do business with such parties could limit our ability to conduct business
with certain potential customers.
Such restrictions have already affected our offerings directly. For example, in June 2026, the U.S. Department
of Commerce imposed worldwide export restrictions on our Fable 5 and Mythos 5 models. In collaboration with
the U.S. government and industry partners, we updated our safeguards, and we re-deployed our Fable 5 and
Mythos 5 models once the U.S. government lifted its restrictions. If similar restrictions were to be imposed in
the future, they may limit our ability to recruit talent, to fully utilize our existing workforce, to continue to
improve our models, and to make our products available internationally. For more information, see the section
titled “Risk Factors—Governmental trade controls, including export and import controls, sanctions, customs
requirements, and related regimes, could subject us to liability or loss of contracting privileges or limit our
ability to compete in certain markets.” Additionally, changes in the scope or application of export controls or
other trade restrictions on AI accelerators and compute could impact our access to the infrastructure necessary
to develop and deploy our models, platform, and applications. As this is an emerging technology area,
governments are continuing to refine and could potentially expand the export controls and other trade
restrictions applicable to AI models
and related technologies. These restrictive governmental actions and any
similar measures that may be imposed on U.S. companies by other governments could limit our ability to
conduct business globally.

Other Matters
In February 2026, in response to our publicly stated position that our technology should not be used for mass
domestic surveillance or fully autonomous weapons, the President of the United States stated that he had
directed that all federal executive agencies cease using our technology. At the same time, the Secretary of War
directed the Department of War to designate Anthropic as a “supply-chain risk to national security” and stated
that “effective immediately, no contractor, supplier, or partner that does business with the United States
military may conduct any commercial activity” with us. On March 4, 2026, the Department of War sent us two
letters—one pursuant to 10 U.S.C. § 3252 and the other pursuant to Section 4713 of the FASCSA—asserting that
our models, platform, and applications present a supply-chain risk. These actions referenced above are defined
herein as “Challenged Actions.” We vigorously challenged the Challenged Actions in
Anthropic PBC v.
Department of War, et al.
(N.D. Cal.) and
Anthropic PBC v. Department of War, et al.
(D.C. Cir.). After first
obtaining an order from the United States District Court for the Northern District of California that
preliminarily enjoined the Department of War’s directive and Section 3252 supply-chain risk designation of us
and preliminarily enjoined the other defendant agencies from implementing the Presidential directive until
final resolution of the lawsuit, we subsequently, on August 27, 2026, obtained an order from the United States
District Court for the Northern District of California that largely granted summary judgment in our favor. The
court ruled that the Challenged Actions were retaliatory acts meant to punish us for speech protected under the
First Amendment to the United States Constitution and violated our rights under the Due Process Clause of the
Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution. The court also held that the Secretary of War’s actions,
particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they were in
excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The court entered final judgment
largely in our favor. The defendants filed a notice of appeal of the preliminary injunction. The D.C. Circuit Court
of Appeals, however, denied our motion to stay the Secretary of War’s Section 4713 designation of us as a
supply-chain risk pending review on the merits. On September 25, 2026, in a 2-1 split decision, the D.C. Circuit
Court of Appeals denied our petition for review, ruling that the Department of War’s Section 4713 supply-chain
risk designation was proper, and that our rights under the First Amendment and Due Process Clause of the
Fifth Amendment were not violated. We filed a petition for rehearing en banc asking the full D.C. Circuit to
review the panel’s decision. We cannot predict the ultimate outcome of these lawsuits. While we continue to
work with government agencies, we cannot be certain that the resolution of these lawsuits will not adversely
affect our ability to sell to government agencies and other customers that sell products and services to the U.S.
government, and thus on our business, financial condition, and results of operations.

Our Governance Structure
and
Its Goals
Our novel capital and corporate governance structure has been carefully designed and differs significantly from
that of other public companies. We strive to help bring humanity safely into an era where transformative AI
exerts tremendous and potentially decisive influence over a broad range of human undertakings. Operating as a
PBC gives our board of directors the necessary latitude to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders,
the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and our Company Purpose. In addition, a
financially disinterested LTBT, which generally has the power to elect and remove a majority of the authorized
members of our board of directors, is designed to supply both the incentives and insights for striking this
balance appropriately. We also believe that our seven co-founders are distinctly equipped to be stewards of our
mission.
Public Benefit Corporation
We are incorporated as a PBC under Delaware law, a structure that enables our commitment to AI safety and
responsibility. PBCs are a class of corporations that are intended to produce a public benefit and to operate in a
responsible and sustainable manner. As a PBC, we are required to balance (i) the pecuniary interests of our
stockholders, (ii) the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose.
This requires our board of directors to weigh multiple factors, including relevant long- and short-term
externalities of decisions, alongside the pecuniary interests of our stockholders. To date, we have found that the
safety and societal benefit of AI and consideration of the best interests of all key stakeholder groups have
generally aligned with our long-term commercial success and stockholders’ long-term monetary interests.
However, as a PBC, we may make decisions that we believe appropriately balance the pecuniary interests of our
stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the Company Purpose, but that
negatively impact the short-, medium-, or long-term performance of our business or the market price of our
Class A common stock. There is limited judicial precedent interpreting the balancing requirement applicable to
PBCs under Delaware law, and there is therefore uncertainty as to how a court would view our directors’
balancing of these potentially competing interests. For a discussion of these risks, see “Risk Factors—Our focus
on the long-term best interests of our company as a PBC, and the duty of our directors to balance the pecuniary
interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those stakeholders materially affected by our conduct, and
our Company Purpose, may conflict with short-, medium-, or long-term financial interests and business
performance, which may negatively impact the value of our Class A common stock” and “Risk Factors—As a
Delaware public benefit corporation, we may be subject to increased litigation concerning our board of
directors’ obligation to balance our stockholders’ pecuniary interests, the best interests of those materially
affected by our conduct and our Company Purpose, the occurrence of which may have an adverse impact on our
business, financial condition, and results of operations.”
In measuring our public benefit performance, our board of directors will consider the objectives set forth in our
five mission pillars: that the technical problems of AI safety are solved, that AI safety is a universal practice
backstopped by law, that AI strengthens democracy and global stability, that AI expands prosperity and human
flourishing, and that AI’s benefits are shared by everyone.
We may also address the additional
interests of our
customers, partners, employees, and other stakeholder constituencies that we may identify from time to time.
Neither our amended and restated certificate of incorporation nor our amended and restated bylaws will
require that we measure our public benefit performance against an objective third-party standard, and our
board of directors will be responsible for establishing and overseeing the standards by which to measure our
public benefit performance against these objectives. We currently expect that our objectives and standards will
be qualitative in nature and may evolve over time as our business grows and as our understanding of our public
benefit impact develops.
As required by Section 366(b) of the DGCL, we will provide our stockholders no less than biennially with a
statement assessing our promotion of the Company Purpose and of the best interests of those materially
affected by our conduct. The statement will set out our objectives and standards and describe the actions we
have taken. We intend to make the statement available to stockholders and the public through our website. We
also expect to demonstrate our progress towards these goals by continuing to publish evidence-based research
on our website regarding our work and its impact.

Long-Term Benefit Trust
We created the LTBT, which was designed to ensure that we are managed in a manner that responsibly
balances our tripartite goals as a PBC: (i) the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, (ii) the best interests of
those materially affected by our conduct, and (iii) the Company Purpose. The LTBT is organized as a common
law “noncharitable purpose trust” under Delaware law and governed by the Long-Term Benefit Trust Amended
and Restated Trust Agreement (the “Trust Agreement”). The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent
body of Trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. The LTBT’s
arrangements are designed to minimize the LTBT’s and the Trustees’ exposure to our financial performance
and grant the Trustees sufficient independence to ensure we are striking this balance appropriately.
Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect
and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our
board of directors. Class T common stock has no economic rights.
Decisions regarding our business and affairs are made by our board of directors. While the LTBT has significant
influence over our board of directors through its ability to generally elect and remove Class T directors, neither
the LTBT nor the Trustees have decision-making authority in the day-to-day management or strategy setting of
the company. The LTBT’s role is to select directors who are well-equipped to responsibly balance our tripartite
goals as a PBC, and to support our management’s decision-making through advice and guidance. Certain
actions, such as a merger, consolidation, or sale of all or substantially all of our assets, will require the approval
of our board of directors pursuant to Delaware law, a majority of whom are elected by the LTBT.
Election and Removal of Directors
As the sole holder of Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class
T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our
Class T common stock will not vote on the election or removal of directors elected by the holders of our Class A
common stock and Class F common stock, who will be elected or removed solely by the holders of Class A
common stock and Class F common stock, voting together. For a discussion of the members of our board of
directors who are currently Class T directors and those that will be Class T directors upon the completion of this
offering, see the section titled “Management—Board of Directors.”
Prior to nominating or removing a director, the nominating party must provide at least 30 days’ notice to our
NGC, which notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion
. Following the completion of this offering,
our NGC will be composed of one Class T director and two directors who are not Class T directors and will act
by majority vote.
With respect to one of the Class T director seats (the “Specified Class T Director”), the LTBT’s ability to
nominate that director, to remove that director without cause, or to change the director designated as the
Specified Class T Director is subject to the concurrence of our NGC. If our NGC does not concur with such
nomination, removal, or change in designation within 15 days of receiving notice, the matter will be submitted
to a vote of the holders of our Class E common stock unless the LTBT elects to withdraw the notice. If submitted
to a vote of the holders of Class E common stock, approval of the LTBT’s proposal will require a majority of the
votes cast by our Class E common stock (subject to a quorum of a majority of our outstanding Class E common
stock). The LTBT may withdraw any notice of nomination, removal, or change in designation at any time before
the taking of such a vote. Any Class T director, including the Specified Class T Director, may be removed for
caus
e, which will be determined in accordance with Delaware law,
without the concurrence of our NGC or the
approval of the holders of our Class E common stock; provided, however, that each of the LTBT and the
Founder LLC has agreed to provide 30 calendar days’ notice to the other stockholder and the NGC prior to
effecting a removal of any director for cause.

Trustees of the LTBT
The LTBT is governed by five Trustees. The Trustees have the authority to appoint the Trustees by majority vote
of the Trustees then in office and to remove the Trustees by majority vote of the total number of authorized
Trustees or by the unanimous approval of the other Trustees then in office and the approval of the NGC,
provided that the LTBT must provide at least 30 days’ prior written notice to our NGC before effecting any such
appointment or removal. The notice period is waivable by our NGC in its discretion. Trustees may also be
removed by order of the Court of Chancery of the State of Delaware upon petition by a person designated by the
Trust Agreement as having the power to enforce the agreement if a Trustee has engaged in disqualifying
conduct and removal would best serve the purpose of the LTBT. Trustees will serve annual term
s, and there is
no limit to the number of terms a Trustee may serve.
Trustees are selected based on their expertise in areas
relevant to the LTBT’s purpose, including AI safety, national security, public policy, social enterprise, and
related fields. In practice to date, the Trustees and company executives have collaborated closely on sourcing,
interviewing, and selecting Trustees. Of the five authorized seats for Trustees, one is currently vacant.
Dr. Neil “Buddy” Shah
has served as a Trustee and Chair of the LTBT since June 2023. Dr. Shah will also serve
as an initial manager of the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund. Dr. Shah has served as Chief Executive Officer of the
