Variable Interest Entities
The Company evaluates its ownership, contractual, and other interests in entities to determine if it has a
variable interest in an entity.
These evaluations are complex, involve judgment, and use estimates and
assumptions based on available historical and prospective information, among other factors.
If the Company
determines that an entity for which it holds a contractual or ownership interest is a VIE and that the Company
is the primary beneficiary, the Company consolidates such entity in its consolidated financial statements. An
enterprise having a controlling financial interest in a VIE must consolidate the VIE if it is considered the
primary beneficiary, which is described as having both (1) the power to direct the activities of a VIE that most
significantly impact the VIE’s economic performance and (2) the right to receive benefits or the obligation to
absorb losses of the VIE that potentially could be significant to the VIE. The Company consolidates certain VIEs
formed to finance and deploy compute and infrastructure capacity. Refer to
Note 7
for further information.
Long-Term Benefit Trust
In 2023, the Company established the Long-Term Benefit Trust (“L
TBT
”). The LTBT is intended to operate as
an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public
policy, and social enterprise. In connection with establishing the LTBT, the Company created a class of common
stock (the
“Class T common stock”
) that is held exclusively by the LTBT and gives the LTBT authority to elect
and remove certain of the Company’s directors.
The LTBT is considered a consolidated VIE as it relies on the Company for financial support. The Company is
the primary beneficiary of the VIE as it has the power to direct the activities that most significantly impact the
LTBT’s economic performance, provides financial support to the LTBT, and would receive the LTBT’s financial
assets (other than the Class T common stock) in the event that the LTBT terminates. The Company consolidated
the VIE at inception and will perform on-going reassessments of the VIE based on any reconsideration events
to reevaluate whether a change to the consolidation conclusion is required each reporting period.
The
consolidated balance sheets as of
December 31, 2024
and
2025
and June 30, 2026 (unaudited) include assets of
the LTBT, which can only be used to settle obligations and liabilities of the LTBT. As of
December 31, 2024
and
2025
and June 30, 2026 (unaudited), total assets and liabilities of the LTBT were
not material
.
Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments
Fair value is defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an
orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. In accordance with Accounting
Standards Codification (“ASC”) 820,
Fair Value Measurement
(“ASC 820”), the Company uses the fair value
hierarchy, which prioritizes the inputs used to measure fair value. The hierarchy, as defined below, gives the
highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities and the lowest
priority to unobservable inputs. The three levels of the fair value hierarchy are set forth below:
Level 1: Observable inputs such as quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities.
Level 2: Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in
active markets, quoted prices in markets that are not active or inputs other than the quoted prices that are
observable either directly or indirectly for the full term of the assets or liabilities.
Level 3: Unobservable inputs in which there is little or no market data and that are significant to the fair
value of the assets or liabilities.
The Company’s financial instruments include accounts receivable, short-term investments, prepaid expenses
and other current assets, other assets, accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities,
convertible notes payable, SAFE liabilities, and certain derivative contracts. The estimated fair value of other
financial instruments, including cash and restricted cash, are stated at their carrying value which approximates
fair value due to the short time to the expected receipt or payment date. Additionally, the carrying amounts of
accounts receivable, prepaid expenses and other current assets, accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other
current liabilities approximate fair value due to their short-term nature.

The Company regularly monitors collections and payments from customers and maintains an allowance for
credit losses for estimated losses resulting from the inability of customers or channel partners to make or remit
required payments. Management estimates the Company’s allowance for credit losses by considering factors
such as historical credit loss experience and current conditions, the length of time accounts receivable are past
due, customer payment histories, any specific customer collection issues identified, and current market
conditions which may affect customer financial condition. This assessment is performed on an aggregate basis
when similar characteristics exist within a customer group and on an individual basis when specific customers
with collectability risks are identified. The Company writes off accounts receivable against the allowance when
management determines a balance is uncollectible and no longer actively pursues collection of the receivable.

Property and Equipment, Net
Property and equipment is stated at cost less accumulated depreciation. Depreciation is recorded using the
straight-line method over the estimated useful lives of the related asset, ranging from
three to five years
.
Leasehold improvements are amortized over the
shorter of estimated useful life or the remaining lease term
.
The Company estimates the useful lives of property and equipment upon initial recognition and periodically
evaluates the useful lives and whether events or changes in circumstances warrant a revision to the useful lives.
Maintenance and repair costs that do not extend the useful life of the assets are expensed as incurred.
When assets are retired or otherwise disposed of, the cost and accumulated depreciation are removed from the
accounts and any resulting gain or loss is reflected in the consolidated statements of operations in the period
realized.
Software Development Costs
Software development costs include costs to develop advanced AI models and related software solutions used to
deliver the Company’s services to external users. Software development costs also include costs to develop
software solely for internal use and applications used to support the Company’s operations. Model development
costs are generally expensed as incurred due to the significant development uncertainty inherent in the
development process.
The Company capitalizes qualifying software development costs when (i) management, with relevant authority,
has authorized and committed to fund the software project and (ii) it is probable that the project will be
completed and the software will be used to perform its intended function. Capitalization ceases when the
software is substantially complete and ready for its intended use, including the completion of all significant
testing. Software development costs capitalized were not significant for the years presented.

Evaluation of Long-Lived Assets for Impairment
Long-lived assets, such as property and equipment, right-of-use (“ROU”) assets, and finite-lived intangible
assets subject to amortization, are reviewed for impairment whenever events or changes in circumstances
indicate that the carrying amount of an asset or asset group (collectively, the “asset group”) may not be
recoverable. Recoverability of asset groups to be held and used is measured by comparing the carrying amount
to the estimated undiscounted future cash flows expected to be generated. If the carrying amount exceeds the
undiscounted cash flows, the asset groups are determined to be impaired, and an impairment charge is
recognized as the amount by which the carrying amount exceeds its fair value.
Intangible Assets, Net
Intangible assets which are subject to amortization are amortized on a straight-line basis over their estimated
useful lives, which range from
one
to
six years
. The Company reviews intangible assets which are subject to
amortization for impairment under the long-lived asset model.
Goodwill
Goodwill represents the excess of the purchase price in a business combination over the fair value of net
tangible and intangible assets acquired. Goodwill is not subject to amortization but is tested for impairment on
an annual basis, performed in the fourth quarter of each year, or whenever events or changes in circumstances
indicate the carrying value of the reporting unit may be in excess of the reporting unit’s fair value.
Goodwill is tested for impairment at the reporting unit level by first assessing the qualitative factors to
determine whether it is more likely than not that the fair value of the Company’s single reporting unit is less
than its carrying amount. Qualitative indicators assessed include consideration of macroeconomic, industry,
and market conditions, the Company’s overall financial performance, and personnel or strategy changes. Based
on the qualitative assessment, if the Company determines that it is more likely than not that the Company’s
single reporting unit’s fair value is less than its carrying amount, a quantitative analysis is performed by
comparing the fair value of the Company’s single reporting unit to its carrying value. If the carrying amount of
the reporting unit exceeds its fair value, an impairment loss is recognized in an amount equal to that excess,
limited to the total amount of goodwill allocated to the reporting unit. The Company did not recognize any
goodwill during the years ended
December 31, 2023
and
2024
. No impairment losses related to goodwill were
recognized during the year ended
December 31, 2025
or the six months ended June 30, 2026 (unaudited).
Acquisitions
The Company accounts for acquisitions of entities or asset groups that qualify as businesses in accordance with
ASC 805,
Business Combinations
(“ASC 805”). The purchase price of the acquisition is allocated to the tangible
and intangible assets acquired and liabilities assumed based on their estimated fair values at the acquisition
date. The excess of the purchase price over those fair values is recorded as goodwill. During the measurement
period, which may be up to one year from the acquisition date, the Company may record adjustments to the
assets acquired and liabilities assumed with the corresponding offset to goodwill. Upon the conclusion of the
measurement period or final determination of the values of assets acquired or liabilities assumed, whichever
comes first, any subsequent adjustments are recorded in the consolidated statements of operations.
Leases
The Company determines if an arrangement is a lease at inception. The Company evaluates the classification of
leases at commencement and, as necessary, at modification. The Company, as the lessee, classifies leases with
lease terms longer than
12
months as either operating or finance. A lease is
classified
as a finance lease if it
meets any of
the finance lease classification
criteria in ASC 842 at lease commencement
; all other leases are
classified
as operating leases. The Company’s finance leases are generally those leases that allow the Company
to utilize the asset for a major part of its estimated economic life, that have discounted lease payments that are
substantially all the estimated fair value of the asset, or that include a purchase option which the Company is
reasonably certain to exercise.
The Company leases facilities and equipment under operating and finance leases. The Company determines
whether an arrangement is or contains a lease at inception and records lease liabilities and right-of-use assets
F-20
Table of Contents
Anthropic, PBC
Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
(Continued)
on its consolidated balance sheets at lease commencement. Where the Company’s leases do not provide an
implicit rate, the Company determines its incremental borrowing rate based on the information available at
commencement date in determining the present value of lease payments. The determination of the incremental
borrowing rate is based on an estimate of the Company’s unsecured borrowing rate, adjusted for tenor and
collateralized security features. Lease liabilities are recognized at the present value of the future lease payments
at the lease commencement date. ROU assets are measured based on the corresponding lease liability adjusted
for (i) payments made to the lessor at or before the commencement date, (ii) initial direct costs incurred and
(iii) tenant incentives received, incurred or payable under the lease. The Company does not assume renewals or
early terminations of its leases unless it is reasonably certain to exercise these options at commencement.
Operating lease cost is recognized on a straight-line basis over the lease term. Finance lease ROU assets are
amortized on a straight-line basis over the shorter of the estimated useful life of the underlying asset or, where
title does not transfer at the end of the lease term and the Company is not reasonably certain to exercise a
purchase option, the lease term, and are recognized within operating expenses based on the nature of the leased
asset. The interest component of a finance lease is recognized using the effective interest method over the lease
term and is presented separately from the amortization of the related ROU asset.
Operating lease ROU assets and operating lease liabilities are presented separately on the consolidated balance
sheets. Finance lease ROU assets are included in property and equipment, net. Finance lease liabilities are
included in accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities, and in other noncurrent liabilities.
The Company’s lease agreements may contain lease and non-lease components. Non-lease components related
to the asset being leased are not separated from the lease components and are accounted for as a single lease
component for all existing classes of assets.
The Company made an accounting policy election for lease agreements with a term of 12 months or less and
does not recognize ROU assets and lease liabilities in respect of those agreements. Any payments related to
short-term leases are expensed as incurred.
Variable lease payments are expensed as incurred and are mainly composed of utilities, common area
maintenance, and other operating expenses.
Similar to other long-lived assets discussed above, management assesses ROU assets for impairment whenever
events or changes in circumstances indicate that the carrying amount of such assets may not be recoverable.
Finance lease ROU assets are assessed for impairment together with the Company’s other property and
equipment. For leased assets, such circumstances would include the decision to enter into a sublease for which
estimated cash flows do not fully cover the costs of the associated lease.
Revenue Recognition
The Company generates revenue from customers, including enterprises and
prosumers
, utilizing its intelligence
service, which enables customers to submit text, documents, and other materials (“Prompts”), and receive AI-
generated results (“Results”) from its proprietary Claude model family. Prompts and Results are measured in
the number of tokens consumed. The Company provides the intelligence service through its web, mobile, and
desktop interfaces and APIs as well as through
CSP marketplaces
that distribute the intelligence service to the
Company’s customers. The intelligence service is not available for on-premise download or hosting by
customers.
The Company accounts for revenue under ASC 606,
Revenue from Contracts with Customers
. Revenue is
recognized based on the amount of consideration the Company expects to receive when the Company provides
its intelligence service to customers. Revenue excludes amounts collected on behalf of third parties, such as
sales and indirect taxes, as well as estimated concessions, credits, and refunds.
The Company’s intelligence service is provided on a consumption or subscription basis. Revenue is recognized
when customers use the Company’s intelligence service, based on the quantity of tokens consumed. Intelligence
service provided on a subscription basis is subject
to usage
limits that reset over short periods, which results in
revenue being recognized ratably over the subscription period, which is generally 12 months or less. Payment
terms vary by customer and sales channel but are generally less than 60 days. Subscription fees are generally
prepaid. Certain enterprise contracts may include minimum spend commitments.

When the Company utilizes
CSP marketplaces
that distribute the intelligence service to customers, the
customer receives the same intelligence service as is available through its web, mobile, and desktop interfaces
and APIs, and the intelligence service represents a single promise in customer contracts. In these arrangements,
the Company is the principal and recognizes revenue on a gross basis because the Company has a direct
contractual
relationship with customers, is primarily responsible for providing the intelligence service to
customers, and establishes pricing. The
CSPs in these arrangements
do not obtain control of
the Company’s
intelligence service at any point prior to transfer to the customer.
Deferred Revenue
Deferred revenue consists of amounts billed or received in advance of the Company satisfying its performance
obligations, and is recognized as revenue as services are delivered to customers. Deferred revenue relates
primarily to subscriptions that are subject to usage limits that reset over short periods, which results in revenue
being recognized ratably over the subscription period, which is generally 12 months or less.
Compute and Infrastructure
Compute and infrastructure expenses primarily consist of costs attributable to operating the Company’s
technology infrastructure, which supports the full range of workloads for the Company’s models, including
research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. These costs primarily consist of
cloud compute fees paid to CSPs under committed and on-demand arrangements, including storage,
networking and connectivity, and related support costs, infrastructure costs associated with serving customer
workloads through partner channels, colocation facility costs, equipment leases and committed power costs
associated with the Company’s data center operations, and third-party application infrastructure software costs
directly related to the Company’s compute operations.
Personnel
Personnel expenses primarily consist of stock-based compensation, including expense related to stock options,
restricted stock units (“RSUs”), and restricted stock awards, cash compensation, including base salaries and
bonuses, employee benefits, including health and welfare benefits, and employer payroll taxes.
Bartz Settlement
Bartz settlement consists of the charge the Company recorded in 2025 to settle the Bartz copyright
infringement suit
. Refer to Note 13 for further information.
Sales, Marketing, and Partnerships
Sales, marketing, and partnerships expenses primarily consist of channel partner costs and marketing and
advertising costs, including media and public relations spend.
Advertising costs are expensed as incurred. Advertising expenses were
$33 million
and
$147 million
for the
years ended
December 31, 2024
and
2025
, respectively. Advertising expenses incurred in
2023
were
not
material
.
Other Operating and Administrative
Other operating and administrative expenses primarily consist of charitable donations expense related to the
Company’s donation matching program, vendor costs related to data quality and performance evaluation
services, information technology and cloud software costs, payment processing and platform fees, facility and
occupancy costs, non-income taxes, professional services costs, bad debt expense, and depreciation and
amortization related to non-data center assets.
Stock-Based Compensation
The Company’s equity incentive plan provides for the granting of stock options, RSUs, and restricted stock
awards to employees, consultants, officers, and directors. The Company measures compensation cost for stock-
based awards at grant-date fair value and recognizes it over the requisite service period. The Company accounts

for forfeitures when they occur. The fair value of stock-based awards, granted or modified, is determined on the

Stock Options
Stock-based compensation expense is recognized on a straight-line basis over the period during which an
employee is required to provide services in exchange for the award (generally the vesting period of the award).
The Company determines the fair value of stock options on the date of grant using the Black-Scholes-Merton
option pricing model which is impacted by the estimated fair value of the Company’s common stock, as well as
changes in assumptions regarding a number of highly complex and subjective variables. These variables are
summarized as follows:
•
Fair value of common stock
– Until the Company’s common stock is publicly traded, the Company
must estimate the fair value of common stock. The Company’s board of directors (the “Board”)
considers numerous objective and subjective factors to determine the fair value of the Company’s
common stock including: contemporaneous third-party valuations of the Company’s common stock,
price paid by investors for the Company’s common and redeemable convertible preferred stock, actual
and forecasted operating and financial performance, market conditions, performance of comparable
publicly traded
companies, developments and milestones within the Company, the rights, preferences,
and privileges of the Company’s common and redeemable convertible preferred stock, and the
likelihood and timing of achieving a liquidity event, among other factors.
•
Expected volatility
– Expected volatility is a measure of the amount by which the stock price is
expected to fluctuate. Since the Company has no trading history of its common stock, it estimates the
expected volatility of its underlying common stock as of the grant date of its stock options by taking the
weighted-average historical volatility of a group of comparable
publicly traded
companies over a period
equal to the expected life of the options.
•
Expected term
– Expected term represents the period over which the Company anticipates stock-based
awards to be outstanding. The Company estimates the expected term based on the options’ vesting
term and contractual terms, such that the expected life is equal to the average of the stock-based
award’s weighted-average vesting period and its contractual term.
•
Risk-free interest rate
– The risk-free interest rate used is based on the implied yield in effect at the
time of grant of U.S. Treasury securities with maturities similar to the expected term of the stock
options.
•
Expected dividend yield
– The expected dividend yield is zero, as the Company has never declared or
paid any dividends and has no current plans to do so.
Restricted Stock Units
The Company measures and recognizes stock-based compensation expense for RSUs based on the estimated
fair value of the underlying common stock on the date of grant. The Company’s RSUs vest upon the satisfaction
of both service and performance conditions. The service condition for these awards is generally satisfied over a
four-year vesting period. The performance condition is satisfied upon the occurrence of either (i) a qualifying
change in control of the Company or (ii) a listing of the Company’s equity securities on an established securities
market (including through a traditional public offering, direct listing, or business combination with a special
purpose acquisition company), in each case, on or before the seventh anniversary of the grant date, as further
defined in such RSU agreements. If the performance condition is not satisfied within seven years of the grant
date, all unvested RSUs are forfeited. Compensation cost related to these RSUs must be recognized over the
F-23
Table of Contents
Anthropic, PBC
Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
(Continued)
requisite service period using the accelerated attribution method, if it is probable that the performance-based
vesting condition will be satisfied. The performance-based vesting condition will be deemed probable of being
satisfied upon either the consummation of an acquisition or change in control or the Company’s initial public
offering. As of
December 31, 2025
and June 30, 2026 (unaudited),
no
stock-based compensation expense had
been recognized for the RSUs because management determined that it is not probable that the performance
condition will be achieved.
Redeemable Convertible Preferred Stock
The Company records shares of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
at their respective fair values on the
dates of issuance, net of issuance costs. The
redeemable convertible preferred stock
is recorded outside of
permanent equity because it is not mandatorily redeemable and redemption is contingent upon the occurrence
of certain deemed liquidation events that are not solely within the Company’s control. The Company has not
adjusted the carrying values of the
redeemable convertible preferred stock
to the liquidation preferences of such
shares because it is not probable that a deemed liquidation event would occur that would obligate the Company
to pay the liquidation preferences to holders of shares of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
. Subsequent
adjustments of the carrying values to the liquidation preferences will be made only when it becomes probable
that such a deemed liquidation event will occur.
Foreign Currency
The functional currencies of the Company’s foreign subsidiaries are the local currency or the U.S. dollar
depending on the nature of the subsidiaries’ activities. Monetary assets and liabilities, and transactions
denominated in currencies other than the functional currency are remeasured to the functional currency at the
exchange rate in effect at the end of the period and are recorded in the current period consolidated statements
of operations. Gains and losses resulting from remeasurement are recorded in foreign exchange gains (losses),
net within other income (expense), net in the consolidated statements of operations. Subsidiary assets and
liabilities with non-U.S. dollar functional currencies are translated at the month-end rate, retained earnings and
other equity items are translated at historical rates, and revenue and expenses are translated at average
exchange rates during the year. Cumulative translation adjustments are recorded within accumulated other
comprehensive income (loss), a separate component of total stockholders’ deficit in the Company’s consolidated
balance sheets.
Loss Contingencies
The Company is periodically involved in various legal claims, proceedings and other regulatory and
administrative proceedings that may arise in the ordinary course of business. Certain of these matters may
include speculative claims for substantial or indeterminate amounts of damages. The Company routinely
reviews the status of each significant matter and assesses its potential financial exposure. The Company records
a liability when it believes that it is both probable that a loss has been incurred and the amount can be
reasonably estimated. If the Company determines that a loss is reasonably possible and the loss or range of loss
can be reasonably estimated, the Company discloses the possible loss in the consolidated financial statements.
Because of inherent uncertainties related to these legal matters, significant judgment is required to determine
both the probability and the estimated amount of loss. These estimates have been based on the Company’s
assessment of the facts and circumstances at each balance sheet date and are subject to change based on new
information and future events. As additional information becomes available, the Company reassesses its
potential liability and may
revise
its estimates. If one or more matters were resolved against the Company for
amounts in excess of management’s expectations, the Company’s results of operations and financial condition,
including in a particular reporting period in which any such outcome becomes probable and estimable, could be
materially adversely affected.
Share Repurchase
Share repurchases are recorded on the trade date. When shares are immediately retired, the value of
repurchased shares is deducted from stockholders’ deficit through common stock with the excess over par value
recorded to accumulated deficit.

Income Taxes
The Company uses the asset and liability method to account for income taxes. Current income tax expense or
benefit represents the amount of income taxes expected to be payable or refundable for the current year. Under
this method, deferred income tax assets and liabilities are determined based on differences between the
financial statement reporting and tax bases of assets and liabilities and net operating loss and credit
carryforwards. Deferred tax assets and liabilities are measured using enacted tax rates applied to taxable
income in the years in which those temporary differences are expected to be recovered or settled. Valuation
allowances are established when necessary to reduce deferred tax assets to the amounts that are more-likely-
than-not expected to be realized based on the weighting of positive and negative evidence. Future realization of
deferred tax assets ultimately depends on the existence of sufficient taxable income of the appropriate character
(for example, ordinary income or capital gain) within the carryback or carryforward periods available under the
applicable tax law. The Company regularly reviews the deferred tax assets for recoverability based on historical
taxable income, projected future taxable income, the expected timing of the reversals of existing temporary
differences and tax planning strategies. The Company’s judgment regarding future profitability may change due
to many factors, including future market conditions and the ability to successfully execute the business plans
and/or tax planning strategies. Should there be a change in the ability to recover deferred tax assets, the
Company’s income tax provision would increase or decrease in the period in which the assessment is changed.
The Company treats Net CFC Tested Income (formerly referred to as Global Intangible Low-Taxed Income or
“GILTI”) as a period cost.
The Company accounts for uncertain tax positions in accordance with ASC 740-10,
Accounting for Uncertainty
in Income Taxes
. The Company recognizes the tax effects of an uncertain tax position only if such position is
more likely than not to be sustained based solely on its technical merits as of the reporting date and only in an
amount more likely than not to be sustained upon review by the tax authorities. The Company recognizes
accrued interest and penalties related to unrecognized tax benefits in the provision for income taxes in the
consolidated statements of operations.
Net Loss per Share
Basic and diluted net loss per share attributable to common stockholders is computed in conformity with the
two-class method required for participating securities. The two-class method requires income available to
common stockholders for the period to be allocated between common stock and participating securities based
upon their respective rights to receive dividends as if all income for the period had been distributed.
The Company considers all series of its redeemable convertible preferred stock to be participating securities as
the holders of such stock have the right to participate on a pari passu basis in any distributions to common
stockholders.
The holders of the redeemable convertible preferred stock would be entitled to dividends in preference to
common stockholders, at specified rates, if declared. Any remaining dividend amounts would then be
distributed to the holders of common stock, restricted common stock, and the holders of the redeemable
convertible preferred stock on a pro-rata basis assuming conversion of all redeemable convertible preferred
stock into common stock. These participating securities do not contractually require the holders of such shares
to participate in the Company’s losses. As such, net losses for the periods presented were not allocated to the
Company’s participating securities.
Basic net loss per share is computed by dividing the net loss attributable to common stockholders by the
weighted-average number of shares of common stock outstanding during the period, less shares subject to
repurchase. The diluted net loss per share is computed by giving effect to all potentially dilutive securities
outstanding for the period using the treasury stock method or the if-converted method if the effect is dilutive.
For periods in which the Company reports net losses, diluted net loss per share is the same as basic net loss per
share, because all potentially dilutive securities are anti-dilutive.

(Subtopic 350-40): Targeted Improvements to the Accounting for Internal-Use Software
(“ASU 2025-06”).
ASU 2025-06 modernizes the guidance for costs incurred in connection with internal-use software by removing
references to prescriptive development stages. Under ASU 2025-06, an entity may begin capitalizing internal-
use software costs when (a) management, with the relevant authority, implicitly or explicitly authorizes and
commits to funding a computer software project and (b) it is probable that the project will be completed and the
software will be used to perform the function intended (the “probable-to-complete recognition threshold”). ASU
2025-06 is effective for annual reporting periods beginning after December 15, 2027, and interim periods
within those annual reporting periods; early adoption is permitted. The ASU may be adopted prospectively,
retrospectively, or via a modified prospective transition. The Company early adopted ASU 2025-06, effective
January 1, 2025, applying the guidance on a prospective basis. This ASU did not have a significant impact to the
Company’s consolidated financial statements.

During the years ended
December 31, 2024
and
2025
and the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026
(unaudited), the Company had no transfers between levels of the fair value hierarchy of its assets measured at
fair value.
The Company measures cash equivalents and
short-term investments
at fair value. Level 1 instrument
valuations are based on quoted market prices of the identical underlying security. Level 2 instrument valuations
are obtained from readily available pricing sources for comparable instruments, identical instruments in less
active markets, or models using market observable inputs.
During the year ended
December 31, 2025
, the Company entered into a contract to receive warrant rights to
acquire common shares of a
privately-held
company as consideration under an agreement entered into but not
yet commenced. The warrant rights are freestanding financial instruments that meet the definition of a
derivative as they contain a net settlement feature. The warrants have not been designated as hedging
instruments and will be granted and recognized as lease incentives upon commencement of the related
arrangements and recognized as a reduction of the related ROU assets. The Company estimated the fair value of
the warrant rights using a probability-weighted expected return method. In applying this method, the Company
utilized
Level 3
valuation inputs based on information available, including terms and features of the warrant
rights and other outstanding classes of the issuer’s equity securities, observable transactions in the issuer’s
securities such as its most recent financing round, estimates of equity volatility, and expected time to a liquidity
event. The initial fair value of the warrant rights was recognized as a derivative asset classified within other
assets on the consolidated balance sheets, with a corresponding deferred liability classified within other
noncurrent liabilities.

The estimated fair value of the note purchase agreements was determined by using a probability-weighted
expected return method. The fair value of the
Series G-2 redeemable convertible preferred stock
was
determined by using a hybrid approach comprising a contingent claims analysis (“CCA”) and a common stock
equivalent (“CSE”) method. Assumptions included assumed future liquidity and financing events, the terms and
features of the agreement, weights applied to each scenario, discount rates, applicable risk free rates, the fair
value of the Series G-2 redeemable convertible preferred stock, and a discount for lack of marketability.
Level 3 liabilities consist of the SAFE liabilities (
Note 9
), convertible notes (Note
9
), derivative liabilities (
Note
9
), donation matching program liability (Note
10
), and a holdback liability for a portion of shares issuable in the
acquisition of Codeblog Corp. (“Bun”) (
Note 15
). There is no current market for these liabilities such that
determination of fair value requires significant judgment or estimation. Changes in fair value measurements
categorized within Level 3 of the fair value hierarchy are analyzed each period based on changes in estimates or
assumptions and recorded as appropriate. The Company recorded a
$3 million
change in fair value of the
holdback liability during the year ended
December 31, 2025
in other income (expense), net in the consolidated
statements of operations.
The SAFE liabilities are recorded at fair value, which is determined based on a third-party valuation utilizing a
scenario-based analysis and
a CCA
, that considers specific scenarios that factor in timing, probability, and
financing size. This model takes into account the contract terms as well as multiple inputs, such as the
Company’s redeemable convertible preferred stock price, risk free interest rates, and expected volatility, some
of which the Company could not corroborate with observable market data. Th
e as
sumptions used in valuing the
SAFE liability upon conversion on December 31, 2023 and on January 30, 2024, include volatility, risk free
interest rate, and term to liquidity. Changes in the fair value measurement of the SAFE liabilities relate to the
conversion scenarios and are recorded as change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and
SAFEs in the consolidated statements of operations. All SAFEs have been converted as of
December 31, 2024
.
The estimated fair value of the convertible notes is determined by using a hybrid approach comprising a CCA
and a CSE method. The analysis estimates the fair value of the convertible notes based on the probability-
weighted expected future investment returns, considering possible outcomes available to the note holder,
including conversions to
redeemable convertible preferred stock
, Class N common stock, and maturity.
Assumptions include weight applied to the CCA and CSE methods, assumed volatility, time to a liquidity event,
need for and terms of financings or expected financings, and the risk free interest rate. Changes in fair value of
the convertible notes are recorded as change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs
in the consolidated statements of operations.

Convertible Notes, Revolving Credit Agreement and SAFEs
Convertible Notes
The Company has entered into note purchase agreements which provide for the issuance of one or more
convertible notes. To the extent that the note purchase agreements create an obligation to issue notes in the
future, these obligations are accounted for as
derivative liabilities on the consolidated balance sheets until the
related note is issued.
Google
Google 2023 Note Purchase Agreement
In
September 2023
, the Company entered into a note purchase agreement (“
Google 2023 NPA
”) with Google
LLC (“Google”), for the issuance of convertible promissory notes in an aggregate principal amount of up to
$2.0
billion
, issuable in three tranches. The Company issued the first tranche of notes in an aggregate principal
amount of
$500 million
in September 2023, the second tranche of notes in an aggregate principal amount of
$750 million
in September 2024, and the third tranche of notes in an aggregate principal amount of
$750
million
in September 2025.
The notes issued under
Google 2023 NPA
bore
interest at a rate of
10.0%
per annum, compounded annually,
and payable upon maturity,
48 months
after the respective issuance date. The Company also has a commercial
agreement with Google for the provision of intelligence service.

SAFEs
During the year ended December 31, 2023, the Company issued SAFEs with an aggregate purchase amount of
$122 million that entitled investors to participate in future equity financings through share-settled redemption
of the amount invested. Of this amount, $1 million converted into shares of Series C-1 convertible preferred
stock during the year ended December 31, 2023, and $121 million converted into shares of Series D-1 and D-2
convertible preferred stock during the year ended December 31, 2024. Conversion prices were determined
F-43
Table of Contents
Anthropic, PBC
Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
(Continued)
based on the purchase amount divided by the per-share price of the applicable series of preferred stock,
multiplied by a stipulated discount rate, if applicable.
The Company determined that the SAFEs are not legal form debt (i.e., no creditors’ rights). The monetary
settlement amount of the SAFEs is based upon a fixed or determinable amount known at inception, and the
number of equity shares received upon conversion is variable. In such circumstances, equity classification is not
appropriate because such contracts that are settled based upon a fixed amount do not expose the holder to risks
and rewards similar to those of an equity-holder, therefore, the SAFEs would have been classified as marked-to-
market liabilities pursuant to ASC 480.
As of
December 31, 2024
and 2025, as well as June 30, 2026 (unaudited), the Company had no outstanding
SAFEs.
Fair Value Option
The Company elected to account for the SAFEs and the convertible notes using the fair value option pursuant to
ASC 825 and changes in fair value related to the SAFEs and convertible notes are recorded in change in fair
value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the Company’s consolidated statements of
operations (
Note 4
). The Company elected to account for the convertible notes using the fair value option
pursuant to ASC 825 to eliminate the accounting complexity that would otherwise result from separately
accounting for the liability and equity components of the convertible notes under the traditional bifurcation
model.
The estimated fair value of the convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs is determined by using a
scenario-based analysis that estimated the fair value of the convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs
based on the probability-weighted present value of expected future investment returns, considering possible
outcomes available to the SAFE and convertible note holder, including conversions to
redeemable convertible
preferred stock
, Class N common stock and maturity. Issuance costs were expensed as incurred and are
reflected in other income (expense), net in the consolidated statements of operations. Changes in fair value of
the SAFEs and convertible notes and accrued interest are recorded as change in fair value of convertible notes,
derivative liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statements of operations.
There were no changes in fair value attributable to credit risk recognized as of December 31, 2023, 2024, and
2025, as well as
June 30, 2026 (unaudited).
Derivative Liability
As of December 31, 2024, the Company had a derivative liability representing the subsequent note tranche
rights on
Amazon 2024 NPA
. The Company applied the terms of the subsequent note tranche rights for a
written call option and purchased put option scenarios and calculated a derivative liability. The changes in the
fair value of the derivative liability were recorded as change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative
liabilities, and SAFEs in the consolidated statements of operations. Upon the second closing and third closing of
the
Amazon 2024 NPA
during 2025, the related tranche rights were exercised and thus the derivative liability
was settled and derecognized in full through the issuance of the convertible notes, with no remaining tranche
rights outstanding as of
December 31, 2025
.
Revolving Credit Agreement
On May 14, 2025, the Company entered into a credit agreement (the “Credit Agreement”), by and among the
Company, the lenders from time to time party thereto (collectively the “Lenders”), and Morgan Stanley Senior
Funding, Inc., as Administrative Agent and Collateral Agent for the
Lenders
. The Credit Agreement provides for
a senior secured revolving credit facility in an aggregate principal amount of
$2.5 billion
, with a
$400 million
letter of credit sublimit.
The obligations under the Credit Agreement mature on May 14, 2030, subject to an
earlier springing maturity date that is contingent upon the outstanding amount of convertible notes issued by
the Company on the date that is 91 days prior to the maturity of such notes.
The proceeds of the credit
facility
may be used for working capital, general corporate purposes, and other lawful purposes. The Company may
request borrowings in U.S. dollars or certain other agreed currencies, subject to the terms of the Credit
F-44
Table of Contents
Anthropic, PBC
Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
(Continued)
Agreement. Borrowings under the Credit Agreement bear interest at rates based on either the Alternate Base
Rate, Term SOFR or other applicable benchmarks, plus an applicable margin
.
The Company is required to pay commitment fees on the unused portion of the credit
facility
and fees in
connection with letters of credit. The obligations under the Credit Agreement are guaranteed by certain
subsidiaries of the Company and are secured by substantially all of the assets of the Company and the
subsidiary guarantors, subject to certain exceptions and exclusions set forth in the Credit Agreement. The
Credit Agreement contains customary affirmative and negative covenants, including, but not limited to,
restrictions on additional indebtedness, liens, asset sales, investments, mergers, and restricted payments. The
Company is also subject to a financial covenant which requires the Company to maintain liquidity of at least
$500 million
as of the last day of each fiscal quarter. The agreement also includes customary events of default,
which, if triggered, could result in the acceleration of amounts due under the credit
facility
.

.

Dividend Rights
The holders of the outstanding shares of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
are entitled to receive, when
and if declared by the
Board
, and prior and in preference to dividends on the Company’s common stock,
dividends at the per annum rate of
6%

F-47

shall not be cumulative. After payment of such dividends, any additional dividends shall be distributed among

in proportion to the number of shares
of common stock that would be held by each such holder if all shares of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
were converted to common stock calculated on the record date for determination of holders entitled to such

Liquidation Preference
In the event of any Liquidation Transaction (defined, generally, as any voluntary or involuntary liquidation,
dissolution or winding up of the Company or deemed liquidation event), the holders of
redeemable convertible
preferred stock
shall be entitled to receive, prior and in preference to any distribution of any of the assets of the
Company to the holders of common stock, by reason of their ownership thereof, an amount per share equal to
the OIP for each outstanding share of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
then held (as adjusted for stock
splits, stock dividends, reclassifications and the like), plus any declared but unpaid dividends on such shares. If,
upon the occurrence of such event, the assets and funds thus distributed among the holders of
redeemable
convertible preferred stock
shall be insufficient to permit the payment to such holders of the full aforesaid
preferential amounts, then the entire assets and funds of the Company legally available for distribution shall be
distributed ratably among the holders of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
in proportion to the
preferential amount each such holder is otherwise entitled to receive, and provided that the holders of
redeemable convertible preferred stock will be treated on an as-converted basis if, as a result of an actual
conversion, such holder would receive, in the aggregate, an amount greater than the amount that would be
distributed to such holder if such holder did not convert such series of preferred stock into shares of such series
of common stock.

Voting
The holders of Series A, Series C-1, Series D-1, Series D-2, Series E-1, Series F-1, Series G-1, and Series H-1
redeemable convertible preferred stock shall be entitled to the same voting rights and powers as the holders of
the Class A common stock and to notice of any stockholders’ meeting in accordance with the bylaws of the
Company, and the holders of Class A common stock and the holders of Series A, Series C-1, Series D-1, Series
D-2, Series E-1, Series F-1, Series G-1, and Series H-1 redeemable convertible preferred stock shall vote together
as a single class on all matters. Each holder of Series A, Series C-1, Series D-1, Series D-2, Series E-1, Series F-1,
Series G-1, and Series H-1 redeemable convertible preferred stock shall be entitled to the number of votes equal
to the number of shares of Class A common stock into which such shares of Series A, Series C-1, Series D-1,
Series D-2, Series E-1, Series F-1, Series G-1, and Series H-1 redeemable convertible preferred stock,
respectively, could be converted.
The holders of Series B, Series C-2, Series D-3, Series E-2, Series E-3, Series E-4, Series E-5, Series F-2, Series
F-3, Series F-4, Series G-2, Series G-3, Series G-4, Series H-2, Series H-3, and Series H-4 non-voting
redeemable
convertible preferred stock shall not be entitled to vote and shall have no voting rights, except as
required by law or as specifically set forth in the certificate of incorporation, and shall have no right to vote in
any election of the Board.
Redemption
The holders of the
redeemable convertible preferred stock
have no voluntary rights to redeem shares. The
redeemable convertible preferred stock
holders have liquidation preferences in the event of any Liquidation
Transaction (defined, generally, as any voluntary or involuntary liquidation, dissolution or winding up of the
Company or deemed liquidation event). Although the
redeemable convertible preferred stock
is not
mandatorily or currently redeemable, a deemed liquidation event could constitute a redemption event outside
the Company’s control. Therefore, all shares of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
have been presented
outside of permanent equity.
The Company recorded shares of
redeemable convertible preferred stock
issued for cash at their respective
issuance price less issuance costs on the dates of issuance. Shares of redeemable convertible preferred stock
issued upon conversion of convertible notes were recorded at the fair value of the respective convertible note
immediately prior to conversion. The carrying values of the Company’s
redeemable convertible preferred stock
have not been accreted to their redemption values as the liquidation event is not considered probable of
occurring. Subsequent adjustments of the carrying values to redemption values will be made only if and when it
becomes probable the convertible preferred stock will become redeemable.

Restricted Stock Units
The Company grants RSUs to employees and the RSUs vest upon the satisfaction of both a service condition
and a performance condition. The service condition for these awards is generally satisfied over a
four
-year
vesting period. The performance condition is satisfied upon the occurrence of an “initial event” which is defined
as either (i) a qualifying change in control of the Company or (ii) a listing of the Company’s equity securities on
an established securities market (including through a traditional public offering, direct listing, or business
combination with a special purpose acquisition company), in each case, on or before the seventh anniversary of
the grant date, as further defined in such RSU agreements. If the performance condition is not satisfied within
seven years of the grant date, all unvested RSUs are forfeited.
As of
December 31, 2025
and June 30, 2026 (unaudited),
no
stock-based compensation expense had been
recognized for the RSUs because management determined that it is not probable that the performance
condition will be achieved. If management had determined the performance condition was probable of
achievement as of
December 31, 2025
and June 30, 2026 (unaudited), the Company would have recognized
$671 million
and
$2.9 billion
, respectively,
of cumulative stock-based compensation expense as of the
respective dates and would have had
$5.2 billion
and
$23.7 billion
, respectively,
of unrecognized compensation
cost that represents the RSUs that have not satisfied the service condition for vesting. As of June 30, 2026
(unaudited), unrecognized compensation cost
is expected to be recognized over a weighted-average period of
2.1 years
.

cumulative net losses incurred since inception and has concluded that it is more likely than not that the
Company will not realize the benefits of the deferred tax assets. Accordingly, a full valuation allowance was
established against the Company’s U.S. and foreign net deferred tax assets as of

.

Net Loss per Share
The Company computes net loss per share utilizing the two-class method required for participating securities.
The rights, including the liquidation and dividend rights, of the holders of the Company’s Class A common
stock and Class N common stock are identical, except with respect to voting. As a result, the basic and diluted
net loss per share of Class A common stock and Class N common stock are the same and therefore presented on
a combined basis.

Legal Matters
The Company is involved from time to time in claims, proceedings, and litigation, including the following:
In August 2024, various authors filed suit against the Company alleging infringement of copyrighted books in
the case of Bartz, et al. v. Anthropic in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California (“Bartz”).
The complaint alleged, among other things, copyright infringement related to the use of literary works used in
the training of the Company’s large language models. The complaint sought certification as a class action,
unspecified amounts of damages, injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees, costs, and interest. The Company reached a
settlement in the amount of
$1.5 billion
and the interest earned thereon, which was approved by the district
court in July 2026. The Company paid $300 million during the year ended December 31, 2025 and recorded
liabilities of
$750 million
in accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities and
$450 million
in other noncurrent liabilities on the consolidated balance sheets as of December 31, 2025, and
$1.2 billion
in
accounts payable, accrued expenses, and other current liabilities as of June 30, 2026 (unaudited).
In October 2023, Concord Music Group et al. filed a complaint against the Company in the U.S. District Court
for the Middle District of Tennessee (“Concord I”). The complaint alleges, among other things, that in the
process of building and operating the Company models, the Company unlawfully copied and disseminated
copyrighted lyrics controlled by the publishers. It also asserts a claim for unlawful removal of copyright
management information. The complaint seeks unspecified amounts of damages, injunctive relief, attorneys’
fees, costs, and interest. The case was later transferred to the Northern District of California. Both parties filed
motions for summary judgment and the court held a hearing on October 21, 2026. The Company disputes the
allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in this matter.
The Company is also subject to four copyright actions in Canada. In May and July 2025, two putative class
actions were filed on behalf of purported classes of Canadian authors - one in British Columbia (“MacKinnon”)
on behalf of all Canadian authors, and one in Québec (“Grescoe”) on behalf of all Québec authors - each alleging
violations of Canada’s Copyright Act based on the Company’s copying and use of copyrighted books to train its
large language models. Grescoe has been stayed pending a final judgment in MacKinnon. In July 2026, La
Presse Inc., a Québec news publisher, filed a copyright infringement action against the Company in the Québec
Superior Court alleging that the Company reproduced its journalistic works in the data used to train the
Company’s models. In October 2026, a group of Canadian news publishers filed a claim against the Company in
the Ontario Superior Court of Justice. The plaintiffs allege the Company copied their content from their
websites to develop its Claude models. They further allege the Company breached the websites’ terms of service
and circumvented technological protection measures. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and
intends to defend itself vigorously in these matters.
In June 2025, Reddit, Inc. filed suit against the Company in California state court alleging various claims,
including breach of contract and trespass to chattels, stemming from allegations about the Company’s use of
Reddit data in building and operating its models. In September 2026, the state court narrowed the case to
Reddit’s breach of contract, interference with contract, and unfair competition claims. The Company disputes
the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in this matter.
Between January and October 2026, several complaints were filed against the Company in the U.S. District
Court for the Northern District of California by various music publishers and their affiliated entities, including
Concord Music Group, Universal Music Publishing Group, ABKCO Music, BMG Rights Management (US) LLC,
Round Hill Music LP, Sony Music Publishing (US) LLC, Warner Chappell Music, Inc., and others (collectively,
the “Music Publisher Matters”). The complaints allege, among other things, that the Company unlawfully
copied the plaintiffs’ copyrighted song lyrics and musical compositions, and assert claims for direct and indirect
copyright infringement based on both the acquisition and use of copyrighted materials to train the Company’s
F-60
Table of Contents
Anthropic, PBC
Notes to Consolidated Financial Statements
(Continued)
large language models and the outputs of those models, as well as claims for removal of copyright management
information. Certain of the complaints also assert claims for unauthorized downloading and distribution of
copyrighted works, circumvention of technological protection measures, and violations of the Digital
Millennium Copyright Act, and certain of the complaints also name two Company executives as defendants. The
complaints seek unspecified amounts of damages, injunctive relief, attorneys’ fees, costs, and interest. These
matters are in preliminary stages. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend
itself vigorously in these matters.
The Company is subject to several putative class action complaints alleging that it markets and sells
subscription plans for Claude through false, misleading, and deceptive advertising practices. These matters are
generally in the early stages. The Company disputes the allegations of wrongdoing and intends to defend itself
vigorously in these actions.
Various authors and publishers have opted out of the class action and settlement reached in Bartz and filed
individual suits against the Company, generally alleging claims of direct copyright infringement, contributory
copyright infringement, and removal of copyright management information related to the use of literary works
used in the training of the Company’s large language models. The Company disputes the allegations of
wrongdoing in these remaining opt-out actions and intends to defend itself vigorously in all matters. These
proceedings remain in various stages.
The Company has received notices, demands, and other communications from several authors and individual
rights-holders, publishers (including, but not limited to, book, news, and music publishers), platforms and
website operators, and trade associations, in the United States and other jurisdictions (collectively, “Rights-
Holders”) alleging unauthorized acquisition or use of content, removal of copyright management information,
violation of terms of service, and violation of copyrights. Some Rights-Holders have also sought to have their
content removed from the Company’s training corpus or sought more information on how their content was
used in the development of the Company’s models. Other Rights-Holders have argued that the mere crawling of
their sites has harmed them. The Company expects to continue to receive similar notices from Rights-Holders,
which may ultimately result in litigation against the Company. The Company disputes the allegations of
wrongdoing and intends to defend itself vigorously in these matters.
From time to time, the Company is subject to inquiries, investigations, subpoenas and requests for information
from federal, state, and foreign governmental authorities, including the U.S. Federal Trade Commission and
state attorneys general, regarding, among other things, consumer protection, data protection and privacy, and
the safety and security of the Company’s products.
In addition, from time to time, the Company is subject to claims, litigation, and other proceedings, including
potential regulatory proceedings, involving patent and other intellectual property matters, taxes, labor and
employment, competition, privacy and data protection, consumer protection, commercial disputes, and services
offered by the Company, and other matters. The outcomes of the Company’s legal proceedings and other
contingencies are inherently unpredictable, subject to significant uncertainties, and could be material to its
operating results and cash flows for a particular period. The Company evaluates, on a regular basis,
developments in its legal proceedings and other contingencies that could affect the amount of liability,
including amounts in excess of any previous accruals and reasonably possible losses disclosed, and makes
adjustments and changes to its accruals and disclosures as appropriate. For the matters the Company discloses
that do not include an estimate of the amount of loss or range of losses, such an estimate is not possible or is
immaterial, and the Company may be unable to estimate the possible loss or range of losses that could
potentially result from the application of non-monetary remedies. Until the final resolution of such matters, if
any of the Company’s estimates and assumptions change or prove to have been incorrect, the Company may
experience losses in excess of the amounts recorded, which could have a material effect on its business,
consolidated financial position, results of operations, or cash flows.

Segment and Geographical Information
The Company’s chief operating decision maker (“CODM”) is the leadership team consisting of the Company’s
Chief Executive Officer and President. The Company operates its business in one operating segment and,
therefore, has one reportable segment. The CODM utilizes financial information presented on a consolidated
basis for purposes of making operating decisions, assessing financial performance, and allocating resources
including, but not limited to, the Company’s consolidated net loss.
The CODM uses consolidated net loss as the measure of segment profit or loss. The CODM uses consolidated
net loss to evaluate overall financial performance, monitor budget-to-actual results, assess the return on the
Company’s investments in compute and infrastructure, personnel, and other operating activities to inform
decisions regarding the allocation of capital and personnel resources across the Company’s operations. There
are no other expense categories regularly provided to the CODM that are not already included in the primary
consolidated financial statements, except that stock-based compensation expense is separately provided to the
CODM as a discrete component within the Personnel line item. Stock-based compensation expense was
$29
million
,
$192 million
, and
$1.2 billion
for the years ended
December 31, 2023
,
2024
, and
2025
, and
$286
million
and
$2.2 billion
for the six months ended June 30, 2025 and 2026 (unaudited), respectively. The
CODM does not evaluate operating segments using asset information.
Long-lived assets, which consist of property and equipment, net, and operating lease right-of-use assets, by
geographic location are based on the physical location of the assets. As of

one-year

The incremental expense recognized as a result of these stock option modifications was not material.
•
A portion of the Company’s revenue is derived from contracts with various agencies of the United
States Government (“USG”). On February 27, 2026, the President of the United States ordered the
USG to stop using the Company’s models and the U.S. Department of War designated the Company as
a Supply-Chain Risk to National Security (the “Risk Designation”). The Company may experience
material revenue losses or business disruptions attributable to these events. On March 9, 2026, the
Company filed a complaint in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California challenging
the Risk Designation as unlawful and simultaneously filed a petition for review in the U.S. Court of
Appeals for the D.C. Circuit. The U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California has largely
granted summary judgment in the Company’s favor, ruling that the Department of War’s actions were
retaliatory acts meant to punish the Company for speech protected under the First Amendment to the
United States Constitution and violated the Company’s rights under the Due Process Clause under the
Fifth Amendment to the United States Constitution, and that the Secretary of War’s Risk Designation,
particularly with respect to 10 U.S.C. § 3252, violated the Administrative Procedure Act because they
were in excess of statutory authority, contrary to law, and arbitrary and capricious. The defendants
have filed a notice of appeal of the preliminary injunction. The D.C. Circuit Court of Appeals, however,
in a 2-1 split decision, has denied the Company’s petition for review, ruling that the Department of
War’s Risk Designation was proper under
Federal Acquisition Supply Chain Security Act (“FASCSA”)
Section 4713, and that the Company’s rights under the First Amendment and Due Process Clause of the
Fifth Amendment were not violated. The Company is evaluating its next steps with respect to the D.C.
Circuit’s decision.

Item 14.
Indemnification of Directors and Officers.
Section 145 of the DGCL authorizes a corporation’s board of directors to grant, and authorizes a court to award,
indemnity to officers, directors, and other corporate agents.
We expect to adopt an amended and restated certificate of incorporation, which will become effective
immediately prior to the completion of this offering, and which will contain provisions that limit the liability of
our directors and certain officers for monetary damages to the fullest extent permitted by Delaware law.
Consequently, neither our directors nor certain officers will be personally liable to us or our stockholders for
monetary damages for any breach of fiduciary duties as directors or officers, as applicable, except liability for
the following:
•
any breach of the director’s or officer’s duty of loyalty to our company or our stockholders;
•
any act or omission not in good faith or that involves intentional misconduct or a knowing violation of
law;
•
for our directors, unlawful payments of dividends or unlawful stock repurchases or redemptions as
provided in Section 174 of the DGCL;
•
any transaction from which the director or officer derived an improper personal benefit; or
•
for our officers, any action by or in the right of the corporation.
Any amendment to, or repeal of, these provisions will not eliminate or reduce the effect of these provisions in
respect of any act, omission, or claim that occurred or arose prior to that amendment or repeal. If the DGCL is
amended to provide for further limitations on the personal liability of directors or officers of corporations, then
the personal liability of our directors and officers will be further limited to the greatest extent permitted by the
DGCL.
II-2
In addition, we expect to adopt amended and restated bylaws, which will become effective immediately prior to
the completion of this offering, and which will provide that we will indemnify, to the fullest extent permitted by
law, any person who is or was a party or is threatened to be made a party to any action, suit, or proceeding by
reason of the fact that they are or were one of our directors or officers or is or was serving at our request as a
director or officer of another corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust, or other enterprise. Our amended
and restated bylaws are expected to provide that we may indemnify to the fullest extent permitted by law any
person who is or was a party or is threatened to be made a party to any action, suit, or proceeding by reason of
the fact that they are or were one of our employees or agents or is or was serving at our request as an employee
or agent of another corporation, partnership, joint venture, trust, or other enterprise. Our amended and
restated bylaws will also provide that we must advance expenses incurred by or on behalf of a director or officer
in advance of the final disposition of any action or proceeding, subject to limited exceptions.
Further, we have entered into or will enter into indemnification agreements with each of our directors and
executive officers that may be broader than the specific indemnification provisions contained in the DGCL.
These indemnification agreements require us, among other things, to indemnify our directors and executive
officers against liabilities that may arise by reason of their status or service. These indemnification agreements
also require us to advance all expenses incurred by the directors and executive officers in investigating or
defending any such action, suit, or proceeding. We believe that these agreements are necessary to attract and
retain qualified individuals to serve as directors and executive officers.
The limitation of liability and indemnification provisions that are expected to be included in our amended and
restated certificate of incorporation, amended and restated bylaws, and the indemnification agreements that we
have entered into or will enter into with our directors and executive officers may discourage stockholders from
bringing a lawsuit against our directors and executive officers for breach of their fiduciary duties. They may also
reduce the likelihood of derivative litigation against our directors and executive officers, even though an action,
if successful, might benefit us and other stockholders. Further, a stockholder’s investment may be adversely
affected to the extent that we pay the costs of settlement and damage awards against directors and executive
officers as required by these indemnification provisions.
At present, we are not aware of any pending litigation
or proceeding involving any person who is or was one of our directors, officers, employees
, or other agents or is
or was serving at our request as a director, officer, employee, or agent of another corporation, partnership, joint
venture, trust, or other enterprise, for which indemnification is sought, and we are not aware of any threatened
litigation that may result in claims for indemnification. Under Delaware law and our amended and restated
certificate of incorporation, in the absence of a conflict of interest, no failure to satisfy the balancing obligations
associated with our status as a PBC shall, for purposes of the exculpation, advancement, and indemnification
rights of our directors and officers, constitute an act or omission not in good faith, or a breach of the duty of
loyalty.
We have obtained insurance policies under which, subject to the limitations of the policies, coverage is provided
to our directors and executive officers against loss arising from claims made by reason of breach of fiduciary
duty or other wrongful acts as a director or executive officer, including claims relating to public securities
matters, and to us with respect to payments that may be made by us to these directors and executive officers
pursuant to our indemnification obligations or otherwise as a matter of law.
Certain of our non-employee directors may, through their relationships with their employers, be insured or
indemnified against certain liabilities incurred in their capacity as members of our board of directors.
The underwriting agreement to be filed as Exhibit 1.1 to this registration statement will provide for
indemnification by the underwriters of us and our officers and directors for certain liabilities arising under the
Securities Act or otherwise.

Item 17.
Undertakings
.
Insofar as indemnification for liabilities arising under the Securities Act may be permitted to directors, officers,
and controlling persons of the registrant pursuant to the foregoing provisions, or otherwise, the registrant has
been advised that in the opinion of the Securities and Exchange Commission such indemnification is against
public policy as expressed in the Securities Act and is, therefore, unenforceable. In the event that a claim for
indemnification against such liabilities (other than the payment by the registrant of expenses incurred or paid
by a director, officer, or controlling person of the registrant in the successful defense of any action, suit, or
proceeding) is asserted by such director, officer, or controlling person in connection with the securities being
registered, the registrant will, unless in the opinion of its counsel the matter has been settled by controlling
precedent, submit to a court of appropriate jurisdiction the question whether such indemnification by it is
against public policy as expressed in the Securities Act and will be governed by the final adjudication of such
issue.
The undersigned registrant hereby undertakes that:
(1)
For purposes of determining any liability under the Securities Act, the information omitted from the
form of prospectus filed as part of this registration statement in reliance upon Rule 430A and
contained in a form of prospectus filed by the registrant pursuant to Rule 424(b)(1) or (4) or 497(h)
under the Securities Act shall be deemed to be part of this registration statement as of the time it was
declared effective.
(2)
For the purpose of determining any liability under the Securities Act, each post-effective amendment
that contains a form of prospectus shall be deemed to be a new registration statement relating to the
securities offered therein, and the offering of such securities at that time shall be deemed to be the
initial bona fide offering thereof.
